articles.title: Macron’s nuclear throwdown, Mossad’s man in Germany, Ukraine in flames: RT stories that shaped the week
articles.body:
Macron’s nuclear throwdown, Mossad’s man in Germany, Ukraine in flames: RT stories that shaped the week
Macron sends a nuclear message
When France’s military test-fired its latest nuclear-capable ballistic missile, the submarine-launched M51.3, on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron chose to milk the spectacle for every last drop of propaganda value. “To be free, we must be feared,” he said. “And to be feared, we must be powerful.”
The launch, Macron said, was intended as “a clear message… for wherever it must be received.”
The missile may have splashed down in the north Atlantic, but the message was received “loud and clear” in Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the following day. “Problems should be resolved through dialogue, not demonstrative missile launches,” but Russia will take “all necessary measures” to protect its strategic security, Peskov added.
France is currently modernizing and expanding its nuclear arsenal amid a broader rearmament push, but it remains unclear how Paris intends to pay for its remilitarization. This week, RT looked at France’s looming sovereign debt crisis and the violent riots tearing the country apart from within.
This domestic turmoil isn’t unique to France, nor is it something that can be fixed with minor policy tweaks. As RT examined on Friday, mass migration has already pushed European housing, security, and welfare systems to the breaking point. With native Europeans set to become minorities in their own countries in the coming decades, the social and political consequences could be deadly.
Germany’s enemies within
France is not the only European power gearing up for conflict abroad while its political and economic foundations disintegrate at home. Germanys’ foreign intelligence chief opened the week with a warning to lawmakers: Moscow is waging “a shadow war” against Europe, and “Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia.”
The Kremlin views accusations of “shadow war” and “hybrid war” – which are unprovable by nature – as “hastily cobbled-together provocations,” designed to serve “Kiev and the militaristic wing of the European political class.”
They’re provocations that Berlin is looking less and less able to follow through on. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is going from one electoral humiliation by the right-wing AfD to another, anti-war protests are spreading, and conscientious objections to a proposed military draft have tripled.
However, the German government can’t trust the loyalty of its own intelligence agents. Former spymaster August Hanning was charged with treason and espionage this week, in what appears to be the country’s worst spy scandal since the Guillaume affair of the 1970s.
German prosecutors aren’t revealing which foreign services Hanning allegedly collaborated with, but as RT explored in the latest installment in our ‘Wired for War’ series, all the signs point to Israel’s Mossad.
Russia reminds Zelensky what it’s capable of
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky is also on shaky ground this week. “Disappointment” and “shame” are now the most common feelings Ukrainians associate with him. US President Donald Trump blamed him for the worldwide diesel fuel shortage while Zelensky doubled down on silencing his critics, stepping up his long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries.
He soon learned that Russia always responds. Russian forces pounded data centers, logistics hubs, weapons depots, and missile factories across Ukraine this week, including production plants of Ukraine’s flagship ‘Flamingo’ cruise missiles. “People in Ukraine should blame only the head of the Kiev regime for this. It is Zelensky who bears full personal and political responsibility for it,” the Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement.
The strikes continued all week, as Zelensky prepared to fly to Miami for a meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Friday. Witkoff and Kushner were bringing “new ideas and proposals” aimed at resolving the conflict. The two could travel to Moscow later this month for another round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Although Zelensky’s situation at home may be deteriorating, he can still count on the support of his backers in Europe. Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk, who has been sanctioned by Ukraine and the EU over his war reporting, was detained in Montenegro on Friday. Zvinchuk founded the ‘Rybar’ Telegram channel, and was reportedly preparing to film a report on Montenegro’s plans to align its visa policy with EU standards. To the country’s pro-EU government, that now counts as “hybrid activity.”
‘Muslim NATO’ triggers article 5: Saudi Arabia calls for backup
Saudi Arabia’s renewed conflict with Yemen’s Houthis is not going well for Riyadh. After conquering a swathe of new territory along the Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the Houthis declared Saudi airspace a “theater for military operations” this week, and struck Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport multiple times to make their point.
After an emergency meeting on Monday, Pakistan and Türkiye decided to deploy military forces to Saudi Arabia – the first deployment of the newly-formed “Muslim NATO.” Britain has also agreed to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi warplanes; France is sending troops, radar, and air-defense systems; and Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former jihadist, is reportedly considering entering the conflict on the Saudi side.
RT examined why the long-dormant Saudi/Houthi conflict is flaring up again, and compared the manpower, resources, and weaponry that Yemen’s Saudi-backed government and the Houthis bring to the table, as the government prepares for a ground offensive against the militants.
India hits a wall with Washington
Russia and the Soviet Union “stood by us in many ways when our security, when our territorial integrity were under threat,” Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar told a gathering of foreign policy experts last weekend. These ties are “not easily forgotten,” he said, adding that India is not going to sever its relations with Russia under Western pressure. That pressure looms in the shape of the so-called “sanctions from hell” Washington is threatening to unleash upon Russia’s trading partners.
A spat over work permits has driven another wedge between New Delhi and Washington. After US Vice President JD Vance lashed out at eight US and Indian tech giants for using H-1B visas to hire “indentured servants” from India over American workers, India’s Foreign Ministry slammed Vance for his “deeply offensive” comments.
“Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive,” the ministry said.
At the same time, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Indian “oligarchs” of wielding undue influence over the country’s telecoms regulators, as his bid to introduce Starlink internet access to the Indian market remains stalled. India’s Communications Ministry called his allegations “baseless and misconceived,” but Musk doubled down on Thursday, asking whether telecoms and media tycoon Mukesh Ambani was “the real boss of India?”
And finally…
India has chosen to play a central role in the emergence of a new, multipolar world order. Last month’s BRICS summit in New Delhi showed just how seriously India takes this role, ending with a joint declaration – drafted despite sharp differences between BRICS nations – on the Middle East, global governance, and opposition to unilateral sanctions.
BRICS could face its biggest political test yet, however, if Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva loses his upcoming runoff election against Flavio Bolsonaro, son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro. Should Bolsonaro win, he is likely to pull Brazil into the orbit of the US, where Trump has made no effort to conceal his hostility toward BRICS.
Russian analyst Fyodor Lukyanov broke down what a Bolsonaro victory would mean for the multipolar project, and with two weeks to go until the runoff election, we’ll be keeping a close eye on Brazil.

articles.title: Spain and Greece refuse to transfer Patriot systems to Ukraine whose service life is nearing its end - media
articles.body:
Spain and Greece refuse to transfer Patriot systems to Ukraine whose service life is nearing its end - media
Kyiv • UNN
Greece and Spain have Patriot PAC-2 missiles whose service life is expiring. NATO and the EU are calling on them to transfer them to Ukraine.
Greece and Spain possess stocks of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems whose expiration dates are approaching. These missiles could be transferred to Ukraine, but the countries have so far refused, reports UNN, citing The Telegraph.
The publication notes that Greece and Spain— two NATO countries—have some of the largest stocks of such missiles in Europe, while Kyiv is persistently asking for additional means of protection against Russia's plans to carry out the most severe long-range mass strikes of the war.
Ukrainian officials have disclosed information about intercepted Russian plans for a new campaign aimed at destroying the country's energy system, with the goal of plunging cities into darkness and testing the population's resilience during the winter period.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly called on allies to provide more interceptor missiles for the American Patriot systems currently in Ukraine—the most effective systems for shooting down enemy warheads.
Kyiv fears that Russian forces could use a thousand missiles, drones, and aerial bombs against electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, as well as the infrastructure of Ukraine's three operating nuclear power plants.
According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine needs between 300 and 360 Patriot interceptor missiles to withstand Russia's winter campaign.
Given the urgent need to provide Ukraine with the necessary means, efforts have focused on encouraging Greece and Spain to transfer part of their stocks.
NATO and EU representatives have tried to persuade Greece and Spain to transfer Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles to Ukraine whose expiration dates are approaching.
Greece is believed to have at least 200 Patriot PAC-2 missiles, whose service life—calculated at 23 years—will soon expire.
The exact number of missiles in Spain's reserve is unknown, although last month the country's foreign minister announced that Madrid would transfer five interceptors to Kyiv.
Participants in the talks are reluctant to name the two countries publicly, fearing that this could damage relations with them.
EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas raised the issue during talks in Ireland last month, stating: "We know that some countries have interceptor missiles whose expiration dates will soon pass. So it would be very good if they were transferred to Ukraine."
As a diplomatic source told The Telegraph, the approach chosen is to ask Greece and Spain: "How can we help you make this decision?"
"It would be logical if at least those interceptor missiles whose expiration dates are approaching were sent to Ukraine," the interlocutor added.
Interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, like other missiles, have a specified storage life during which the manufacturer guarantees their effectiveness.
Fabian Hoffmann, a missile-weapons expert from the University of Oslo, said: "The manufacturer guarantees that the missile will function properly for a certain period of time. After this period ends, the missiles must undergo recertification.
During recertification, components whose expiration dates have passed—such as batteries or rocket engines—are replaced, and the operability of the remaining systems is also checked.
Of course, missiles may function even after their expiration date, but if they fail, the manufacturer bears no responsibility for this."
Ukraine receives 95% of its Patriot missiles through a NATO-led initiative that involves using European funds to directly purchase these interceptors from the United States.
However, the war with Iran has caused a global shortage that even Washington is finding difficult to overcome.
According to some estimates, the United States and its allies used at least 800 Patriot interceptor missiles in the first days of the conflict that erupted in February.
At the time, senior Ukrainian officials said that Kyiv had received only 600 such missiles over four years.
Earlier this year, the Ukrainian Air Force stopped publishing daily data on the number of intercepted ballistic missiles amid an increasingly acute shortage of ammunition.
Anonymous sources cited by The New York Times suggest that the U.S. stockpile of Patriot missiles may total fewer than 1,700 units.
This raised questions about the Pentagon's readiness to replenish Ukraine's supplies at a time when the United States itself is engaged in hostilities against Iran.
The Telegraph approached the defense ministries of Greece and Spain for comment.

articles.title: Iran's Houthi allies step up deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
Live Updates: Iran's Houthi allies kill 3 in strike on Saudi airport as Trump rules out pre-midterms strikes
What to know about the Iran war today:
- Three Saudi citizens were killed Thursday in an attack by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Riyadh's main airport. Fighting between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen has escalated this week in what appears to be the new epicenter of the wider war in the Middle East.
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that Tehran had revised its proposals to initiate peace talks with the U.S. and stood ready to finalize them through mediators. President Trump rejected a "7-day plan" offered by Iran in late September to get both sides back around the negotiating table.
- The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, eased Friday to around $103 a barrel after Mr. Trump promised the U.S. would not resume attacks on Iran before the U.S. midterm elections early next month. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he offered no specifics.
Trump says Iran can either "give us everything or they don't exist any longer"
During a rally in upstate New York, President Trump said, "Iran will be very quick, one way or the other. Either they give us everything, or they don't exist any longer. They know that"
The president made the comments while criticizing the Nobel Peace Prize committee for not awarding him the prize — a frequent complaint by Mr. Trump. Calling the body "crooked," Mr. Trump attacked it for giving the prize to former International Criminal Court Judge Navanethem Pillay, whom the president called a "mystery person."
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision," he said. "The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization."
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed more than 100 Houthi targets
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Saturday it destroyed more than 100 military targets in a "large-scale operation" against the Iran-backed group.
"We are carrying out a large-scale operation targeting the personnel and capabilities of the Houthi terrorist militia," Turki al-Maliki, spokesperson for the Saudi coalition, wrote on X.
"We destroyed 136 military targets in areas controlled by the Houthi terrorist militia," he said in a separate post.
The Houthi's Almasirah TV channel reported that Saudi missiles targeted areas in the northwestern Yemeni governorate of Saada.
The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government — which Saudi Arabia supports — reignited in July, and has since spilled over into the neighboring kingdom.
In addition to seizing territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have attacked transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world's largest crude exporter with drones and missiles.
Trump says Russia will release millions of tons of diesel
President Trump said Russia has agreed to provide the world with millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months in a bid to decrease skyrocketing global prices.
In a Truth Social post, the president said he had just gotten off the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately. He said another 500,000 tons of diesel would be released in November, followed by 1 million tons in December.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump continued.
The Treasury Department also announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
Mr. Trump had earlier Friday teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks at a Columbus Day celebration.
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.
Trump teases "big announcement" on diesel fuel
President Trump teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks Friday at a Columbus Day celebration, but offered little information to speculate on what the announcement would be about.
Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."
"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "It's gonna — we're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.
Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.
The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.
Sri Lanka has no plans to help 19 Iranian tankers stuck due to blockade, foreign ministry says
Sri Lanka's government says it has no immediate plans to help 19 Iranian ships that have been anchored in the international waters near the island nation facing food, water and fuel shortages.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Thushara Rodrigo said Sri Lanka will put its national interest first before considering any help, and the companies that supply ships are aware of possible secondary sanctions from the United States.
He said, however, there hasn't been any communication from the U.S. warning of repercussions should Sri Lanka decide to help.
Rodrigo said the ships are stationed 24 nautical miles from Sri Lanka's coast and have reported shortages of food, water and fuel.
Sri Lankan Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath told local Sunday Times newspaper the ships are Iranian oil tankers and they have been anchored off Sri Lanka for the past several months after the U.S. resumed its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving dozens of Iranian vessels stranded and unable to return home.
U.K., France, Germany, Australia and Canada advise against travel to Saudi Arabia after attacks
The U.K., France, Germany, Australia and Canada have advised their citizens against travel to parts of Saudi Arabia following a wave of Houthi attacks, including one that killed three civilians at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
The U.K. Foreign Office now advises against all but essential travel to the Riyadh region, Najran, Jizan and Aseer provinces, Taif city and Taif International Airport, and against all travel within six miles of the Yemeni border.
France says travel to Najran, Abha, Khamis Muhsait and Djizan in the south of the kingdom "remains strongly discouraged," and Germany, Australia and Canada have all advised against all travel to the country.
The U.S. has also tightened restrictions, requiring government employees to obtain special authorization to use Riyadh airport, and barring them from all travel within 20 miles of the Yemen border. U.S. government employees also require "special authorization for travel to the provinces of Jizan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu, and Taif."
There is currently no warning for U.S. nationals more broadly to avoid Saudi Arabia, but the U.S. embassy in Riyadh urged Americans across the Middle East to "exercise heightened vigilance due to the complex security environment."
Yemen's Saudi-backed military claims it has taken back Bab el-Mandeb Strait
Yemeni government forces, backed by air support from the Saudi-led coalition, have taken control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and Mayyun Island from the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, a Saudi diplomat said Friday.
Saudi Arabian Ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed Al Jaber, said in a post on X that the strait had been "cleansed" of remaining Houthi forces.
Fighting escalated dramatically this week after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive to retake territory held by Houthis, including some coastline around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that was seized by the rebels only weeks ago. The Houthis have held a vast portion of Yemen, including its capital Sanaa, for over a decade.
Yemeni forces claimed earlier this week to have retaken other key territory along the Red Sea coast, north of the strait, but the Houthis insisted Tuesday that their fighters still had "full control over all their gains on the ground."
Houthis appear to taunt Saudi Arabia, say Riyadh humanitarian flights require their authorization
The Iran-backed Houthis appeared to taunt Saudi Arabia on Friday, as the group's spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree declared that humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh's airport would be allowed only with authorization from the Yemeni rebel group.
"Humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh airport will be allowed for all flights that have obtained a permit from the Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center in the capital, Sanaa," Saree said in a post on X.
The statement was a challenge to Saudi Arabia's control of its own airspace. It came just a day after a Houthi attack killed three people at Riyadh's King Khaled International Airport, including a Saudia Airlines captain.
The Houthis warned international airlines on Monday that "operating in the skies of Saudi Arabia" would be "unsafe as long as the Saudi aggression against our country continues."
The statement from the Houthis' Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center (NOCC) said "the skies of Saudi Arabia will be a theater for operations by our armed forces," declaring that the rebel group would accept "no responsibility after this announcement" for anything that happens to aircraft.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it struck a gas tanker in the Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday that its navy had struck a liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tanker after it allegedly attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz via what it considers an illegal route through the waterway.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said the vessel, identified as NV Sunshine, was struck "a few hours ago" as it "intended to cross via the illegal route," referring to a U.S.-backed lane that skirts close to the Omani coast.
On Wednesday, a senior IRGC advisor said Iran would soon block what it considers "illegal routes" through the Strait of Hormuz.
Brig. Gen. Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the IRGC commander-in-chief, reiterated Iran's stance that the strait is closed and that Iranian armed forces have "full control" over it, adding that the situation would continue until Iran's "legitimate demands" are met.
The Trump administration insists the strait is open and that the southern route is safe for commercial vessels. The U.S. military has escorted some ships through that route for weeks, helping energy shipments from the Persian Gulf, which have been severely impeded by the ongoing war with Iran, rebound.
Germany to release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, crude and heating oil
Germany is going to release up to 15 million barrels of diesel, crude and heating oil, the country's economy minister said Friday.
"Diesel and heating oil will be the first, with crude oil to follow," Katherina Reiche told the Reuters news agency, adding that Germany would implement an agreement reached by the G7 last week to release 100 million barrels of diesel oil.
"We must always have the entire supply chain in mind. Available crude oil alone is not enough," she said.
The Trump administration has pressured Europe to draw on its emergency reserves.
Mr. Trump had threatened to ban U.S. diesel exports, a move that would push global diesel prices even higher, saying in late September that he had "called for" such a ban. But after the G7 announcement last week the president said "we were never going to do" it.
Iranian proxies "must stop their reckless and violent acts," says EU leader
The president of the European Union's governing commission, Ursula von der Leyen, condemned on Friday the deadly Houthi missile attack on Saudi Arabia's main international airport the previous day, calling on Iran's proxy groups to "stop their reckless and violent acts."
The attack Thursday on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed three Saudi civilians. The Houthis, a rebel group based in Yemen, said they targeted the airport several times this week, including on Thursday.
"Houthis have once again struck Riyadh's airport, taking three innocent lives," von der Leyen said in a post on X. "We stand in full solidarity with the people of Saudi Arabia and all our Gulf partners."
"Attacks on civilian infrastructure are unacceptable," the EU leader said. "Iran's proxies must stop their reckless and violent acts."
Airlines cancel flights to Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes
Multiple airlines have suspended flights to Saudi Arabia's capital after strikes claimed by the Iran-backed Houthis hit Riyadh's main airport this week, including a missile attack that killed three civilians Thursday.
Lufthansa, Air India, Pakistan International Airlines, FlyDubai, Etihad Airways, Emirates and Air Arabia are among the airlines that have suspended flights to Riyadh.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency on Friday advised against airlines operating in some parts of Saudi airspace, saying in an updated bulletin that "recent attacks have demonstrated the ability and intent of the Houthis to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory."
Iran's Vatican envoy urges Pope Leo to oppose U.S. sanctions
Tehran's ambassador to the Vatican, Mohammad Hossein Mokhtari, urged Pope Leo XIV to use his moral and diplomatic influence to oppose U.S. sanctions and air restrictions on Iran that he says threaten ordinary people's access to medical treatment, education, family and religious pilgrimage.
In a letter addressed to the leader of the Catholic Church on Thursday, Mokhtari called for a public defence of humanitarian air routes and urged the Pontiff to press Washington to assess the human consequences of its policies.
The letter comes amid renewed U.S. sanctions against Iran and restrictions targeting Iranian airlines. Washington imposed new sanctions on 27 Iranian airlines in September, threatening measures against airports and companies worldwide that provide services to them. Tehran has condemned the measures as "economic terrorism."
"When decisions by the unwise and inhumane U.S. president lead to sweeping air restrictions and make people's travel more difficult, the issue is no longer merely about flight routes or political relations," Mokhtari wrote.
Saudia Airlines mourns captain killed in Riyadh airport attack
Saudi national carrier Saudia Airlines announced the death of aircraft captain Hamoud bin Ali Al-Kalthami Friday following a strike on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh the previous day.
Saudi authorities have not said who carried out the Thursday attack on the airport, which killed two other civilians in addition to Al-Kalthami, but the Iran-backed Houthis claimed they targeted the airport on the same day, as they have previously this week.
In a statement, the airline paid tribute to the slain captain's professional service, saying it remembered "with appreciation and pride what the deceased contributed throughout his professional career in serving the national carrier, and the good reputation he left among his colleagues."
The airline extended its condolences to his family, relatives and colleagues.
Pakistan says it has a "substantial number of forces" deployed in Saudi Arabia
Pakistan has a "substantial number of forces" deployed in Saudi Arabia in a defensive capacity, Pakistan's foreign ministry spokesman said Friday.
"From Pakistan already we have substantial number of forces as well as resources in town, in Riyadh," spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan told journalists, according to the French news agency AFP, without specifying whether the deployment had grown under a major defense pact that Pakistan signed this year with Turkey and Saudi Arabia.
He added that Pakistani military personnel in the kingdom "would not be crossing the borders of the other side for an attack on the Houthis, but of course [they are acting] in the defense of the territory."
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have launched barrages of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia this week, including attacks on Riyadh's international airport Thursday that killed three people.
Pakistan signed the defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey in August, committing the three countries to come to each other's aid in the event one is attacked.
Khan declined to say whether additional Pakistani forces had arrived in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom's fight with the Houthis intensified in recent weeks, saying that "how much and when and where" forces would be deployed would be up to the trilateral alliance, which is headquartered in Riyadh with a retired Pakistani general as its secretary general.
Khan noted that Pakistan's forces had been deployed in Saudi Arabia regularly since the 1980s, including after the signing of a bilateral agreement between Islamabad and Riyadh in 2025.
CBS/AP
Saudi authorities say 3 civilians killed in attacks on Riyadh airport claimed by Houthi rebels
Three Saudi citizens were killed and several other people "of different nationalities" were wounded in attacks targeting Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a Saudia Airlines aircraft, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said Friday.
Thursday's attack was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom and allied forces in neighboring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend aimed at retaking territory seized by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
It was a significant escalation in what appears to be the new epicenter of the wider war in the Middle East sparked by the joint U.S.-Israeli assault on Iran in late February.
The first attack Thursday afternoon targeted airport facilities, while the second struck the aircraft, which was empty at the time, the Saudi statement said. It did not identify those responsible, though the Houthis have claimed to target the airport repeatedly this week with ballistic missiles, including on Thursday.
Among the dead was Capt. Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, the Saudia Group said in a statement seen by the Associated Press. It appeared to be the first confirmed attack on the Saudi national carrier since the new offensive against the Houthis began.
The Saudi aviation agency, GACA, said in its statement that injuries to citizens and people of other nationalities "ranged from minor to serious."
The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they have declared a theater for military operations.
On Wednesday, Saudi officials said attacks on the Riyadh and Abha airports claimed by the Houthis had killed three people.
CBS/AP
Iran says it has revised proposals to renew peace talks with U.S.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that Iran had revised its proposals for negotiations with the United States and was ready to finalize them through intermediaries.
"We have made our revisions to these proposals. Once they are finalized, we are supposed to sit down through the mediators and consolidate them," Pezeshkian said during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
He said Iran had put forward proposals, and the U.S. had also presented new ones, but he accused Washington of repeatedly scuppering diplomatic efforts.
"Every time we hold talks with the U.S., they attack again," Pezeshkian said.
Addressing Putin, Pezeshkian thanked Russia for its positions on regional issues, including at the United Nations.
"Our efforts are aimed at ending the war and ensuring that the rights of the Iranian people are respected within the framework of international law," Pezeshkian said. "But if the United States seeks to proceed through unilateralism, it will not be possible."
USS Lincoln returns home to San Diego for first time in over 10 months
The USS Abraham Lincoln and its more than 4,500 sailors returned home to San Diego on Thursday for the first time in 321 days, a jubilant homecoming after a long deployment that included months in the Middle East.
Braving the heat, hundreds of family members and friends waited for hours in the sun to greet their loved ones. As the ship pulled into the harbor, a roar of cheers erupted from a pier. Sailors stood at attention on the deck for the aircraft carrier's long approach, and after they were released, smiles and waves broke out as sailors took out their phones to call people on the pier.
In one such reunion, McKenzie Adkins held her 10-week-old son Declan as she waved to her husband, Alexander, on the ship's deck, before the new father met his son for the first time.
The Lincoln carrier strike group had been deployed for more than 10 months, including more than 250 uninterrupted days at sea this year. Much of that time was spent in the Middle East, where the aircraft carrier and its escort ships supported the U.S. war against Iran. It left the region in late August.
Read more here.
U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia issues new security alert over airport attacks
The U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia is warning Americans to "exercise heightened vigilance" if they are traveling through King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh due to attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militant group.
"The Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including against civilian airports, and the military conflict has the potential to escalate," the embassy wrote on X. "U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."
The Houthis have launched attacks on the airport, hundreds of miles into interior Saudi Arabia, four times this week. Three people were killed at airports on Oct. 6 and 7 in Saudi Arabia, including one at King Khalid International Airport, according to the country's aviation authority.
The embassy had already warned citizens not to travel near the Yemeni border. U.S. government employees are banned from traveling within 20 miles of the border. On Thursday, the embassy also said government officials now require special authorization to travel through King Khalid International Airport.
Trump says U.S. won't attack Iran before midterms, touts oil coming through strait
President Trump has promised the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, which take place on Nov. 3. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.
"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd," he wrote on Truth Social.
Several outlets reported on Thursday that Mr. Trump was considering new strikes on Iran before the midterms.
The Trump administration has consistently provided numbers for the millions of barrels being escorted out of the Strait of Hormuz under U.S. military protection. Moving out 22 million barrels of oil in one night would mark a total similar to prewar levels.
Brent crude, the international standard, was up to $105 a barrel, about a 4% increase from close Wednesday, before Mr. Trump's post on social media. After the post, it dropped to $103 a barrel.

articles.title: German Spy Scandal – Could Ukraine and NATO Be at Risk?
articles.body:
The arrest of Germany’s former intelligence chief August Hanning in one of the country’s most serious espionage scandals in decades has exposed a suspected Azerbaijani connection – and raised broader questions about the vulnerability of Western intelligence networks as Russia intensifies its shadow war against Europe.
Hanning, 80, who headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was arrested on Tuesday, Oct. 6, on suspicion of espionage, attempted treason and illegally obtaining state secrets.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
German prosecutors say he acquired nearly 2,000 intelligence documents through a former senior aide who continued working at the BND long after Hanning left office.
The documents reportedly included sensitive intelligence relating to Russia’s military activities, Iran’s nuclear program and information shared by Western intelligence partners.
German magazine Der Spiegel reported that investigators were examining whether Hanning used classified material to prepare an analysis for an Azerbaijani intelligence operative.
Azerbaijan has denied involvement, while German prosecutors have not publicly identified the foreign intelligence service concerned.
The case has emerged at a particularly sensitive moment for Germany, which is confronting growing Russian intelligence and hybrid threats while remaining a major supporter of Ukraine.
Budanov Heads to US With Ukrainian Negotiating Team for ‘Important Meetings,’ European Leaders Set to Join
How nearly 2,000 intelligence documents allegedly left the BND
At the center of the investigation is Hanning’s former office manager, identified by German prosecutors as Manfred D.
According to prosecutors, the two arranged in 2010 for Manfred D. to provide confidential information to Hanning in exchange for payment.
Manfred D. remained employed at the BND, working for successive intelligence chiefs until March 2026, giving him continued access to sensitive internal documents.
Prosecutors say he supplied Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents through June 2022, including material classified as secret.
Hanning allegedly used information from the documents to prepare analyses intended for foreign intelligence contacts.
The suspected breach is especially serious because some of the material was intended for Germany’s highest political leadership, including the chancellor’s office.
It also reportedly included intelligence originating from Germany’s allies, raising concerns about whether information shared by the CIA and other partner agencies was compromised.
Hanning denies wrongdoing. His lawyer has acknowledged that he possessed classified material but disputes allegations that he paid for or improperly disseminated it.
A German court ordered Hanning and Manfred D. to remain in custody on Wednesday, Oct. 7, pending further proceedings.
The Azerbaijan connection – what investigators know
The possible involvement of Azerbaijani intelligence has become one of the central questions surrounding the scandal.
According to Der Spiegel, investigators suspect Hanning was in contact with an Azerbaijani intelligence operative and prepared an analysis using information obtained from the BND.
Whether the analysis reached its intended recipient remains under investigation.
Azerbaijan rejected the allegations, describing the reports as unfounded and an attempt to damage German-Azerbaijani relations.
Hanning’s connections with Azerbaijan, however, extend beyond the current investigation.
He served on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum, an organization promoting ties between Berlin and Baku.
German newspaper Die Tageszeitung reported that Hanning was re-elected to the organization’s board as recently as August 2025.
Russia and Azerbaijan – a formal intelligence partnership
The suspected Azerbaijani connection has drawn attention to Baku’s established intelligence cooperation with Moscow.
On July 19, 2022, five months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) Director Sergey Naryshkin announced that the Russian and Azerbaijani foreign intelligence agencies had signed a cooperation agreement in Baku.
Naryshkin described the agreement as a framework for strengthening intelligence cooperation between the two countries.
The relationship continued despite Russia’s war against Ukraine.
During an April 2025 visit to Baku, Naryshkin met the heads of Azerbaijan’s Foreign Intelligence Service and State Security Service.
The Russian SVR subsequently described bilateral intelligence cooperation as constructive, mutually beneficial and based on trust.
The relationship raises a question in the Hanning case: If sensitive German intelligence reached an Azerbaijani intelligence operative, could it subsequently have been shared with Moscow?
There is no evidence that such a transfer occurred. However, classified BND assessments on Russia’s military activities or information supplied by Western partners could be particularly valuable to Moscow if obtained.
Secret German-Russian talks in Baku – Aliyev confirms meetings
The alleged Azerbaijani connection emerged months after another controversy involving confidential contacts between former senior German officials and figures close to Russian President Vladimir Putin in Baku.
A joint investigation by German weekly Die Zeit and public broadcaster ARD revealed that former German officials had been meeting Russian representatives in Azerbaijan since 2024.
The most recent gathering took place in July 2026.
Among the German participants were Ronald Pofalla, former head of Chancellor Angela Merkel’s office, and Matthias Platzeck, a former premier of Brandenburg.
Russian participants included Viktor Zubkov, a former Russian prime minister and senior Gazprom figure, and Valery Fadeyev, chairman of Russia’s Presidential Human Rights Council.
According to the German investigation, security agencies viewed the meetings as a potential Russian influence operation aimed at shaping Berlin’s approach to Moscow and its war against Ukraine.
The controversy reached the highest political level on July 21, when Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev was questioned about the meetings during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin.
Merz said he had no knowledge of the contacts.
Aliyev, however, acknowledged that Azerbaijan’s border authorities had confirmed the participants’ visits.
Aliyev maintained that his government had not been informed of the meetings.
“Our territory was simply used without our knowledge,” he said, adding that the overlapping travel records suggested a secret gathering had taken place.
“If this meeting serves to end the Ukrainian-Russian war, we, of course, welcome it,” Aliyev said.
Hanning traveled to Russia seven times after Crimea’s annexation
Further questions about Hanning’s international contacts emerged after independent investigative outlet The Insider identified at least seven trips he made to Russia between 2015 and 2019 – following Moscow’s illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014.
Some visits lasted less than 24 hours.
On July 6, 2016, Hanning flew from Munich to Moscow and returned to Berlin the following afternoon.
A similar short visit took place in May 2019.
The purpose of the trips and the identities of those he met remain unknown.
Significantly, the visits occurred during the period when prosecutors say Hanning was receiving classified documents from his former aide.
In September 2019, Hanning also attended an international Arctic-related gathering in Russia involving senior officials and representatives of foreign governments, according to reporting cited by Russian independent media.
He was reportedly invited as an honorary guest, separately from the official German delegation.
Russia’s shadow war – an alarming coincidence
The arrests occurred just one day after Germany’s current intelligence chief, Martin Jaeger, delivered a warning about Russia’s expanding covert campaign against Europe.
Speaking before lawmakers on Monday, Oct. 5, Jaeger said the threat posed by Moscow had entered a more dangerous phase.
He warned that Germany faced the possibility of direct confrontation as Russia intensified espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks and drone operations against European countries.
Jaeger described Russia’s activities as a shadow war threatening Germany’s security institutions and critical infrastructure.
German authorities have also examined suspected Russian involvement in drone-related incidents, including an attempted attack at Leipzig airport in August.
What could be at stake for Ukraine and NATO?
The suspected breach carries consequences far beyond Germany.
The BND is a major participant in Western intelligence cooperation, sharing assessments with NATO allies and partner agencies monitoring Russian military activities.
Germany has also become one of Ukraine’s most important European military supporters, providing weapons, air defense systems and other assistance as Kyiv continues resisting Moscow’s invasion.
Reuters reported that Hanning’s arrest had raised concerns among European intelligence services about potential damage to Germany’s intelligence-sharing relationships.

articles.title: British nuclear subs have only fire hoses as drone defense – media
articles.body:
British nuclear subs have only fire hoses as drone defense – media
British sailors are drilling to fend off potential drone attacks against £4 billion ($5.3 billion) Vanguard-class subs using fire hoses as the only onboard “air defense weapon,” The Sun has reported.
The hoses, known as “center fed reels” are placed on submarine decks as a precaution when the vessels are moored at the British naval base Clyde in Scotland, the UK’s most sensitive military site, the tabloid reported on Thursday, citing anonymous sources. The equipment has pistol-grip nozzles that would allow sailors to direct water at approaching drones.
“You have to use what you’ve got,” the tabloid cited one of its sources as saying.
The Royal Navy’s four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines are the only British platforms equipped to carry and launch Trident II nuclear missiles, which deliver the UK’s only operational nuclear weapons. According to The Sun, the Navy insists that layered defenses, including “physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone capabilities,” protect the subs.
The report comes as the Royal Navy is facing what a former senior commander has described as its worst crisis in 350 years.
The UK’s entire fleet of nuclear-powered Astute-class attack submarines are not fit for combat duty, retired chief of the Naval Staff, Lord Alan West, told The Sun earlier this year. Five of the vessels are facing maintenance and availability delays, while the sixth, according to the Royal Navy, is still undergoing sea trials ahead of returning to service.
West described the number of ships the Navy has as “pathetic.” The fleet has just five operational frigates and no amphibious assault ships, while former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government retired four frigates, two assault ships, two tankers, and a nuclear-powered submarine during his time in office, The Sun reported in July.
This year, the UK has pledged an additional £15 billion in military funding, citing alleged threats from Russia. London has also seized and aided in seizing ships it has accused of being part of the so-called Russian ‘shadow fleet’ – a practice Moscow has denounced as “piracy.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Moscow wants to attack NATO and has accused Western European leaders of escalating tensions with Moscow, pointing to their statements about preparing for a possible war with Russia in 2029 or 2030, repeated military exercises in the Baltic Sea, and attempts to detain Russian vessels. “This is all escalation,” he said last week.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Drones strike another Yandex data center in Russia
articles.body:
Key developments on October 09:
- Second Russian Yandex data center damaged by drone attack in two days, company says
- Twenty Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on Donetsk, independent monitors claim
- Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
- Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
- Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities
A drone attack damaged a Yandex data center in Russia's Kaluga Oblast overnight on Oct. 9, disabling several modules at the facility and threatening further disruptions to the company's services.
Several modules of the data center were completely disabled, Yandex said in a statement carried by pro-government Russian newspaper Vedomosti.
"Some Yandex services may experience disruptions as a result," the company said, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Yandex reported no injuries at the facility.
The attack came as drones struck other parts of Kaluga Oblast overnight, injuring nine people, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He also reported damage to houses in two districts of the oblast. Russian authorities claimed to have shot down 26 drones over the region.
Ukraine has not publicly confirmed responsibility for the attack on the Kaluga data center.
The strike marks the second reported attack on a Yandex data center in Russia in two days.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at a major Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing the facility to suspend operations and disrupting parts of Yandex's cloud infrastructure.
The Sasovo facility houses tens of thousands of servers and two of the company's three supercomputers used to develop artificial intelligence models. Yandex said it was still assessing whether damaged equipment could be restored.
The attack coincided with reports of widespread internet disruptions across Russia, affecting banking services, transport websites, and online platforms.
Responding to questions about the Sasovo strike on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would continue retaliating against Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
"We responded to them," he added. "I cannot share all the details."
Russian forces struck several Ukrainian internet providers and data centers in Kyiv in late September, disrupting internet access for approximately 100,000 households, according to Ukrainian officials.
read also
Record 20 Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on headquarters in Donetsk, monitors say
Ukrainian missile strikes on Russian army command posts in Donetsk on Aug. 26 killed more Russian officers than in any other single attack during the war, independent monitors claim.
Mediazona, an independent Russian outlet that tracks Russian military deaths in collaboration with the BBC Russian Service, identified 20 officers killed in the attack.
Each of the dead Russian officers was identified by name, age, and rank by Mediazona. Seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain, and one senior lieutenant were killed in the strikes, which hit the headquarters of the Central Military District and the 41st Combined Arms Army in occupied Donetsk.
According to Mediazona, 18 of the Russian officers died immediately in the missile strike, while two succumbed to their injuries.
Denis Pushilin, the head of the Russian illegal occupation administration in Donetsk Oblast, confirmed in a post on Telegram that Ukraine had launched an attack on targets in Donetsk on Aug. 26, claiming that Anglo-French "Storm Shadow" air-launched cruise missiles were used, and that eight civilians were injured.
Mediazona also identified two other instances of "mass casualties" amongst staff officers of the 41st Combined Arms Army, according to their research, eight officers were killed on Aug. 4, with an additional four killed on Sept 8, 2025.
At least 276,113 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine since 2022, according to Mediazona, which tracks individuals killed by searching through obituaries, posts on Russian social media networks, and leaked Russian databases.
read also
Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
Russian forces forcibly removed 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territory in Kharkiv Oblast to an unknown destination, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 9.
The civilians, including children, young people, and elderly residents, were taken from an area of the oblast where active fighting continues. Their current whereabouts and the conditions in which they are being held remain unknown, Lubinets said.
"Russia calls this an 'evacuation.' But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated, and left with no choice, it is not a rescue. It is coercion," Lubinets said.
The ombudsman did not specify which settlement the civilians were taken from or where they had been transported.
According to Lubinets, Russian forces published footage of what they described as a rescue operation on their Telegram channels. He said the footage showed signs of intimidation and pressure on civilians who had not consented to being relocated.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the circumstances of the reported removals.
Lubinets also warned that Russian occupation authorities had created a Telegram bot to collect personal information under the pretext of evacuation, potentially putting civilians and their relatives at risk.
Forcible transfers and deportations of civilians from occupied territory are prohibited under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Lubinets said he had appealed to Russia's human rights commissioner, demanding information about the 25 civilians, their whereabouts and conditions, and measures to secure their return to Ukraine.
He also appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the United Nations, and other international organizations for assistance.
Russia has repeatedly forcibly transferred and deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territories since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In March 2026, a United Nations commission concluded that Russia's deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children amounted to crimes against humanity.
read also
Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
Several Moscow airports temporarily suspended flights on Oct. 9, as suspected Ukrainian drones and balloons entered airspace around the Russian capital.
Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports all halted operations during the alleged Ukrainian raid, disrupting flights and causing long delays.
According to FlightRadar24, an open-source air traffic monitoring website, multiple Russian government aircraft from the Rossiya Special Flight Detachment, which transports top-level Russian government officials, were scheduled to fly into Moscow's airports on Oct. 9.
At least one of the aircraft, an Ilyushin Il-96-300PU flying from Türkmenbaşy in Turkmenistan to Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, was reportedly forced to divert to St. Petersburg, according to FlightRadar24.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed "the Ministry of Defense's air defense forces repelled an attack by 15 UAVs" on the Russian government's messaging app, MAX.
A number of unknown balloons, which both Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels claimed were launched by the Ukrainian military, were also seen in the Russian skies.
Local Russian Telegram channels showed mysterious balloons in the skies near Moscow, and air defense activity.
Russian outlet BAZA claimed that, "reconnaissance balloons launched from Ukraine," were shot down over Yaroslavl Oblast, a region of Russia north of Moscow.
By 5:42 p.m. Moscow time, Russian wire service RIA Novosti reported that Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports had reopened.
On Sept. 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced a plan to close Russia's skies.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said, as he warned "every airline that uses Russian airspace" against flying over the country.
"The Russian sky will be de facto closed," he added.
In the weeks following the announcement, Ukrainian drone raids have caused severe disruption to Russian air travel, but the result has fallen short of the complete closure Zelensky promised.
read also
Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said.
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+, citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said.
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Command decisions: CENTCOM chief Brad Cooper's ups and downs in shaping Trump's war on Iran
articles.body:
While US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu make their next decisions on Iran and the Middle East conflict strategy, The Jerusalem Post now reveals the major impact that US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Adm. Brad Cooper has had in this regard.
In April, the Post reported that Cooper has, in some ways, taken a more passive role than his predecessor, Gen. Michael “Erik” Kurilla, in communicating his broad strategy views to Trump, preferring instead to convey them to US Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman Gen. Dan Caine.
The Post can now add that, at times, some say that Cooper conveys views directly to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio or to US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, along with Caine, depending on the issue.
Cooper, the Post understands, views this as his proper role as a theater combat commander and says communicating with these top officials, rather than Trump, lets him get his concerns heard at the highest decision-making levels.
All parties credit Cooper with tremendous success as deputy chief of CENTCOM in the June 2025 war with Iran, where he worked closely with top Israeli officials and managed much of that relationship and coordination.
All parties also credit Cooper with excellent military operational planning and execution in many areas as CENTCOM chief during the early 2026 war with Iran.
They have also been impressed by his ability to capitalize on his special naval expertise during the ongoing Strait of Hormuz conflict.
However, questions remain about his role and impact in areas where the American public is critical of the war’s results.
The Post now reveals a range of Cooper, CENTCOM, US military, and Israeli military views about areas where many Americans have criticized the results of the war.
Much of Iran’s closure of Hormuz ‘fake’ until April
The biggest black eye for the Trump administration has been the Strait of Hormuz. Whether current US operational control there succeeds going forward, the US and the world economy have been shaken by Iran’s closure of the strait for much of 2026.
Many experts have slammed Trump and US military officials for failing to secure the strait in the opening plays of the war.
If questioned about why the US military did not focus its first moves in early March on cleaning up or blocking any Iranian efforts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, the Post understands that Cooper would explain that the strait “clean up” could not happen until the main drone, ballistic missile, and large vessel Iranian naval threats were cleared.
Estimates were that this was going to take at least a month. Several US military officials argue that many observers wrongly superimpose the situation now when they go backward to analyze the state of play way back in early March.
They fail to consider the months it took to wear down the broader Iranian threats, such that there can be a more surgical focus on the strait now. In other words, there was no way to immediately neutralize the strait problem.
Based on this, Cooper would argue that such backseat quarterbacking is misinformed and irrelevant.
Questions do remain about whether the US, Israel, and CENTCOM could have pursued a different operational strategy, as Gen. Kenneth Franklin McKenzie Jr. told the Post on April 9.
McKenzie suggested seizing Kharg Island, or using consistent firepower to prevent Iran from operating there or around the Strait of Hormuz.
But given the limits of Trump not wanting to lose marines or hobble Iran’s non-military economic capabilities longer term, it is unclear exactly how some of those other operational options would have played out.
In addition, in a staggering revelation, when Iran announced that it had closed the Strait Hormuz in early March, Cooper would assert that this was a partially fake declaration.
Iran’s declaration was real in the sense of the danger felt by ships worldwide that stopped traveling through the strait and regarding the threat of hundreds of daily missiles and thousands of daily drones.
However, the Post can now disclose that Iran’s claims that it was already mining the strait back then were mostly fictitious.
Over time, the US Navy inspected suspicious objects in the sea and found that the vast majority of the supposed 80 mines were duds, the Post has learned.
What about reports by The Wall Street Journal, CNN, and others in early and mid-March claiming that Iran had already laid significant quantities of mines in the ocean and that the US was facing difficulty in removing them?
According to American sources, while the missile and drone threats were real and the US military was dealing with those from the start of the conflict, it later turned out that any reports backing Iran’s claims of heavily mining the strait in early March were untrue.
The Post can now disclose that it understands that Iran did not deploy mines in Hormuz before the April 7 initial ceasefire.
This might seem like too convenient an answer for US sources to give, since they can blame any shortcomings on the absence of continuous military operations.
But one significant piece of evidence for this narrative is that no reports show ships damaged by sea mines. By May 2026, CENTCOM said it had destroyed over 90% of over 8,000 Iranian sea mines (many were destroyed before they could be deployed).
New dimensions to the Cooper call to Zamir to eliminate Tangsiri
It has recently been reported that around March 19, Cooper made a secret call to IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir to request that Israel eliminate IRGC Navy chief Alireza Tangsiri, considered a serious threat to Hormuz and the naval conflict in general.
Zamir approved, and on March 26, Israel assassinated Tangsiri.
This incident raises the question: Why would Cooper secretly call Zamir on March 19 to ask him to remove Tangsiri as a threat, if US sources want to claim that Iran was not carrying out significant, real sea mining until the conflict paused sometime in mid-April?
The Post has learned that the US was confused and had varying levels of confidence when it learned of Iranian discussions about what Tehran was really thinking about doing regarding mining.
Whatever the concerns were, both Israeli and American sources have acknowledged that they were not the same as issuing actual orders on the matter.
In that sense, the Post understands that Cooper’s call to Zamir was, in many senses, a call for a preemptive move to head off a possible future strategic problem.
The Post also reported earlier on Thursday that some top Israeli officials worried Tangsiri could emerge as the next head of the IRGC and that he would be a much tougher adversary than Ahmad Vahidi, who eventually became the new IRGC chief.
In contrast, many top Israeli officials viewed Tangsiri as a highly creative and resourceful commander. Vahidi was largely seen as a deputy to a deputy of top commanders, lacking the power to shape the broader security posture.
What role or influence has and will CENTCOM have on the war’s strategic goals over time?
There are multiple parts to this question, starting with resolving the Hormuz crisis. The other parts involve regime change and Iran’s nuclear program.
Regarding regime change, even at the start of the war, American voices opposing or doubting that regime change plans pushed by Israel would pay off leaked out.
As the war has drawn out, the divergence between US and Israeli strategy and focus on these issues has grown even larger.
Even the targeting carried out by the two militaries during the main conflict saw Israel assassinating Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian officials. At the same time, the US mostly stayed away from that, focusing on degrading Iranian military capabilities.
A disconnect on the US side over regime change complicates the picture.
Trump himself has repeatedly made comments encouraging regime change or using metaphors about wiping out Iran as a functional nation.
However, the Post has learned that behind the scenes, Trump and his other top lieutenants have given zero directives to the military and CENTCOM about making efforts toward achieving this.
Also, US sources would note Trump has made at least as many or more statements demurring from regime change as a goal – it just happens to be that this American president does not try to keep a consistent public message on the issue.
However, the nuclear dilemma is different.
All US officials and most of the world know that getting Iran to make nuclear concessions (once negotiations were viewed as having failed) was the minimum primary strategic goal and starting point for the war with Iran.
In that sense, the purpose of striking Iran’s drones, missiles, and navy has been to remove Iran’s strategic threats that have held back the US, the West, and Israel from confronting it about the nuclear program more directly all these years.
Striking Iran’s military programs had benefits on their own, but the real goal was to pressure Tehran into nuclear concessions.
How would Cooper and CENTCOM judge overall success on these goals at this point?
The jury is out, but the story isn’t over yet.
What does that mean?
It means that Cooper and CENTCOM, like Israel and much of the world, are waiting to see what Iran’s breaking point is, given all of the economic and military pressure it has been under.
This last point may make sense after a few weeks or a few months, but seems problematic after seven months.
Yes, Iran has been hit much harder. But American bases, soldiers, allies, and the US and world economy have also been hit hard for seven times longer than Trump publicly promised this conflict would go on for.
Is there a point where Cooper and CENTCOM would press Trump harder and more directly to either end the conflict or reengage militarily to break the logjam?
The Post’s understanding is that even if this conflict is stuck for a full year or even a few years (however unlikely), Cooper’s and CENTCOM’s position would not change: strategic feedback should come only through lower channels, including Caine, Rubio, and Hegseth.
Former CENTCOM chief McKenzie warned US bases would be vulnerable to sustained Iranian attacks
In 2024, McKenzie, discussing American military bases in the region, warned that “the United States will not be able to maintain these bases in a full-throated conflict, because they will be rendered unusable by sustained Iranian attack.”
Previously, the Post and others have reported that CENTCOM and the US in general did not heed McKenzie’s warnings.
Cooper only took over CENTCOM fully in August 2025, so there is only so much he could have done, but his previous efforts on the issue had not been reported in any significant fashion.
In contrast, the Post has learned that there is a counter-narrative on the issue.
According to it, the winding down of many US bases and assets in the region did start before the war, especially in Iraq and Syria.
Since the war, more winding down has occurred in Iraq and Syria, and eventually in Kuwait as well. Notably, the US has not talked about reducing its footprint in Jordan and Saudi Arabia, though its bases there have been hit hard and repeatedly.
Another area where Cooper’s and CENTCOM’s narrative would likely differ from the narrative reported by most of the media to date relates to how unexpected the billions in damage to US bases from Iran have been.
Another disconnect within the administration is that Hegseth has often publicly denied the extent of the damage and has been accused of trying to cover it up.
But the CENTCOM view would be that such damage was, in fact, expected.
CENTCOM would ask rhetorical questions like: Since when has there been a war with no damage to one of the sides?
In addition, CENTCOM would note that a modern war in which bases were spread like peanut butter across a region was obviously vulnerable, and anyone who did not recognize this grossly misunderstood the weaknesses of America’s basing posture, a leftover from earlier eras of warfare.
But decades of basing cannot be changed overnight, especially in the enormous US military, which is known for being slow to transfer large forces between bases or military theaters.
It seemed to be implied that the much more recent expanded and evolving drone threat changed the security posture for US basing much more rapidly and radically than the decades-old missile threat.
Alternatively, elements of the Trump administration may not have thought Iran would succeed at firing off as many missiles at US bases as it did.
In contrast, Cooper would take significant pride in the success of America’s regional air-defense architecture with its Middle Eastern allies.
Meanwhile, the war might have heavily degraded the US supply of interceptors for missiles and drones. Some internal US defense establishment reports have said there could be shortages if there is a war in the near future with another adversary like Russia or China.
Cooper might have communicated this risk to Caine and Hegseth. However, both the US defense secretary and Trump have denied any combat impact from interceptor shortages – without explaining how a shortage would affect combat readiness.
In addressing these problematic byproducts of the war, the Post understands that Cooper’s view is that what matters most is that Iran was hurt by the war exponentially more than the US.
Put simply, Iran lost $200-$300 billion in its defense sector from US and Israeli attacks, while the US lost only around $5b.
In addition, some have said that absent the superior US-allied air defenses, Iranian missile fire could have potentially killed millions of people in worst-case scenarios.
Other estimates put the risk from Iranian missile fire more in the tens of thousands. But either way, the point about how ready Iran was to commit mass murder across the region, absent strong CENTCOM regional air defense, remains clear.
Some American sources have questioned whether this is the right way to evaluate the mission’s and the war’s success or failure.
They ask: What if Washington had an option to achieve its strategic goals with Iran without losing $5b. in damages to its bases?
US military sources believe that part of the problem with the public perception of the war could be that portions of them thought the Iran war would go as quickly and as easily as America’s effective coup in Venezuela in January of this year.
Unspoken by US military officials in this criticism, but obvious from public comments by the US president about how surprised he has been that Iran did not “crack” sooner, is that many military officials believe that Trump himself was swept up by the quick “win” in Venezuela.
Trump administration claimed Iran's ballistic missile threat would soon be eliminated
During the war, Trump, Caine, and Hegseth repeatedly made public claims indicating that Iran’s ballistic missile apparatus had been decimated and that its threat would almost entirely disappear within days or weeks.
Israeli defense and intelligence officials also told the Post in March and April that Iran’s missile capacity had fallen to possibly as few as several hundred missiles.
Iran fell from 2,500 missiles to 1,600, and its production capacity fell from an expected 2,000 by the end of 2026 to original pre-war estimates that, absent outside intervention, it might reach 6,000 missiles by the end of the year.
In that sense, the Post has learned that CENTCOM’s view would be that Iran’s missile threat is substantially weaker now than pre-war.
However, the predictions by Trump, Caine, and Hegseth seem substantially off base.
Even the predictions by Israeli defense and intelligence officials have turned out to be significantly overly optimistic.
If Iran is “not the same Iran,” as CENTCOM and Israel would both argue, it has still managed to fire dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at will throughout the Middle East. This includes firing on American ships during any period of renewed military conflict between Tehran and Washington.
These missile launches have paled in comparison to the hundreds of missiles and thousands of drones Iran was able to launch per day at the start of the war. They have been far more than the drizzle that some American and Israeli officials predicted, and remain a strategic-level threat.
Certainly, Iran cannot threaten the region as a “bully” the same way it could before. But the US and Israel are still refraining from going directly to control Iran’s remaining nuclear assets by force out of fear of what remains of the Islamic Republic’s capabilities.
All of this paints a nuanced picture of CENTCOM under Cooper as the region’s lead shaper in some respects, but one that avoids sticking its neck out too much in others.
Many top American generals who have spoken up when they disagreed with some aspect of Trump’s or Hegseth’s ideas have been summarily dismissed in numbers unseen in years.
Cooper’s preference for conveying his views through Caine, Hegseth, and Rubio has not only been a way of operating within the chain of command, but has also saved him so far from the rash wave of firings.
It will be years before history can fully judge the mix of undeniable major contributions Cooper has made to Middle East security, alongside major dilemmas where he steered clear of rocking the boat too much.
In the meantime, much of the region is thankful that, even if Trump and Washington are wildly unpredictable, they have the benefit of Cooper’s steady hand.

articles.title: The two elections that revolve around Iran
articles.body:
The two elections that revolve around Iran
Israel is now formally in campaign mode. The Knesset dissolved on July 17, and voters go to the polls on October 27, 2026. A week later, on November 3, American voters decide the composition of Congress.
