The overlap is almost exact, and it has turned the relationship between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump into something closer to a competition than an alliance. What helps one man survive politically threatens to sink the other.
Netanyahu needs Iran to dominate the Israeli campaign. His best path back to power runs through a public that feels an immediate security threat and a prime minister positioned as the only leader capable of ordering military action at scale. Trump needs the opposite: proof to American voters that a long war is over, that gasoline prices are falling, and that no more Americans are dying for someone else’s fight. The result is a near-perfect zero-sum bind. A new round of escalation could hand Netanyahu a path to victory while costing Republicans their House majority. A negotiated end to the conflict could hand Trump a signature achievement while leaving Netanyahu exposed to hostile polling and an unresolved domestic reckoning.
An opposition advantage that doesn’t guarantee a government
On paper, Netanyahu’s position looks weak. The Knesset has 120 seats, a governing coalition needs 61, and any party must clear a 3.25% threshold to enter parliament at all – meaning the real battle isn’t just for vote share but for keeping allied parties above the line.
As of October 8, 2026, Israeli polling presents a mixed picture, with neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Zionist opposition securing a parliamentary majority in the latest surveys. A Channel 13 poll published on October 7 put Netanyahu’s bloc at 55 seats, the Zionist opposition at 50, and Arab parties at 15. The Yashar party of former IDF Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot and Netanyahu’s Likud were tied at 20 seats each, although Eisenkot retained a personal lead as the preferred prime minister, with 44% support against Netanyahu’s 40%.
A Channel 12 poll published on October 5 showed a different balance: 49 seats for Netanyahu’s bloc, 54 for the Zionist opposition and 13 for Arab parties. Yashar led Likud by 23 seats to 21, while Eisenkot led Netanyahu by 41% to 38% on suitability for prime minister.
A summer survey on whether Netanyahu should even run again found that 61% of Israelis opposed his participation in the upcoming election, while 35% supported it. Among Jewish respondents, 57% opposed another candidacy and 39.5% supported it.
None of this makes his defeat inevitable, because the opposition’s real problem is forming a coalition. Eisenkot, the Bennett-Lapid alignment, Avigdor Liberman’s party, and the left could plausibly out-poll Netanyahu’s bloc and still lack a workable majority without leaning on Arab parties, an arrangement much of the Jewish opposition leadership is unwilling to commit to publicly. A Netanyahu bloc stuck around 50 seats doesn’t automatically mean a change of government; it leaves room for him to peel off defectors, split rivals, or force a repeat election.
His current partners – the ultra-Orthodox Shas and United Torah Judaism, along with the far-right Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism – are disciplined blocs, but keeping them requires continuing to push yeshiva exemptions from military conscription, expanding executive influence over the judiciary and media, and holding a hard line on the Palestinians. Those same moves alienate the center, military reservists, and secular Israelis. The conscription fight in particular has repeatedly brought the coalition to the brink of collapse, and in its final weeks before dissolution the outgoing Knesset pushed through several contested measures on conscription, judicial authority, and media regulation.
War helps Netanyahu
Security remains the one lever capable of reshaping the campaign overnight. On the normal political agenda, Netanyahu has to answer for the October 7, 2023 intelligence and defense failure, the strain of prolonged reserve-duty mobilization, a difficult economy, and years of domestic polarization. A fresh war pushes all of that into the background and reframes the election as a referendum on wartime leadership.
The pattern has already played out once. After what Israelis broadly regarded as a successful twelve-day war with Iran in summer 2025, Likud’s support hit its highest point since the 2022 election. But by July 2026 the party had slid back down to roughly 21-24 seats.
Israeli public opinion is a genuine paradox here: war-weary, yet unwilling to accept a settlement seen as premature. Only 38% of respondents believe Israel’s security position has actually improved since the war with Iran. Polling from the Institute for National Security Studies finds 43% believe the war ended without a clear result, 37% consider Iran the winner, and just 15% consider Israel the winner. Separately, 66% viewed the US-Iran memorandum signed in June as unfavorable to Israel, and a majority of Jewish respondents have said ending the war on its current terms is incompatible with the country’s security interests.
This paradox gives Netanyahu an opening to argue the war produced nothing decisive because Washington called off the pressure too early. New war with Iran, in this framing, is finishing an unfinished job: dismantling nuclear infrastructure, ballistic missile production, IRGC command targets, and the logistics networks supporting Iran-aligned militias.
Such an escalation could pull wavering right-of-center voters back from Eisenkot and Bennett toward Likud. But Eisenkot himself is a former chief of staff with his own security credentials, which means a strike alone won’t be enough – Netanyahu needs a fast, unambiguous result he can credibly claim as his own achievement.
A drawn-out or inconclusive operation would do the opposite. Israelis are already skeptical of what has been achieved so far; further destruction, extended mobilization, and strikes on the home front risk changing the question from “is Netanyahu decisive enough” to “why, after years of fighting, has this government still not delivered lasting security.”
There’s an economic constraint layered on top. The Bank of Israel’s forecast projects 4% GDP growth in 2026, a budget deficit of 4.9% of GDP, and public debt near 69% of GDP – but that assumes no new war with Iran and a cooling of hostilities in Lebanon. The central bank has warned that a proposed defense-spending increase of up to 25 billion shekels (about $8.1 billion) would push up the deficit, debt, and inflation simultaneously. A new war could therefore improve Netanyahu’s electoral standing while it undermines the macroeconomic recovery his government depends on.
What Netanyahu wants from Trump
Netanyahu needs to persuade Trump of three things: that any diplomatic pause gives Tehran time to rebuild its missile and nuclear capacity; that limited strikes around the Strait of Hormuz don’t resolve the underlying strategic problem; and that any agreement must include dismantling enrichment capacity, removing stockpiled material, capping the ballistic missile program, and weakening Iran’s regional proxies.
Israel’s regional strategy much more than just Iran, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza, Iran-backed militias in Iraq and Yemen, strategic competition with Türkiye, and preserving military superiority amid the possible sale of F-35s to Ankara. Trump’s agenda is even wider: freedom of navigation, energy prices, the relationship with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye, expanding the Abraham Accords, and casting himself as the president who ended the war. Israel remains a central ally in that picture, but no longer the only crucial player.
A new war is dangerous for Trump
At home, however, election math is pulling Trump in the opposite direction. Republicans are defending an extremely narrow majority in the November 3 midterms. The House currently stands at 218 Republicans to 214 Democrats, one independent, and two vacancies. The Senate split is 53 Republicans to 45 Democrats and two independents caucusing with Democrats – and of the seats up for election, 22 are held by Republicans against just 13 held by Democrats, which is obviously structurally unfavorable for the Republicans.
A war with Iran is itself an electoral liability. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found only about a third of Americans support it, against 62% opposed. Roughly 69% of respondents, including 40% of Republicans, say Trump has failed to explain the operation’s objectives. Earlier Pew and Quinnipiac surveys told a similar story, with 59% to 60% calling the use of force a mistake or not worth the cost.
For American voters, the war’s most tangible effect is the price at the gas pump. Disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and volatile oil prices pushed the average gasoline price above four dollars a gallon; EIA data puts the national average at $4.35 as of October 5, after peaking near $4.56 in the spring. The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index slipped from 88.6 in August to 81.9 in September, the lowest since 2014.
The link between the war and household costs is especially damaging for a president who campaigned on lowering prices and ending open-ended foreign wars. Even many voters who favor a hard line on Iran don’t see defending Israel as sufficient justification for prolonged US involvement – AP-NORC polling found 67% of Americans call preventing higher fuel prices an important priority, compared with just 39% who say the same about preventing threats to Israel.
Congress has already registered the discontent. On July 23, the Republican-controlled House passed a resolution demanding an end to military action against Iran without congressional authorization, 214 to 208, with four Republicans crossing party lines. The measure is largely symbolic, but it demonstrates how easily the Iran question could split a majority that already has no margin for error.
Two paths forward
The immediate choice facing both leaders has changed from whether to start a fresh offensive or pursue a peace deal, to whether the current pause can survive the election season. On October 8, Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterms, while keeping the blockade in place and describing talks with Tehran as productive. That in turn puts a publicly declared American timetable around Netanyahu’s room for maneuver before Israel’s October 27 vote. It does not amount to a peace agreement, guarantee Israeli restraint, or rule out a response to a new attack.
Escalation remains a risk, but it can no longer be presented as an equally likely, openly US-backed campaign strategy before the elections. Axios reported on October 7 that the Pentagon had ordered preparations for possible renewed combat. If fighting resumes, Netanyahu could try to rally voters around wartime leadership, but the electoral benefit would depend on the outcome. A brief operation with demonstrable gains might help Likud; missile retaliation, civilian losses, and renewed mobilization could instead reinforce doubts about his government’s ability to deliver lasting security.
For Trump, the more immediate objective is to keep the conflict from producing another economic shock before Americans vote. His announcement leaves coercive pressure intact. Shipping through Hormuz also remains vulnerable: Iranian attacks on tankers have resumed even as Washington describes progress in getting Gulf oil to market. Avoiding a new bombing campaign may reduce the risk of a sudden price surge, but it cannot by itself restore normal navigation or ensure cheaper gasoline within weeks.
A diplomatic breakthrough could still improve Trump’s position, especially if it makes shipping safer and brings sustained relief at the pump. Its effect on Netanyahu would depend on the terms. An agreement seen in Israel as leaving Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities insufficiently constrained could expose him to criticism from both rivals and his own right-wing partners. A settlement with credible restrictions and verification could give him an achievement to defend. In either case, a quieter security environment would leave more room for the domestic issues already shaping the campaign: accountability for October 7, ultra-Orthodox conscription, and the confrontation over the judiciary.
The shared-success option rests on sustained pressure producing enforceable concessions without another regional escalation. Both leaders could claim credit for such an outcome. But negotiations, implementation, and verification are unlikely to fit within the remaining days before the election, and neither Washington nor Jerusalem has control over Tehran’s response. A pause that holds through the votes may still leave the central disputes unresolved and renewed fighting possible afterward.

articles.title: Rubio says Trump wants F-35 deliveries to Türkiye
articles.body:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said President Donald Trump wants Türkiye to receive F-35 fighter jets, while stressing that legal barriers linked to Ankara’s Russian S-400 air defense system remain unresolved.
In an interview with Kathimerini published on Oct. 8, Rubio said Türkiye was a NATO ally and had already paid for some aircraft. Trump wanted deliveries to proceed if possible, he said.
However, U.S. legislation imposed strict conditions that Ankara had yet to meet.
“Until those conditions are met, the sale cannot go ahead,” Rubio said, adding that the Turkish side was aware of the restrictions and was seeking solutions.
Rubio also described a conflict between Türkiye and Greece as “unthinkable,” saying it would harm both NATO allies and the United States.
It was “something we could never allow to happen,” he said.
Washington remained in constant contact with Ankara, Rubio said, pointing to Türkiye’s role in hosting talks between Russia and Ukraine.
He suggested that U.S. investment in its relationship with Türkiye could help diplomatic efforts.
On the proposed electricity interconnector between Greece and Greek Cyprus, Rubio said Washington would use private diplomacy to address obstacles to the project, which it considered important for diversifying energy supplies.
The United States and Greece also announced $4 billion in military sales following their strategic dialogue in Athens on Oct. 7.
The package includes upgrades to Greek F-16 fighter jets and purchases of missiles and precision-guided bombs, according to Greek officials.
Asked about Greece’s request for specific advanced weapons for its F-35s, including systems supplied to Israel, Rubio said the matter remained under review and that Trump would make the final decision.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1689: Russia plans up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs against 60 Ukrainian infrastructure sites this winter, Ukraine says
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare. Ukrainian forces combined assaults with drones and ground robots to reclaim territory in Donetsk Oblast while limiting their exposure to Russian fire.
More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit. Russian officials confirmed the fires but named none of the targets.
Ukraine reruns its Vivaldi playbook outside Kramatorsk and pushes Russia back across the Siverskyi Donets, ISW says. Even Russian milbloggers now concede Ukrainian gains east of Sloviansk, including a river crossing toward a key height.
Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant. In Bashkortostan, Ukraine’s General Staff says its forces hit a Gazprom refinery. Salavat’s mayor says an unnamed enterprise there keeps working.
Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says. The faster drones break through Ukraine’s air defenses more reliably, and ISW expects the same strike pattern in Russia’s winter campaign against Ukraine’s energy.
Intelligence and technology
Air-raid sirens cost Kyiv’s weapons makers 61.8 working hours in month, nearly eight days, yet their contract deadlines stay fixed, two groups say. Ukraine’s gunmakers want the government to count real siren downtime against contract deadlines.
Ukrainian producer that neutralized more than 7,000 drones over 100 square kilometers in year, plays enemy in Pentagon contest, and gets invitation to continue. Ukraine’s Phantom Defense built the counter-drone environment for the Pentagon’s Gauntlet II.
Ukraine uses up Europe’s yearly supply of thermal sensors in about five months, so two Ukrainian firms will build their own plants in the West. Their new venture wants to give Western armies their own supply of the chip that lets thermal cameras see body heat in the dark.
Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites. Substations near Ukraine’s western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe, could be among the first targets.
International
Trump says Russia agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel to US and global markets as he blames Ukraine for fuel price hikes driven by Iran war. The announcement comes as Trump pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, which Ukraine targets to weaken Moscow’s war economy.
Head of Russian military propaganda network to be expelled from Montenegro over suspected anti-EU operation. Authorities ordered Mikhail Zvynchuk, founder of the Russian military-focused Rybar network, and four associates to leave the country after seizing drones and recording equipment.
Ukrainian journalists say Austria detained them “like terrorists”: prosecutor says suspicion unsubstantiated. Tkach says armed people smashed the car windows, forced the journalists onto the road, and put a knee on his neck during the detention.
Russia sells cheaper fuel abroad and pays to keep its own pumps running amid Ukraine’s refinery strikes, but crude money still flows. After Ukraine’s drone strikes on refineries, Russia’s diesel exports, once its biggest fuel export, fell to a decade low.
Fought against Ukraine, now claimed to be victims: Kenya’s plea for five men held by Ukraine. Kenya says the men took Russian army contracts under false job promises.
Moldova pulls its border officers off Ukrainian soil again as Russian drones keep hitting crossings. “They will work on the territory of Moldova.” Moldovan Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin, on withdrawing border personnel from Ukraine.
Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization. The move comes as Moscow rejects reports of a new call-up while Ukrainian officials warn Russia is preparing to expand its forces.
80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership. A new poll shows widespread concern over Moldova’s ability to withstand an attack, even as only 4% of respondents see NATO membership as the answer. Russian drones have increasingly crossed Moldovan airspace in recent weeks.
Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion. More than 30 Russian drones entered Polish airspace in September 2025, and some were found carrying Polish SIM cards, RMF24 reports.
Ukraine’s FM links Russian plague scare to history of cover-ups, from anthrax to Chornobyl and COVID-19. Russia’s handling of the suspected case fits a broader pattern of concealing information about dangerous incidents, Andrii Sybiha said.
Humanitarian and social impact
Eggs cost nearly 20 times US prices in occupied Oleshky, where Ukraine’s ombudsman says people die of hunger every day. Residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky cannot leave the city and are waiting for an opportunity to evacuate through a humanitarian corridor.
Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy. Three people were killed and a woman was still missing as the outages spread.
Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter. Russia is once again targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as winter approaches, threatening to leave civilians without power, heat, and water as Moscow ramps up its campaign to cripple the country’s critical systems.
Two 14-year-old boys killed by an explosive device in a field in Sumy Oblast. Residents are being warned that, in addition to constant Russian attacks, there is a risk of encountering explosive devices.
Russia kills 30 in strike on two passenger buses in Kramatorsk. Hours after the strike, the head of Donetsk Oblast ordered public transport in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk halted, saying Russia had made the buses a target.
A 3-year-old girl came to visit her aunt in Pryluky, Ukraine. By morning, a Russian missile had killed her grandmother and uncle. Zlatoslava is in hospital in Chernihiv. Her aunt, a police officer, was wounded in the strike.
Political and legal developments
Investigators say prosecutors shielded scam call centers. Their office has now fired eight people and is checking how its ex-chief left Ukraine. The acting chief also ordered out a deputy at the regional office he ran until September and dropped no-contest hiring of outsiders.
Read our previous daily review here.

articles.title: Zelenskyy blasts US over Russia ties as strikes kill 78 in Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of being unwilling to help Ukraine after Russian strikes killed 78 people and wounded 215 across the country in two days, urging President Donald Trump to increase military support and sanctions against Moscow.
The attacks included a devastating strike on the eastern city of Kramatorsk, where at least 35 people were killed and 20 wounded, according to Ukrainian officials.
The bombardment followed a major Russian drone and missile assault a day earlier that killed dozens, including 22 people in a residential building in Pryluky, about 130 kilometers (80 miles) east of Kyiv.
Speaking to reporters Thursday in Pryluky, Zelenskyy criticized Washington for pursuing potential economic cooperation with Russia while attempting to mediate the war, now in its fifth year.
He also called on the United States to expand Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite communications network, saying it could help Ukrainian forces identify and target Russian ballistic missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran," Zelenskyy said. "Give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table."
The Ukrainian leader questioned U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio's assessment earlier Thursday that the war had reached a stalemate and Washington would continue working toward a settlement.
Zelenskyy argued that Washington's pursuit of economic projects with Moscow contradicted claims that diplomatic progress had stalled.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," he added.
His remarks followed a Reuters report that senior Russian and U.S. officials, including U.S. Special Envoy Jared Kushner, had discussed bringing an American investor into the Nord Stream pipeline network, which transported Russian natural gas to Germany before Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelenskyy urged Trump to increase sanctions pressure on Russia, arguing that stronger support for Ukraine could help bring Russian President Vladimir Putin to the negotiating table.
Ukrainian negotiators are scheduled to travel to the United States on Friday and Saturday for talks. Zelenskyy said he expected European partners to join the discussions, with air defense expected to be a key issue amid continued Russian attacks.
In Kramatorsk, a Russian guided aerial bomb struck the city Thursday, killing dozens and damaging two buses. A subsequent drone attack killed two more people, bringing the reported death toll to 35.
Regional Governor Vadym Filashkin accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting civilians.
"The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible," he said on Telegram.
Images released by officials showed bodies scattered across a debris-covered street beside a charred bus. Some victims had not been identified, Zelenskyy said, warning that the attack would not go unanswered.
Elsewhere, a Russian guided aerial bomb killed two people in a village in southeastern Dnipropetrovsk region, while another person died in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk, local authorities said.
The latest bombardment followed Wednesday's attacks, which killed dozens across Ukraine, including 22 people in Pryluky.
Russia also attacked Kyiv on Thursday morning, killing four people and wounding 19, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The strikes disrupted water and electricity supplies in parts of the capital, with officials warning that restoring services would take time.
Moscow has intensified drone attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting warehouses, data centers and other infrastructure while renewing its campaign against Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter.
Russian technology company Yandex said it could not yet determine whether equipment at a data center hit by a Ukrainian drone attack could be restored.
Zelenskyy did not specifically address the strike on Yandex but said Ukraine was mirroring Russian attacks on data centers.
Ukraine has sought to regain the battlefield initiative as Russian territorial advances have slowed this year. However, Moscow's sustained air campaign continues to threaten civilians, critical infrastructure and the country's energy security.

articles.title: Middle East live: Yemen, Gulf turmoil and Trump's ICC clash
articles.body:
This live blog has now ended. Make sure to follow us for the latest news on Facebook, X, and Instagram.
Here were the top updates:
The International Criminal Court's deputy prosecutor has condemned sanctions imposed by US President Donald Trump, nut said the court's work will continue
IRGC officials say they still retain control over Hormuz, with "nightly operations" conducted on tankers moving through "illegal routes"
The war in Yemen rages on between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, and southern Lebanon despite any alleged ceasefire agreements
Protests in New York as Trump admin defends ICE shooting
Protesters gathered in New York on Friday after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers shot a Dominican man in an incident that has provoked a showdown between the city's Democratic mayor and the Trump administration.
Oscar Bergal, 28, was wounded in the neck during an ICE operation in the Bronx on Thursday, while a five-year-old child who was in his car at the time was physically unharmed.
The shooting drew swift criticism from Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who wrote "Abolish ICE" on X -- a common refrain among the political left opposed to Republican President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.
Mauritanian PM reappointed hours after resignation
Mauritania's prime minister resigned Friday after a scathing report on two major electric facility fires, but he was reappointed hours later and asked to form a new government.
Mokhtar Ould Djay's resignation after more than two years in office came after President Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani received a report Thursday detailing multiple shortcomings leading to the blazes in August.
The two men met later Friday and Ghazouani reappointed him prime minister and tasked him with forming a new government, the official Mauritanian news agency said.
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had secured Russia's agreement for a major release of diesel, as he eased war sanctions on Moscow in a push to lower energy costs ahead of midterm elections.
Moscow has been hit with waves of sanctions by the United States and partners since its 2022 invasion of neighbouring Ukraine, and President Volodymyr Zelensky criticised Trump for an "unworthy" and "weak" move.
Prices at US gasoline and diesel pumps have surged since late February, when US-Israel strikes targeting Iran triggered Tehran's blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for energy transit.
The deal comes weeks before key US elections where Trump's Republican Party risks losing its grip on Congress as voters express frustration over the mounting cost of living.
Saudi-led coalition says carrying out op targeting Houthis
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Friday it was carrying out a wide-ranging operation targeting the elements and capabilities of the Houthis, according to a statement by the coalition spokesperson.
It had destroyed 136 military targets in areas controlled by the Houthis, the spokesperson said, adding the coalition was providing round-the-clock air support to Yemeni government forces.
Turkey jails 2 journalists for fund crisis 'misinformation'
A Turkish court on Friday jailed two journalists pending trial for allegedly spreading misinformation over a sprawling investment fund scandal, while another two were granted conditional release, media reports said.
Turkey has been grappling with the fallout from an investment fund scandal which erupted in mid-September, prompting an investigation into allegations of widespread market manipulation.
The scandal has put pressure on President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling AKP, with one senior party official resigning after allegations about her investment activities.
Exactly one year after a ceasefire was reached in Gaza, over 100 humanitarian, human rights, and other civil society organisations have highlighted Israel's continued attacks on the enclave, stating that the truce has been "meaningless".
Organisations including Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), ActionAid and Save the Children were among those denouncing Israel’s actions since the truce was agreed in October 2025.
At least 1,471 Palestinians have been killed since then, with daily demolitions carried out and civilians targeted.
“What we see on the ground is that the ceasefire exists in name only. A ceasefire is absolutely meaningless when civilians, including children, are being killed every single day,” Alexandra Saieh, Head of Policy and Global Influencing at Save the Children, told The New Arab.
A magnitude-7.7 earthquake rocked Panama on Friday, unleashing panic in the high-rise capital city and causing buildings to collapse in the center of the country.
USGS said the quake was detected at 1756 GMT with an epicenter 10 kilometers (6 miles) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in the south-center of Panama.
It triggered a tsunami warning for Panama and warnings of smaller but dangerous waves along the coasts of other countries in Latin America and the south Pacific.
Lebanon said an Israeli attack on Friday wounded six people as Israel claimed it targeted a "Syrian terrorist" who planned anti-Israel attacks under Iranian instructions.
"The Israeli attack near the town of Hawsh al-Sayyed Ali in the Hermel district led to six wounded, including five Syrian nationals, two of them women, and one Lebanese," Lebanon's health ministry said.
Lebanon's state-run National News Agency reported that "an enemy military drone targeted a car" in the town, located close to the Syrian border, an area largely been spared such attacks since an Israel-Hezbollah ceasefire was agreed in June.
Houthi media says two killed in Saudi strike on airport
Houthi media reported on Friday that Saudi strikes on the airport in the capital Sanaa killed two people, a day after the group launched deadly strikes against Riyadh's own air hub.
Separately, the civil defence agency in the Yemeni capital reported extinguishing four fires caused by Saudi strikes, including one it said destroyed a factory.
Trump taps conservative commentator Zacharia for press sec.
Katie Zacharia, a communications adviser for President Donald Trump's Truth Social platform, has been offered the position of White House press secretary following Karoline Leavitt's departure from the role in August, a White House official said on Friday.
Zacharia did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but if she accepts the role, she would fill a critical role in the Trump administration before next month's midterm congressional elections.
Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Tel Aviv airport
The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a flydubai jet last week had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport, the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor said on Friday.
The Omani co-pilot had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda's September 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the prosecutor's findings published by state media.
"The findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks."
Morocco King defends Spain 'partnership' after Ceuta rush
Morocco's King Mohammed VI defended his country's "partnership" with Spain on Friday, weeks after thousands of migrants swept into Madrid's North African exclave of Ceuta and sparked a political crisis.
"In the face of the irresponsible statements made by certain political and media circles and their blatant instrumentalisation of the situation, we affirm that partnership is a sovereign choice and a voluntary commitment, which cannot be subject to any pressure or threat, nor to any form of blackmail," the monarch told the opening of a new session of parliament.
71 killed in S.Sudan intercommunal violence: govt, witnesses
Inter-communal violence killed 71 people Friday in South Sudan's central town of Rumbek, the interim government and witnesses said.
Several witnesses told AFP that ethnic and community conflict was behind the latest outbreak of violence in the world's youngest country, which won independence from Sudan in 2011.
ICC sanctions 'blow' for international justice: UN chief
UN chief Antonio Guterres on Friday condemned a decision by the United States to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court, adding he is "deeply alarmed by the expected impact" of the measures.
"Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar," spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
"The secretary-general reiterates his unwavering support for the independence of the Court and its officials," he added.
The United Nations on Friday raised the alarm about a displacement crisis in the central Sahel where nearly four million people have been forced to flee their homes in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.
The number is more than double that of six years ago, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) said, before a wave of coups in a region bedevilled by instability and violence.
It includes 818,000 refugees and asylum seekers, it added.
"The crisis is being compounded by continued attacks affecting civilians, climate-related shocks and severe humanitarian funding shortfalls," the UNHCR said in a statement.
PA hails Nobel for Pillay, defender of 'oppressed'
The Palestinian foreign ministry on Friday welcomed the awarding of the Nobel Peace Price to jurist Navi Pillay, saying the recognition honoured "all those who stand firm in defending international law and justice".
"Throughout her distinguished career, she has pursued the truth and defended the rights of the oppressed in South Africa and around the world, including Palestine, with integrity, courage, and honour," the ministry said in a statement.
South African judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize [Getty
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday praised the United States for imposing sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), which has issued a warrant for his arrest over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," Netanyahu's office posted on X.
Netanyahu is wanted by the ICC for alleged war crimes in Gaza [Getty]
EU slams US sanctions on ICC, vows to help carry out work
The European Union on Friday called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court "deeply regrettable" and said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work".
"The EU will work closely with the ICC to ensure it continues to operate effectively," the European Commission said, adding it hoped that the six-month delay before the sanctions applied meant "there is room for dialogue".
Mauritania's prime minister submitted his government's resignation Friday, according to state media, following a scathing report on two electric facility fires that plunged parts of the capital into darkness for several days.
Mokhtar Ould Djay's resignation after more than two years in office came after President Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani received a report Thursday detailing multiple shortcomings leading to the blazes in August.
ICC says sanctions are an assault on the rule of law
The International Criminal Court (ICC) has called sanctions imposed by US President Donald Trump "an assault on the rule of law."
"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," the court's deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, told Reuters. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."
Residents reported hearing a powerful boom on Friday in the vicinity of Aden airport in southern Yemen.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage, and the cause of the sound was not immediately clear.
The airport was attacked earlier this week, Yemen's Transport Ministry said. It said Houthis had targeted it with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones.

articles.title: As Trump mulls new strikes on Iran, what options does he have?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
As Trump mulls new strikes on Iran, what options does he have?
Following renewed US troop movements into the Middle East, the US is reportedly gearing up for a new round of strikes on Iran after weeks of deliberations by President Donald Trump.
Trump has on several occasions stated that he would not launch new strikes until after the midterm elections, the latest being on Thursday, saying on Truth Social that discussions with Iran were "productive."
Yet, according to both The New York Times and Axios, Trump mulled the possibility of further strikes following a meeting with his national security staff in Camp David on 2 October. A final decision is set to occur within the next seven to 10 days, Israel's Channel 12 reported.
The New Arab explores if and how the US military will escalate tensions, and if Iran will retaliate.
What is now in the region?
As it stands, the US has around 50,000 troops and a host of assets in the region, including the 82nd Airborne Division, air defence systems, surveillance, refuelling and strike aircraft that it built up before and during the start of the Iran war.
This includes the USS George Washington aircraft carrier, involved in blockading Iran and escorting shipping out of the Strait of Hormuz, and the USS Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, housing the 11th Marine Expeditionary Group.
In recent weeks, reports have shed light on new deployments, with some stating there will be between 9,000 and 10,000 troops, including the 13th Marine Expeditionary Group aboard the USS Makin Island, stationed alongside the USS Theodor Roosevelt, according to The Wall Street Journal.
This would maintain US carrier deployments to the region at two, following the withdrawal of the USS George H.W. Bush, which has since arrived in Thailand. It is unknown if the George Washington is also set to withdraw.
The US has also sent two additional Patriot missile batteries, used to shoot down incoming ballistic missiles, to prop up the dense web of systems already deployed and further protect Saudi and Qatari energy sites, according to Axios.
What are Trump's options?
According to Dr Andreas Krieg, Senior Lecturer in Defence Studies at King's College London, the deployments signal that the US "wants to restore escalation dominance without yet committing to another major war", with the troop and carrier deployments acting as both deterrence and preparation.
"The US is reinforcing air and missile defence, force protection, ISR [Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance], logistics and command capacity around Israel and the Gulf, while simultaneously giving Trump a much larger menu of strike options," he told The New Arab.
That menu has been reported on by The New York Times, with five plans drawn up focusing on a short, three-day campaign of intense strikes focusing on the drone and missile arsenal of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, their command posts and headquarters, alongside energy facilities.
Strikes on infrastructure are also expected to occur in the event of a US bombardment, and Israel is also expected to take part in an escalation, with Israeli media reporting that Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir is being briefed on US preparations.
The deployment of two carriers is a key aspect of this, with Krieg noting that it gives US military flexibility in any strike campaign against Iran, increasing sortie rates, allowing the US to enforce a blockade and protect shipping, and giving the US options to escalate the campaign targets.
"Trump wants Tehran to believe that rejecting American terms could now carry a much higher military cost," Krieg said, adding "but these deployments also expose the central weakness of the US position: every additional American asset placed in the Gulf creates another target Iran can threaten".
How could Iran respond?
Like in previous rounds of attacks on Iran by the US or Israel, Tehran is likely to retaliate.
Krieg told The New Arab that Iran would likely respond in two stages, the first being a focus on survivability, with the IRGC and military dispersing assets into hardened facilities, using decoys and decentralising command, to survive the initial strikes.
The second would see a horizontal escalation, targeting US bases and logistics hubs, pressuring Gulf infrastructure, and disrupting maritime traffic around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb through its Houthi allies.
"I think Tehran's calculation remains that the Gulf is America's vulnerability. Iran would aim to make any renewed US campaign immediately costly for Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and global energy markets," he said.
"Iran is likely to answer by making clear that such an escalation cannot be geographically contained inside Iran."
This was echoed by Ali Vaez, Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, who told The New Arab that "Iran cannot match the US militarily, so its strategy is to make escalation costly and geographically expansive."
"Its leverage lies in convincing Washington that any attack on Iran will reverberate across the region," he added.
"I fear that a high US casualty event might compel Trump to throw caution to the wind and go after Iran's infrastructure, which will result in Iran scorching the region," Vaez said.
Is this the same as the February attack?
Much of what is being debated is similar to what played out in February when the war began, with Andreas Kreig telling The New Arab, "There is a striking degree of repetition. The United States still essentially has the same coercive menu it had at the beginning of the war."
Those same escalation plans are part of the same "strategic calculus" employed by both sides, Kreig added, noting that the US is continuing to attempt to use military power to shorten the conflict, despite not being able to translate military power into political leverage, while Iran is playing for time.
"Unless one side changes that underlying logic, we are likely to keep seeing variations of the same escalation pattern rather than a genuinely new strategy," Krieg said.

articles.title: Ukraine has returned to the club of ballistic missile-producing countries: what the first combat use of the FP-7 changed
articles.body:
Ukraine has returned to the club of ballistic missile-producing countries: what the first combat use of the FP-7 changed
Kyiv • UNN
Indigenous ballistic missiles give Ukraine new capabilities to strike targets at a considerable distance and reduce its dependence on partners’ long-range weapons.
The first combat use of Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile marked an important milestone in restoring the country’s own missile capabilities. After decades during which ballistic missile production in the country had effectively been lost, Ukraine once again acquired the capability to create such systems. FP-7 may now become the foundation for the further development of Ukraine’s missile program, UNN writes.
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported the first combat use of FP-7, developed by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point. The launch site and target were not disclosed, but it is known that the missile has a range of about 250 km and a warhead weighing approximately 200 kg.
Returning to the ballistic missile producers’ club
Ukraine already had its own missile industry. During the Soviet era, enterprises operating in our country produced, among other things, intercontinental ballistic missiles. After the collapse of the USSR, a significant portion of these production lines was shut down, and the missile industry declined.
We have a very powerful missile school. Even 10–20 years ago, Ukrainian rockets were launching commercial satellites into space
Therefore, the emergence of FP-7 is significant not only as the creation of a separate weapons system. Following the first combat use of FP-7, The New York Times called it "Ukraine’s return to the small group of countries that produce ballistic missiles."
What Ukraine’s own ballistic missile capability provides
The emergence of its own ballistic missile is also directly important for conducting the war. Serial production of FP-7 could expand Ukraine’s ability to strike targets at a considerable distance from the front line. As experts point out, potential targets could include command posts, ammunition depots, logistics hubs, repair bases, air defense systems, and other military facilities that Russia is attempting to move farther away from the front.
Ukraine is indeed gaining new capabilities on the battlefield. This is a new trump card. The emergence of our own ballistic missile capability changes the balance of capabilities and is of strategic importance. We will no longer merely react—we are gaining the ability to respond
According to him, if Ukraine can scale up FP-7 production, it will have greater freedom in choosing targets and will be less dependent on partners’ supplies of long-range weapons.
FP-7 could become the foundation for the further development of an entire line of Ukrainian ballistic missiles. It may be not just one specific product, but a technological base on which subsequent systems can be created—with different characteristics, ranges, warheads, and operational capabilities. The company (Fire Point—Ed.) has every chance of becoming one of the foundations of Ukraine’s ballistic missile program. It has good specialists and the relevant expertise, and, most importantly, it already has practical experience
The next stage for Ukraine could be the development of missiles with a longer range. Fire Point is simultaneously working on FP-9, which will have a greater range and be capable of striking Moscow.
Therefore, the development of FP-7 and subsequent Ukrainian missile systems could become one of the important elements of a long-term system for deterring Russia. But the key word here is serial production. Individual successful launches demonstrate technological capability, while stable mass production creates a real military capability
Thus, the first combat use of FP-7 was not simply a test of a new missile in the war for Ukraine. It marked the country’s return to the narrow circle of states capable of independently creating ballistic weapons.

articles.title: Why won’t the world call Russia’s theft of Ukrainian children genocide? A Ukrainian lawyer has the evidence, and says only the will is missing.
articles.body:
Kateryna Rashevska can trace exactly how one Ukrainian child disappears into Russia: the occupied-territory orphanage, the foster placement with a Kremlin-connected family, the re-education camp, the military uniform, the draft notice that arrives at sixteen. A legal expert at Ukraine's Regional Center for Human Rights, she has filed submissions to the International Criminal Court, documented the cases behind recent EU sanctions, and spent years building the argument that this is not only a war crime but genocide.
The law, she says, is ready. In less than five years of war, Russia has forcibly transferred at least 20,651 Ukrainian children from occupied Ukraine, a crime that has already put President Vladimir Putin and his children's-rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in the dock of the ICC. The 1948 Genocide Convention lists the forcible transfer of children as one of the acts that constitute genocide, and the ICC's Ukraine investigation has been mandated to examine the charge since 2022. More than 150 states have signed that convention. None has been willing to say the word about Russia.
"We don't need to change any legal framework," Rashevska says. "We simply still lack the political will to call the crimes by their proper names." She presses the point because, for her, justice is not an afterthought but a deterrent: "Without justice, Russia will feel this resentment in several years, and they will repeat their actions."
And the court that could deliver that justice is collapsing. The ICC is in the deepest crisis of its existence: its prosecutor, Karim Khan, removed, 13 of its judges and prosecutors sanctioned by the United States, and on 9 October 2026 the court itself sanctioned by Washington for the first time, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing to dismantle it "brick by brick." The court called the move unprecedented and warned that "history will judge this moment."
Meanwhile the children remain. Of the more than 20,000 taken, only 2,665 have been returned, as of 7 October 2026. The rest are placed in Russia's adoption system and foster homes, taught to forget they are Ukrainian, to love Russia, and to be willing to die for it: Rashevska cites 344,000 Ukrainian children drawn into the Movement of the First and 55,000 into the Yunarmiya youth army.
Euromaidan Press spoke with Rashevska on the sidelines of GLOBSEC 2026 in Prague about the machine Russia built to steal a generation, and why the world still won't name it.
Alya: You say that Russia’s forcible transfer of Ukrainian children is the crime of genocide. In international law, genocide is defined by Article 6 of the Rome Statute. What would it take to change this legal framework to include the deportation and militarization of Ukrainian children? And is the Office of the Prosecutor in any position to do that work under current US sanctions and Karim Khan’s leave?
Kateryna: We don’t need to change any legal frameworks to prosecute what the Russians are doing with Ukrainian children. Militarization and political indoctrination, as well as Russification of young Ukrainians, is a part of Russia’s bigger strategy to destroy Ukraine as a sovereign state and to subjugate everything in the Ukrainian nation to the Russian influence and control. I don’t see legal problems; we simply still lack the political will to call the crimes by their proper names.
The UN’s 1948 Genocide Convention posits that all states that signed the convention, 154 as of today, should act to stop it—not only those affected by genocide. If the international community recognized what the Russians are doing as a crime of genocide, it would mean that yet another time in history the international community was not able to prevent genocide, to recognize some early warnings, to react properly to what the Russians did, for example, in occupied Crimea or Donbas before 2022. It is not easy, and the international community and world political leaders should be mature enough to face all these challenges, recognize that they were involved in the commission of these crimes through silence and inaction, and finally stop it.
So that is why, according to the Rome Statute, the Office of the Prosecutor can start an investigation of the crime of genocide in the Ukrainian context. It is possible: the ICC’s Ukraine-situation investigation in March 2022, supported by 43 states, included not only war crimes and crimes against humanity, but also the crime of genocide. So we have all the legal tools and means, but politically it is very difficult.
Recently, there has been a global shift towards this—in the context of the war between Arabian states and Israel, not Ukraine. But for example, Israel’s attacks against Gaza’s education have already been termed "scholasticide," so as a part of the genocidal intent, as a part of the crime of genocide. So for us lawyers and human rights defenders, this is the task—to push the international community to do the same with Russia. It is not easy because Russia is one of the five "world policemen" expected to maintain this international legal order.
I believe that, perhaps in decades, but we will see how Russia’s actions will be recognized as the crime of genocide. The forcible transfer of children from one group to another group is the fifth universally recognized element of the crime of genocide.
Alya: Your organization was involved in documenting this. How does this pipeline actually work?
Kateryna: Yes, let's take Olga Druzhinina, who fostered four children from the occupied territories of Ukraine. Her story is very interesting: first, it seemed that she could be just an ordinary Russian brainwashed by TV shows about children from Donbas. But then we found that Olga is very close to [former Russian President] Medvedev, and through Medvedev to President Putin. Olga is the head of one non-governmental organization, "Semia Arktiki" [Family of the Arctic], and this organization aims to find foster parents for orphans— now including orphans from occupied territories of Ukraine. The co-head of this organization also fostered Ukrainian children.
It is a very well-built, pre-planned architecture of people involved in the commission of this crime—not some sporadic reaction to the full-scale invasion. They planned to do it. And I will not be surprised if, in the future, we find that these families also adopted children from Crimea or from Donbas even before 2022.
Her husband is a veteran of the Russian Armed Forces. He participated in many wars of the Russian regime, including the wars in Chechnya. It was clearly against the child's best interest to be sent to the family of this Russian serviceman and his wife. So their case was widely publicized. We recorded many different details. Later, we found photos of these children in the "Warrior Center" camp in Novosibirsk, and her foster daughter from occupied Ukraine wearing a St.George’s [Russian imperial] ribbon and in military uniform.
So the Ukrainian identity of these children was completely eradicated. It was prohibited to mention that they were Ukrainians, and the main goal of this family was to repress their unloyalty to the Russian state, to re-educate them, mold them into Russian patriots. Unfortunately, I don’t know the fate of these teenagers from Mariupol, but as far as I know, they were not returned to Ukraine. And now they are already young adults—meaning they will soon be conscripted into the Russian army. They have this military duty because they were forcibly given Russian citizenship. And young children also remain under the control of Olga and his husband.
Olga and her husband are members of the so-called "Putin Team." They were recognized many times as the best family of the Yamalo-Nenets region. The governor of Yamal-Nenets is also Putin's person. His candidacy was supported by Putin for re-election to this position. And this governor has many times mentioned that Ukrainian children from the occupied territories of Ukraine were accepted by foster families from his region, even without the proper documents.
It is very difficult to influence their behavior without sanctions. In this sphere of foster care, the balance between placing children in Russian institutions and Russian families is hard to find. Russia presents only two options for the forcibly transferred Ukrainian children: Russian boarding institutions or Russian foster families. And of course, ordinary people think: a family is better than a boarding institution. The truth is that there is a third option: just return these children to Ukraine, to their homes.
And I would like to highlight that, according to the order of Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, these children from institutions will not be returned to boarding institutions in Ukraine. They will inevitably be placed with a foster family, and they can participate in choosing this family or changing it. Ukraine is doing its best to guarantee that its actions comply with the Convention on the Rights of the Child, but unfortunately, Russians are very hard to persuade to return these orphanage children.
Alya: On 11 May 2026, the EU Council sanctioned 16 individuals and seven entities for the systematic unlawful deportation, forced transfer, and forced assimilation of Ukrainian children, including through indoctrination and militarized education. Your organization pushed for these sanctions. Are they working?
Kateryna: In January–February 2026, we criticized the European Union’s sanctions policy. New persons were being added to lists, but we found that the level of coordination and harmonization of sanctions policies was only 5%. Only 13 individuals and three organizations were under sanctions in all jurisdictions analyzed by us: Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, the European Union, Switzerland, and Japan. It was terrifying because sanctions exist, yet they are riddled by many loopholes and are actually inefficient.
Trending Now
That is why we started persuading them to do something with this system. And on 11 May, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union synchronized their sanctions packages: the people are included in all jurisdictions. For us, this is a big achievement.
Another achievement: a shift in their perception of where this vertical of guilty persons ends. Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova—okay; ministers, children's rights ombudspersons at the regional level, heads of the occupation authorities—okay. But what about the "ordinary" Russian people who fostered poor Ukrainian children and now contribute to their militarization? The 11 May sanctions saw the United Kingdom and Canada listing ordinary Russians, like the family from Yamalo-Nenets that fostered four Ukrainian children, including teenagers from Mariupol, and then sent them to re-education camps of the "Center Warrior" to be militarized as Russian soldiers.
If these results of our work seem small, we must remember that for the Russians, it is a very sensitive issue. They are mad because of the sanctions—and this was visible when the “Yolochka” boarding institution in occupied Crimea’s Simferopol, called a “concentration camp” by ordinary Russians, was sanctioned. Already in December 2014 [after Russia’s occupation of east Ukraine], the first Ukrainian orphans were sent to Russian foster families from this “Yolochka.” 12 years later, children from Kherson boarding institutions also went through “Yolochka.”
Alya: You've documented over 20,500 deported children. How many of that cohort are approaching Russian conscription age?
Kateryna: It is hard to tell because the way the Ukrainian side is collecting statistics is not good enough. So you should address this question to the competent bodies of Ukraine.
But according to our calculations, just to describe the situation in general: all Ukrainian teenagers under Russian control start receiving draft notices at the age of 16. According to the Russian legislation, it should be at the age of 17, but they're so afraid that these children will escape or will return to Ukrainian-controlled territories, that they start this process in violation of their own legislation.
Everything is organized around schools. They’re not about education under occupation, but have become additional buildings of the military commissariat. Specific teachers are responsible for this conscription process. Boys aged 16-17 are being brought to the military commissariat in organized groups. You cannot escape, you cannot refuse, because you will hear “knock-knock” on your door: the occupation authorities and your teacher will ask: “Where are you? You should go.”
Another problem: Russia and Belarus started exchanging data, meaning that if this child receives a draft notice at the age of 18, he will not be able to cross the border—which matters because the checkpoint of Mokrany-Domanove between Belarus and Ukraine is the main point of returning Ukrainian children from Russian control. Every year, the Russians amend their legislation to impose more obstacles to the repatriation process.
So the only way for a Ukrainian teenage boy to escape is to do this several days before a "povestka" [draft notice] comes to his house at 16 years.
According to our intelligence, since 2014, 48,000 Ukrainians from occupied territories were forcibly mobilized by Russians, including those from occupied Crimea. Some of them participated in the "special military operation.” Around 20% of all prisoners of war in Ukrainian camps for Russians are originally Ukrainians who were forced to sign a military contract. Many of them were forced, manipulated, or brainwashed, so it was not done of their own will.
But I would like to highlight that the average age of a Russian soldier is 35. This is not the war of young Ukrainians who reached the age of majority and were sent to the battlefield as cannon fodder. We see that the Russians’ main goal is to rebuild the army degraded by the Ukrainian side during the first month of the full-scale invasion, to have officers and other qualified personnel who will develop a strategy and conquer more and more territory. That is why they're investing in all these military patriotic movements and centers.
That is why I was really impressed when I saw that their All-Russian championship on drone racing will be for children aged seven. Should we next expect that children in kindergartens will assemble and disassemble a rifle? Their society is very militarized. This is the biggest problem. And now, Russian soldiers are those who are teaching Ukrainian children to fight tomorrow.
Alya: Thank you so much, Kateryna, for your time.
Read Also
- What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say Ukraine brought peace to world? Norwegian professor who nominated Zelenskyy and Ukrainians for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize takes on tough questions
- NATO no longer deters Russia. A new coalition could
- The US Army’s former commander in Europe is “withholding applause” for Trump’s Patriot pledge—and expects no interceptors before winter.

articles.title: Why South Korea and Ukraine Are Fighting Over Two Prisoners of War
articles.body:
On Sept. 23, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine spoke at the UN General Assembly about the military support Russia was getting from North Korea and the deaths of North Korean soldiers on the Ukrainian front. “Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” he revealed. He seemed to be trying to highlight the global reach of Russia’s war and also hoping that the revelation would increase popular and political support in Seoul for providing weapons and aid to Ukraine.
Zelensky ended up igniting a diplomatic dispute between Ukraine and South Korea. Seoul claimed that Ukraine had agreed to keep the transfer confidential; Kyiv denied that such an agreement existed and downplayed the episode as a misunderstanding. Now South Korea is recalling its ambassador to Ukraine.
The quarrel over diplomatic protocol highlights the human cost paid by two soldiers caught in a geopolitical conflict linking European and Northeast Asian security. Their story captures the complicated geopolitics of the two Koreas now playing out on a European battlefield. It also underscores South Korea’s push for inter-Korean peace, even as North Korea tests Seoul’s patience by launching hypersonic missiles and planting landmines.
The men from North Korea
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured while fighting in the Kursk region of Russia in January 2025. They were part of a 10,000-strong North Korean contingent reinforcing Russian troops on the front line. Shortly after their capture, Ukraine’s military released video footage of the two soldiers. The images helped confirm North Korea’s direct involvement in the Russia-Ukraine war. Human Rights Watch raised concerns about Ukraine’s decision to release the video and expose the soldiers, given the potential repercussions for their families in North Korea, including torture, forced labor, imprisonment, or execution.
North Korean soldiers are instructed to take their own lives rather than risk capture. One of the captured soldiers reportedly attempted suicide before a Ukrainian medic stopped him. In North Korea’s eyes, a soldier who survives by surrendering, or worse by defecting to the South, is a traitor. Under the regime’s well-documented system of collective punishment, three generations of a defector’s family can face retribution through guilt by association.
By revealing the prisoner of war transfer to South Korea in New York, Zelensky offered Pyongyang an incentive to make an example of these soldiers’ families to demonstrate the consequences of defection. This stands in stark contrast to the regime’s response to the deaths of North Korean soldiers in Russia. Kim Jong Un, the leader of North Korea, promised their surviving families a “beautiful life” and granted them new luxury apartments.
The North Korean regime may have already tracked down the families of the prisoners of war after Ukraine confirmed their capture in January 2025. But Zelensky’s disclosure at the United Nations renewed the danger facing the two soldiers now resettled in South Korea, a point Seoul highlighted in its protest to Kyiv. A life in South Korea offers these soldiers personal safety, but one could imagine it might come at a crushing cost: abandoning their homes and living with the guilt that their families may suffer in their place.
Mending the rupture between Seoul and Kyiv
If this episode were only about the two North Korean soldiers, their resettlement might have passed unnoticed. The diplomatic kerfuffle between Kyiv and Seoul is rooted in the different geopolitical narratives that each nation seeks to project, or in Seoul’s case, downplay.
For Ukraine, publicizing the presence and resettlement of North Korean prisoners of war provides a valuable opportunity to solicit support from South Korea, a major arms exporter and a vital partner to NATO. Since 2022, Kyiv has been urging Seoul to supply it with lethal weapons, including Patriot interceptors and 155mm artillery shells. In light of Pyongyang’s direct military support for Moscow, Ukraine has intensified pressure on South Korea to move beyond non-lethal military, humanitarian, and economic assistance.
For South Korea, Ukraine’s public disclosure of the resettlement of these soldiers undermines its diplomatic outreach to North Korea. In his address to the UN General Assembly, President Lee Jae Myung of South Korea reiterated his vision of inclusive, peaceful coexistence built on “respect for each other’s systems” and the restoration of cross-border trust with North Korea. Accepting North Korean soldiers while publicly promoting dialogue weakens Lee’s reassurances to Pyongyang that Seoul desires “stable, peaceful coexistence.”
Pyongyang has maintained silence regarding these two soldiers. But North Korea considers South Korea’s reception of defectors as part of an effort to undermine its regime and eventually bring about unification on Seoul’s terms. While North Korea now defines the Koreas as two separate states, article four of South Korea’s constitution commits the nation to “peaceful unification based on the basic free and democratic order.”
As two nations dedicated to promoting freedom and democratic principles, South Korea and Ukraine must look beyond this diplomatic disagreement to protect their partnership. Seoul provided $400 million in aid to Ukraine in 2024 and announced $2.3 billion in long-term reconstruction aid through 2027. In return, Ukraine offers critical, real-world intelligence on North Korean military tactics and the weapons technology Pyongyang receives from Russia.
Given the complex legal situation of North Korean combatants captured by Ukrainian forces, Kyiv and Seoul must establish a protocol for handling North Korean prisoners of war and non-combatant defectors who seek asylum in South Korea. The need for such a policy will only grow. Similar episodes may unfold as the presence of North Korean troops and laborers in Russia grows, increasing the potential for future defections. Zelensky recently warned that another 10,000 troops from North Korea could soon be deployed in Russia.
With Kyiv’s cooperation, Seoul should affirm its commitment to accept future North Korean prisoners who voluntarily request resettlement, subject to standard security screening. That policy must fully comply with South Korean law and uphold international humanitarian principles and the values of a democratic society. To safeguard these individuals, both governments should protect prisoners’ identities, grant confidential access to impartial humanitarian representatives, and ensure that decisions are not made under coercion. Prisoners of war should not be forcibly repatriated, and public announcements of their transfer must be avoided without their explicit consent.
Crucially, not every captured North Korean soldier will want to go to South Korea. Their wishes must be determined through private, independent interviews conducted without pressure from governments, intelligence agencies, advocacy groups, or the media. Both governments may have followed such protocols. It remains unclear whether Ukraine eventually deviated from the agreed approach script or whether there was simply miscommunication.
Yet for the two soldiers already resettled, no policy can erase the personal toll. They must now rebuild their lives in a country they were raised to view as the enemy while carrying the lingering anguish about the fate of the families they left behind.

articles.title: Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites
articles.body:
Russia is planning a winter strike campaign involving up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting, among other facilities, electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, and boiler houses. The information is contained in a document that, according to sources cited by The New York Times, Ukraine's Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented as an intercepted Russian plan to destroy energy infrastructure systematically. The newspaper reported on 2 October.
Russia has been striking critical infrastructure across Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion. Such attacks have become particularly frequent ahead of and during winter. Ukraine's recent battlefield gains may have prompted Putin to reconsider his strategy and attempt to force Ukraine to surrender through winter strikes, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggest. Russia's reported plans to attack Ukraine's energy, water supply, and sewage systems could threaten the basic living conditions of millions of people. Such strikes could increase pressure on civilians and the Ukrainian economy while forcing the state to divert more resources to emergency infrastructure repairs instead of defense needs.
The New York Times was unable to verify the document's authenticity independently, but noted that it was written in Russian and dated August.
Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy
A representative of Ukraine's defense-industrial sector who has reviewed the document believes it is more of a calculation than a finalized Russian military operations plan, according to Schemes, an investigative journalism project by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), in a report published on 8 October.
60 targets: how Russia could attack Ukraine's critical infrastructure
The document outlines how many missiles, drones, and bombs Russia would need to deprive Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa of electricity, heating, water, and sewage services, Radio Liberty reported on 9 October. The document's full list of priority cities also includes Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia, and Ivano-Frankivsk.
According to the document, Russia plans to begin by attacking substations near Ukraine's western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe. Hydroelectric power plants could be targeted next, followed by facilities intended to shut down Ukraine's three operational nuclear power plants, Radio Liberty reports. The document lists a total of 60 key targets.
According to Schemes, the document states that Russia would need up to 770 Molniya and Geran drones, Dan-T/Banderol missile-drones, 170 FAB guided aerial bombs, and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles to carry out the attacks.
Sewage systems could become Russia's next target
The document devotes particular attention to water supply and wastewater systems. These include pumping stations, treatment facilities, and other infrastructure essential for cities to provide residents with water and dispose of wastewater.
Russia has not previously attacked such facilities on a similar scale, The New York Times notes.
Preparing for possible attacks on water supply and sewage systems is significantly more difficult than protecting energy infrastructure, Oleh Popenko, head of the Ukrainian Union of Utility Services Consumers, told Current Time, RFE/RL's Russian-language network.
“Sewage is a very complex system. There are specific challenges: where to discharge wastewater, how to organize treatment facilities, and so on. Some work is also underway in this sector, but it will be much more difficult here than with district heating utilities,” Popenko says.
Creating alternative routes in case sewage pumping stations are destroyed is an expensive and technically challenging task, he adds. Such construction could cost billions of hryvnias.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
The priority is to equip water utilities with backup power sources so they can continue operating during power outages. However, if Russian strikes damage the sewage system itself, resolving the problem quickly will be much more difficult, Popenko believes. Specific solutions, including wastewater disposal and the operation of treatment facilities, will have to be determined according to the extent of the damage.
Sewage pumping stations play a particularly important role. They pump wastewater onward for disposal and treatment. If such a station is put out of operation by a strike, the city needs an alternative way to divert wastewater while the damaged facility is being repaired, Popenko says. Bypass pipes or channels could be installed for this purpose, but setting up such a system during wartime is far from easy.
Air defenses remain crucial to Ukraine's winter preparations
Preparations for winter are underway, but protection for energy infrastructure remains inadequate, Popenko believes. The main concern is large substations that transmit electricity from nuclear power plants and distribute electricity imported from Europe.
At the same time, some protective measures are already proving effective. Despite drone attacks over two days, one of Kyiv's substations withstood the strikes, and the city did not lose power, although scheduled outages were in effect, the expert says.
Popenko considers a repeat of last winter's scenario, when parts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks, entirely possible. Russian forces continue to attack energy facilities, and in his assessment, strengthening air defenses in Kyiv is the only way to protect its combined heat and power (CHP) plants from large-scale attacks.
“There are no other ways — for example, building some sarcophagi around CHPs or constructing shelters — because Russia can destroy these facilities again through massive strikes. And then the city risks being left 50–60% without heat,” Popenko believes.
Residents are also preparing for winter, but their options vary, he says. Some homeowners' associations participate in government programs to insulate apartment buildings and purchase backup power supplies for elevators and pumping stations. Owners of private houses are buying generators, among other measures. However, such equipment and preparations require substantial funds, meaning not everyone can afford them, he notes.
Ukraine has already experienced prolonged power outages during previous winters, particularly in 2022 and 2023. At the time, some regions went without electricity for 18–20 hours a day, the expert says. This experience may help people prepare for possible disruptions, but it does not eliminate the risk of further attacks and infrastructure damage.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russian Pantsir-S1 Air Defense System, Drone Launch Site and Ammunition Depots
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russian Pantsir-S1 Air Defense System, Drone Launch Site and Ammunition Depots
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense system, a drone launch site, and several military logistics facilities across Russian-controlled territories and Russia on October 8 and overnight on October 9.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported that the strikes targeted multiple military facilities supporting Russian operations against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces hit a Pantsir-S1 self-propelled anti-aircraft missile and gun system near Kudepsta in Russia’s Krasnodar region.
In the Donetsk area, Ukrainian troops also targeted a facility used to store, prepare, and launch Russian attack drones, as well as a command and observation post belonging to a Russian military unit.
