The operations extended to Russian military logistics infrastructure in the occupied territories of eastern Ukraine.
Ukrainian forces struck ammunition and military supply depots near Rubizhne, Sentianivka, and Luhansk in the Luhansk region, as well as near Vesele in the Donetsk region.
Another strike targeted a field fuel and lubricants depot near Stroitel in Russia’s Belgorod region.
The General Staff also provided an update on an earlier operation, confirming that Ukrainian forces destroyed a command and observation post belonging to a unit of a Russian airborne assault division near Ukrainsk in the Donetsk region on October 6.
The latest operations also targeted infrastructure associated with Russia’s missile program. Overnight on October 9, Ukrainian forces struck two missile-related facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region, including sites involved in missile launch systems and the dismantling of intercontinental ballistic missiles.

articles.title: How Real is the Threat of War in Europe?
articles.body:
A growing number of official bodies are warning of the possibility of Russia launching military operations against Europe. Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service said on Monday that there was an increased risk of hybrid attacks by Moscow, and Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken has said the continent faces a “dark winter” and called for drone defence to become top priority. Denmark’s intelligence service has also warned of the growing risk of a limited military attack on a Nato country in the coming months.
Disinformation and panic-mongering
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Moscow is using intimidation tactics, warns Der Standard (Austria) :
“Russia is no longer merely pressing its most dangerous weapon against our foreheads – it has long since pulled the trigger. Its disinformation has been corroding European minds for years now, sowing doubts about Ukraine’s independence – as if it were up to Moscow to decide who governs there and whether or not the country joins Nato. Worse still, Moscow’s fifth column equates perpetrators with victims and stokes fears about an enraged Russia lashing out against Berlin and Vienna if it is further provoked. ... The reasoning behind this is simple: people who feel threatened will think twice before sending weapons to Ukraine.”
Putin targeting German trauma
Putin’s war threats land on particularly fertile soil in Germany, writes the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (Germany) :
Rubio Touts US Power, Calls on Europe to Emerge From ‘Slumber’
“Whereas the war is a political instrument for Putin, for the Germans it must be avoided at any price. The traumas inflicted by two world wars and the Nazi regime run deep, shaping public opinion and security policy decisions to this day. Germans are no more than moderately willing to take up arms to defend the nation. ... Putin is also stepping up his hybrid war as a way to get the political parties in Germany to demand an end to support for Ukraine. This, too, is meant to fuel the Germans’ fear of war and undermine their already limited spirit of resistance.”
Moscow holds the trump cards for now
Political analyst Kirill Rogov warns on Facebook about the Russian weapons that could potentially overwhelm Europe (Russia) :
“Moscow has expanded its arsenal of missile-type weapons. ... This development increases the threat not just for Ukraine, but also for Europe, which right now is virtually defenceless against such missile and drone attacks. With time, Europe will mobilise its resources and develop a response to the challenges from the air. But precisely this increases the incentive for the Kremlin to use this temporary ‘window of opportunity’ to test Europe’s mettle. In other words, it increases the likelihood of an imminent escalation by the Kremlin on the European stage.”
Perilous period ahead of mid-terms
ERR warns (Estonia) :
“Nuclear weapons are Russia’s last resort. Conventional weapons will never be enough to defeat Ukraine, let alone prevail in a conflict that pits it against the whole of Europe. But before that, it will test the effectiveness of hybrid means like sabotage, assassinations, electoral interference, etc. The aim is to intimidate Europeans enough to make them either end or at least reduce their support for Ukraine. A perilous period lies ahead. Russia might feel compelled to take some sort of action against Europe ahead of next month’s mid-term elections in the US. Because these elections could drastically change Washington’s attitude towards Russia, which until now has been very tolerant.”
Zero tolerance for border provocations
According to reports from Latvia, armed individuals attempted to smuggle a group of migrants from Belarus into the country on Wednesday. Shortly afterwards, masked men reportedly entered EU territory illegally, damaging electricity distribution boxes and stealing CCTV cameras in the process. Delfi calls for effective border protection measures for Latvia and Estonia (Estonia) :
“This kind of hybrid pressure fits the picture of the Putin camp and its determination to provoke problems in the West, which supports Ukraine. All it takes is for organised criminal groups to go about their business while the Belarusian authorities turn a blind eye. ... Latvia’s border must be reinforced to ensure that such provocations fail next time. At the same time it serves as a warning to Estonia – our eastern border must also hold firm. It must be rapidly upgraded into a military protection zone.”

articles.title: Lithuania moves to lift constitutional ban on nuclear weapons: What it means
articles.body:
Lithuania’s parliament has taken the first step toward removing a constitutional ban on weapons of mass destruction being present on its territory, a move supporters say would allow the country to participate more fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements.
The Seimas voted 106-18, with six abstentions, in favour of removing Article 137 of the Constitution. The provision prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
The change is not yet final. Under Lithuania’s constitutional amendment procedure, lawmakers must vote twice, with at least three months between votes. The proposal must receive at least 94 votes – two thirds of the total – in favour in each ballot.
Supporters stress that removing the provision would not automatically lead to nuclear weapons being stationed in Lithuania. Instead, they say, it would remove a legal obstacle to participation in NATO deterrence activities, including exercises involving allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons.
Why does Lithuania want to change the Constitution?
Conservative Homeland Union leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, a former defence minister, said Lithuania’s current constitutional restrictions prevent it from participating fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans.
He noted that Estonia, Latvia, Finland and Poland do not have the same constitutional prohibition.
Under the existing provision, nuclear weapons cannot be stationed in Lithuania, and even the flight of aircraft carrying such weapons over Lithuanian territory is prohibited, Kasčiūnas said. The restriction also prevents allied vessels carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country’s territorial waters.
“Given the current restriction, we cannot participate fully in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” Kasčiūnas told parliament, describing nuclear deterrence as a central element of the alliance’s broader deterrence strategy.
Removing the ban would give Lithuania greater flexibility to participate in allied activities intended to deter potential adversaries, supporters argue.
Former Defence Minister Arvydas Anušauskas, also a conservative, said the amendment would enable more comprehensive participation in deterrence exercises, rather than necessarily leading to the deployment of nuclear weapons.
Social Democrat Remigijus Motuzas similarly argued that removing Article 137 would not turn Lithuania into a nuclear-armed state or mean that nuclear warheads would immediately appear in the country.
Would nuclear weapons be stationed in Lithuania?
Not automatically. Removing the constitutional prohibition would eliminate one legal barrier, but it would not itself authorize a decision to deploy nuclear weapons in Lithuania. Liberal Movement leader Viktorija Čmilytė-Nielsen said any future decisions on deploying such capabilities would require separate legislation.
“What specific measures will be needed for our security is something we will decide ourselves, of course together with our allies,” she said.
What about chemical and biological weapons?
Kasčiūnas rejected claims that removing Article 137 would open the door to the use of chemical or biological weapons.
He said Lithuania had ratified international conventions in 1997 and 1998 that have the force of law and prohibit the proliferation, production or use of those weapons.
Who opposes the change, and why?
Opposition to the amendment was concentrated among lawmakers from the opposition Nemunas Dawn party. Fourteen of its members voted against the proposal and two abstained.
Aidas Gedvilas of Nemunas Dawn questioned whether parliament should make such a consequential change without a public vote. He called for a referendum, arguing that alternative approaches were available.
Vitalijus Šeršniovas, a member of the Seimas’ mixed parliamentary group, proposed a narrower solution that would address the need to allow aircraft carrying nuclear weapons to fly over Lithuania without removing the entire constitutional provision.
He also argued that the issue should be decided by referendum.
Three other members of the mixed group and one lawmaker from the Lithuanian Farmers and Greens Union and Christian Families Alliance parliamentary group also voted against the amendment.
The existing Article 137 covers both weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases. The proposal under consideration would remove the provision rather than replace it with a narrower rule.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukrainian Peace Team in Florida Used as ‘Smokescreen’ for US-Russia Diesel Deal
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky delivered a blistering rebuke of Washington on Friday, Oct. 9, after US President Donald Trump struck a separate energy deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin while Ukrainian peace negotiators were in Florida – handing Moscow a massive financial lifeline to sustain its invasion.
The diplomatic contrast could hardly have been sharper. As Ukrainian officials sat down with their American counterparts in Miami to explore ways to halt Russia’s war, Trump spoke directly with the man who launched it, agreeing to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The arrangement stands to generate substantial new revenue for Moscow at a time when Ukraine and its European partners have been pressing for maximum economic pressure to cripple the Kremlin’s war machine.
Speaking to journalists Friday evening, Zelensky sharply questioned Washington’s approach, challenging how the US could credibly mediate peace while simultaneously offering Putin sudden economic relief.
Ukraine seeks ceasefire as Trump cuts deal with Moscow
According to President Zelensky, Ukraine’s negotiating team traveled to Florida to seek a pathway toward ending Russia’s full-scale invasion – or, at the very least, securing an initial ceasefire.
“Right now, our Ukrainian team, our negotiating team, is in Florida, holding talks with the American team about ending this terrible war – or, at the very least, achieving a ceasefire,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine's Inflation Jumps to 10% as Prices Post Sharpest Monthly Spike This Year
He emphasized that an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure could provide an urgent first step toward a broader de-escalation, particularly as relentless Russian strikes threaten Ukrainian homes, the power grid, and essential services ahead of winter.
“An energy ceasefire could be the first step toward a broader ceasefire. This is extremely important for our people, for our families.”
The high-level Ukrainian delegation in Florida includes Presidential Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov, First Deputy Chief of Staff Serhiy Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia. They have been holding talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, alongside representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the EU, and NATO.
But as those sensitive negotiations unfolded in Miami, Trump was pursuing an entirely different conversation with the Kremlin.
“At this very moment, while our team is talking with the American team in Florida, the president of the United States is having a conversation with the Kremlin leader – the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression,” Zelensky stated. “And they reach an agreement under which America allows Russia to export diesel.”
For Ukraine, the decision risks undermining one of the West’s most critical tools for pressuring Putin to end the war.
‘Additional money for this war against us’
Trump defended the arrangement in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, announcing that Russia had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November and 1 million tons afterward.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote, adding that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons of diesel within a short period, depending on the operational condition of its refineries.
Combined with what Trump termed “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” the US president claimed the agreement would rapidly lower domestic fuel costs.
Shortly after Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued General License 135, officially authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The sudden authorization came just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18 – legislation explicitly designed to choke off Russia’s energy revenues and financial networks. Bipartisan US lawmakers had strongly urged Washington to fully implement the law ahead of its mid-October deadlines, warning that the Kremlin was exploiting loopholes to keep bankrolling its front lines.
Zelensky warned that the financial windfall from lifting these sanctions is impossible to separate from the violence on the ground.
“This is additional money, additional money for this war against us, without question,” the Ukrainian president said. “It only fuels Putin and gives him the opportunity to wage even more war.”
“And at this very moment, when we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel,” Zelensky continued. “I don’t know whether we’re talking about millions or billions. In any case, all of it goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us.”
US fuel prices prioritized over sanctions pressure
The White House has framed the deal as a pragmatic response to severe domestic economic pressures. US diesel prices have recently climbed to an average of approximately $6.28 per gallon, squeezing truck drivers, agricultural supply chains, and American consumers.
However, energy analysts and European allies note that the initial shipment of 300,000 tons is modest compared to total US daily consumption, raising doubts about whether the deal can deliver the sweeping price relief Trump promised.
Furthermore, the decision risks severely fracturing the unified Western sanctions strategy.
For nearly five years, the US and its allies have sought to starve Moscow of the energy revenues required to pay military salaries, manufacture missiles, and sustain its occupation.
Allowing Russian diesel back into Western-regulated markets effectively rewards the Kremlin without securing any corresponding concession, such as a halt to attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace’
Zelensky reinforced his criticism in a separate statement on X (formerly Twitter), describing the sudden easing of energy sanctions as an investment in prolonging the war rather than ending it.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world,” Zelensky wrote.
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky was even more direct, calling the arrangement “not fair and not honest,” likening it to a birthday present for Putin, who turned 74 earlier this week.
Zelensky concluded his remarks to journalists by returning to what he characterized as the fundamentally unfair treatment of Ukraine’s negotiating team.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” Zelensky said. “And that is definitely unfair. It is definitely not how partners should behave.”
“And it is a weak decision. Unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners. Glory to Ukraine!”

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami
articles.body:
Ukraine strikes Russian tech giant Yandex’s data centers for a second straight day as new peace talks involving Kyiv, the U.S., and Europe get underway in Miami
Ukrainian drones attacked Russia’s Kaluga region overnight into October 9, Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He said Ukrainian forces struck infrastructure in Kaluga but gave no further details. Nine people were injured, five of whom were hospitalized.
Yandex later said its data center in Kaluga had come under drone attack. No employees were injured, but “several data center modules have been completely disabled.” The company warned that some Yandex services could experience disruptions.
This was the second attack on the Russian tech giant’s data centers in two days. Overnight into October 8, drones struck a data center in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region. A fire broke out, and the data center was shut down completely. Soon after the attack, users began reporting disruptions to Yandex services, media websites, and other services, including Avito, Ivi, Megafon, Russian Railways, and T-Bank.
Responding to the attacks, Yandex said its data centers were the company’s “iron heart” and that keeping them operational was “critical to services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”
“We understand that for our users, clients, and partners, every outage disrupts plans and prevents them from doing things they normally do in their daily lives or at work. Yandex teams are doing everything they can, day and night, to keep services running and help those affected by the incident. This is our most important task right now, but unfortunately, it isn’t easy,” Yandex said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky briefly addressed the attack on Yandex on the evening of October 8: “You all know they [Russian forces] have struck our data centers and are still striking them. We responded. I can’t share all the details.”
Russia has regularly struck data centers in Ukraine in recent weeks. Since late September, Russian forces have damaged or destroyed data centers belonging to at least eight companies. Russia’s Defense Ministry has called these strikes a “forced digital detox.”
The peace process
Ukrainian representatives will meet with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the United States on October 9 and 10. The Ukrainian delegation has traveled to Miami, where the talks will take place. Its members include presidential chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, Davyd Arakhamia, who leads the Servant of the People parliamentary faction, and Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov. Reuters reported that Washington had invited national security advisers from the United Kingdom, France, and Germany, as well as representatives of NATO and the EU.
According to Axios, Kushner and Witkoff plan to present the Ukrainian delegation with “new ideas and proposals” for ending the Russia–Ukraine war. No details were given. The two presented the proposals to President Donald Trump at a meeting on October 8.
An Axios source said Witkoff and Kushner could travel to Moscow in October for further talks with Vladimir Putin.
Shortly before the Miami talks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there were currently no prospects for a peaceful settlement of the Russia–Ukraine conflict. He said the war had reached a “strategic stalemate”: Russia continues to insist on full control of the Donbas, a condition Ukraine finds completely unacceptable.
Rubio said the situation could be resolved in only two ways: through a negotiated settlement or escalation by one or both sides.
In response, Zelensky said breaking the stalemate would require increasing economic pressure on Russia, allowing Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and refusing to reach agreements with Moscow on any future projects:
It would cost them nothing, absolutely nothing, to help Ukraine. And I’ve said frankly: Give us that. Help us defend our airspace and dominate it. Then Putin will come to the negotiating table. Why? Because he’ll lose everything. He’ll lose everything. Three months, two months — he’ll lose everything.
But instead, we’re waiting for the Chinese to develop their equivalent and hand it over to the Russians. So where’s the truth in that? Where’s the honesty? Where is any of it? What dead end? What dead end? This isn’t a dead end. It’s called unwillingness. It’s not a dead end.
In mid-September, Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure. In practice, however, that did not happen. Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Russia agreed to stop striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
The Kremlin called an energy ceasefire “a very good idea.” Sources told The Kyiv Independent that Russia had demanded U.S. sanctions relief during talks on a possible energy ceasefire. It is unclear which sanctions were involved.
The war in photographs: the aftermath of a Russian strike on Zaporizhzhia
On the morning of October 9, Russian forces struck Zaporizhzhia with aerial bombs. Mykhailo Semikin, head of the Zaporizhzhia regional military administration, said six aerial bombs had been dropped on the city. Homes and cars were damaged. According to Ukraine’s State Emergency Service, a 50-year-old man was killed and 14 people were injured.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: In Russia, Missile Systems Research Institute and Center for Elimination of Ballistic Missiles Have Been Struck — General Staff
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Armed Forces struck the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes and the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region.
This was reported on October 9 by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on its Facebook page.
The facility near the village of Dalne Konstantinovo-5 belongs to the V. P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes—a subsidiary of JSC Ground-Based Space Infrastructure Operation Center Facilities (TsENKI).
The company is engaged in the development and production of launch and technical complexes, refueling equipment, as well as ground-, air-, and sea-based missile and space complexes. This is stated on their official website.
Another facility reported as having been destroyed by the General Staff was the Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center near the village of Surovatikha in the same region.
The center is involved in the disposal of missile weapons, as well as the production, preparation, storage, and transportation of rocket fuel. In addition, the facility maintains and repairs missile delivery systems.
The General Staff noted that the strike on this facility was aimed at weakening the Russian military-industrial complex’s capabilities to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
Gleb Nikitin, governor of the Nizhny Novgorod region, confirmed the nighttime drone attack on the region. According to him, infrastructure facilities were damaged by falling debris, but he described the damage as minor.
The Russian official also reported the death of a serviceman from the Bars-NN unit, who had participated in repelling the attack alongside forces from the Ministry of Defence of the Russian Federation and the National Guard of Russia.
According to reports from the Russian monitoring resource UAV Russia, drones were detected in several districts of the Nizhny Novgorod region on the night of October 9, specifically in the Sosnovsky and Kulebatsky districts. The threat was declared neutralized at 06:39.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that on October 9, Ukrainian drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant in Russia’s Tver region, which manufactures rocket fuel components.
The TsENKI is a Russian organization responsible for operating the ground-based infrastructure of the rocket and space industry. Its structure includes enterprises that develop launch complexes, work with rocket fuel components, and maintain the relevant equipment.
The Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes was established in 2010 through the merger of two design bureaus. Its predecessors participated in the creation of launch infrastructure for the Soviet R-7 intercontinental ballistic missile and rocket and space complexes.
The Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Elimination Center in the village of Surovatikha was established in 1993 on the basis of a missile neutralization and dismantlement station. Initially, its activities were related to the implementation of agreements on the reduction of strategic offensive weapons between Russia and the United States.
In 2009, the center became part of the JSC Ground-Based Space Infrastructure Operation Center Facilities (TsENKI). The organization’s 2018 report noted that, during the facility’s operation, 448 intercontinental ballistic missiles had been dismantled, and its activities also included work to extend the service life of missile systems.
