articles.title: Zelensky and Kiev mayor trade blame over Russian strikes
articles.body:
Zelensky and Kiev mayor trade blame over Russian strikes
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has slammed Kiev city authorities for an “almost complete failure” to protect the capital’s critical infrastructure from Russian attacks, escalating his longstanding feud with Mayor Vitaly Klitschko, who blames central government corruption.
In a social media post on Friday, Zelensky reported “extensive damage” to power grids following Russian strikes and criticized delays in strengthening infrastructure defenses across Ukraine, singling out Kiev for failing to take the necessary precautions.
His remarks came a day after Klitschko urged residents to consider temporarily leaving the capital, warning that the city was in “survival mode” as winter approaches.
In an interview with AFP on Thursday, Klitschko said Kiev was stockpiling food, drinking water and fuel. He urged residents with friends or relatives outside the capital to consider staying with them temporarily. However, he ruled out a full evacuation.
The mayor issued a similar warning in January, when a severe energy crisis left thousands of residential buildings without heating in freezing temperatures. The appeal sparked a public confrontation with Zelensky, who accused city authorities of failing to prepare adequately.
Speaking to AFP, Klitschko again blamed some of the shortcomings in Kiev’s winter preparations on Zelensky’s government. Rejecting accusations that city officials had fallen behind, he argued that “finding scapegoats won’t make people warmer.”
In a separate interview with Germany’s Bild published on Wednesday, Klitschko criticized corruption scandals linked to Zelensky’s administration, warning that wartime graft was “a real poison” for Ukraine.
The dispute comes amid escalating long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine. Last week, Zelensky pledged to intensify attacks on Russian oil refineries, prompting Moscow to announce expanded strikes on Ukrainian military and defense-industrial facilities and supporting infrastructure, including in Kiev.
Moscow has said its strikes are in retaliation for Ukrainian drone and missile attacks on civilian targets inside Russia. According to Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik, 29 people, including two children, were killed in such attacks in the week ending October 4.
Klitschko warned that even extensive preparations might prove insufficient if the capital’s air defenses failed to repel further strikes.
Zelensky acknowledged a “big deficit” in air defenses on Thursday, appealing to Western backers for more interceptor missiles ahead of winter. Multiple media reports have linked shortages of Patriot interceptors in US and allied stockpiles to the US-Israeli war with Iran.

articles.title: British Nuclear Submarines to Be Protected From Drones With Fire Hoses
articles.body:
In the United Kingdom, crews of Vanguard-class strategic nuclear submarines are being trained to use high-pressure fire hoses to defend against drone attacks.
The Sun reports this, citing sources in the Royal Navy.
Fire hoses are placed on the submarines’ decks while they are docked at HMNB Clyde in Faslane, Scotland. They are intended to serve as the last line of defence against drones that manage to get past shore-based counter-drone systems.
The hoses are fitted with pistol-grip nozzles that allow crews to direct a powerful jet of water at aerial targets. According to a source cited by the publication, in the event of an attack by small and medium-sized FPV drones, crews are expected to try to shoot them down or deflect them off course.
Drones pose a particular threat to submarines when they are docked in port or operating on the surface. HMNB Clyde is located in the narrow Gare Loch, which is about one kilometre wide. The surrounding terrain, as well as the presence of public roads and hills near the base could leave defenders with limited time to respond to drones launched from close range.
The UK Ministry of Defence stressed that protecting military facilities involves a multi-layered system that includes physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, and counter-drone measures. The agency also announced an additional £470 million investment over the next four years to strengthen the security of military facilities.
Militarnyi previously reported that suspicious sensors, which may have been used by Russia to track submarines, were discovered near the routes taken by British nuclear submarines leaving HMNB Clyde. The Vanguard-class submarines, armed with Trident II D5 ballistic missiles carrying nuclear warheads, are of particular interest.

articles.title: Drone Strike Hits Russian Plant Making Fuel Components for Kh-101 Cruise Missiles
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Drone Strike Hits Russian Plant Making Fuel Components for Kh-101 Cruise Missiles
Strike drones attacked the Redkinsky Experimental Plant in Russia’s Tver region, triggering explosions and a fire at a chemical facility linked to the country’s defense industry and production of components used in long-range cruise missiles, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ on October 9.
Footage published after the attack showed drones flying over the area, followed by explosions and a fire near the industrial complex. Residents also reported hearing Russian air defenses operating during the raid.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Tver regional governor Vitaly Korolev later confirmed that a fire had broken out at the plant in the town of Redkino following a drone attack. He said employees had been evacuated to shelters in time, no one was injured, and emergency crews subsequently extinguished the blaze.
The Redkinsky Experimental Plant is one of the larger chemical manufacturing facilities in the Tver region and specializes in small-volume specialty chemicals. It produces more than 40 types of products used by Russia’s aviation, aerospace, and other industrial sectors.
Among its products are ferrocene derivatives used as combustion catalysts in solid-fuel rocket engines, as well as specialized materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives. These chemicals have applications across both civilian and military manufacturing.
According to Ukraine’s Security Service, the plant also produces components for Decilin-M, a specialized synthetic fuel used by Russian Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles. The facility is additionally linked to the production of additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
The Kh-101 is one of Russia’s principal air-launched long-range cruise missiles and has been used extensively in strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure throughout the full-scale war.
The plant’s role in Russia’s defense and chemical sectors has already drawn international sanctions. The United Kingdom imposed restrictions on the enterprise in September 2025, citing its activities in sectors considered strategically important to the Russian government and its military-industrial base.
Previously, Russia’s far northern Yamalo-Nenets region started offering mobile fire groups $12,000 for every incoming drone they destroy, underscoring growing concern over Ukrainian long-range strikes reaching some of the country’s most remote oil and gas infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Fuel Plant, Oil Depot and Yandex Data Center as Moscow Claims 505 Drones Downed
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant producing fuel for Russian cruise missiles, an oil depot near the border region of Belgorod and infrastructure in the Kaluga region southwest of Moscow overnight on Oct. 9, Russian officials and Ukrainian monitoring channels reported.
In the Tver region, which is situated between Moscow and St. Petersburg, drones hit the Redkino Experimental Plant and sparked a fire. The facility is the region’s largest chemical enterprise, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The facility manufactures Decylin-M, a specialized rocket fuel component used in Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, Kyiv Post sources within Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) said in February, after the first strike on the enterprise.
Both missile types are among Russia’s primary long-range weapons used in strikes on Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure.
Regional Governor Vitaly Korolev said the fire had been extinguished and plant employees had been evacuated to a shelter. No workers were injured, he added.
Oil depot fire reported near Belgorod
In the Belgorod region, two people were killed and four others, including a child, were injured when shells struck private homes in the Belgorod district, the regional operational headquarters said.
Following the attack, NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at an oil depot north of Belgorod, Exilenova+ reported.
Trump May Leave 100,000 Ukrainians in US Immigration Limbo Rather Than Renew Protections
The depot supplies fuel to industrial and agricultural enterprises and gas stations across the region, according to its website.
Yandex data center damaged in Kaluga
A Yandex data center in Kaluga was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack overnight, marking the second consecutive day that the Russian technology company’s data centers have come under attack, RBC-Russia reported, citing the company’s press service.
Several modules at the Kaluga facility were completely disabled, potentially disrupting some services, Yandex said.
On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones struck another Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan region, where servers host services used by the company and its clients. Operations at that facility were completely halted.
Kaluga Regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said nine people were injured in the overnight attacks across the region, five of whom were hospitalized.
Drones targeted four municipal districts and the regional capital, Kaluga. Shapsha said the drones struck what he described as the city’s “infrastructure.” Private homes were also damaged in two municipal districts and in Kaluga.
Shapsha said Russian air defenses intercepted 26 drones over the region.
Moscow claims 505 drones downed
Russia’s defense ministry claimed its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 505 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight over 19 Russian regions, occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas.
The ministry reported drone activity over Kaluga, Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Tula, Tver, Smolensk and Moscow regions, as well as Krasnodar Krai and Tatarstan.

articles.title: Ukraine reportedly targets Russian cruise missile fuel plant in Tver Oblast
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said.
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+, citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said.
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Iran slams Macron’s double standard on nuclear deterrence
articles.body:
In a post on X on Friday, Esmaeil Baghaei said that during a test of a ballistic missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, Emmanuel Macron said that in order to be free, one must be feared, and to be feared, one must be powerful.
“Yet, he himself asserts, regarding Iran, which has never sought to acquire nuclear weapons: ‘Iran must never possess nuclear weapons. Neither today, nor in five years, nor in ten years. Never.’”
The spokesperson stressed, “The question is not why France possesses a nuclear deterrent force. The real question is why a logic that guarantees France’s security and freedom suddenly becomes a ‘threat’ when it comes to Iran, including when speaking of a civil, peaceful nuclear program subject to international monitoring.”
Baghaei said the harsh reality is that “they do not want peace for all.” “They want to preserve the monopoly of power that inspires fear and the monopoly of legitimacy to intimidate.”
He added that they intend to remain powerful themselves, armed with nuclear weapons and, of course, formidable, while imposing restrictions on others, including countries that merely seek to use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, by raising the specter of a supposed “nuclear threat.”
“A peace in which nuclear powers regard their own weapons as guarantors of their freedom and security, but label the same logic a threat when invoked by others, is not true peace. It is a monopoly of power based on a sense of superiority.”
“An international order that does not recognize everyone’s right to security and peace encourages the domination of a small circle of powers more than it protects peace itself,” he concluded.

articles.title: Fought against Ukraine, now claimed to be victims: Kenya’s plea for five men held by Ukraine
articles.body:
Kenya wants five of its citizens captured fighting for Russia in Ukraine to be treated as victims of human trafficking rather than prisoners of war, Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi told Kenyan lawmakers on 8 October, Bloomberg reported. Botswana is also seeking a citizen's return.
In 2025, Ukrainian ambassador Ivan Kholostenko called Russia's role in Africa neocolonialism. As Africa Corps troops prop up friendly regimes, the Kremlin is carrying out "a typical colonial practice of resource extraction," taking gold, diamonds, bauxite, and uranium, according to Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence. Russia also uses the continent as a recruiting ground for its war: nearly 500 Africans have died fighting for Russia, Ukraine says.
Five Kenyans in a Ukrainian camp
Kenya is negotiating to bring the five men home, and President William Ruto has raised the matter with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Mudavadi told the Senate. One has been held since November 2025, the others since March and April. The youngest is 23, Bloomberg reported. Kenya's honorary consul found them held in humane conditions at the Zakhid-1 camp, with access to medical care, the government said. Ukraine also holds the remains of four Kenyans.
Victims or fighters for hire
African governments say some of their citizens went to Russia for promised work as drivers, security guards, or cooks and were then forced into military service. The Kenyans "report having been recruited under false promises of employment," Mudavadi said.
"The circumstances of their recruitment and conscription are consistent with trafficking in persons," he said.
Ukraine's POW authority sees most foreign recruits differently. "The main motive for most of these mercenaries is financial gain," Dmytro Usov, secretary of Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, said in November 2025, while stressing that many had ended up in Russia's army through fraud or coercion.
Ghana negotiates Ukrainian drone deals as 1,780 Africans fight—and die—in Russia’s ranks
Ukraine holds that prisoners of war go home through exchanges, but Russia has never asked to trade for any foreign fighter except North Koreans, the headquarters said in May, adding it may consider other solutions if diplomats and lawyers find one.
Thousands of foreigners in Russia's ranks
Russia has recruited more than 28,000 foreigners from 135 countries, and more than 5,000 have been killed, a Ukrainian government website cited by Bloomberg says. Ukraine holds at least 213 foreign prisoners of war, not counting Russians and North Koreans, 37 of them African, according to documents Bloomberg saw. Russian dictator Vladimir Putin claimed on 3 September that people are "coming forward voluntarily and signing contracts."
Kenya's government counts 354 citizens linked to the war: 84 killed or missing, 34 hospitalized in Russia, and 62 repatriated. Petitioners told senators that 841 Kenyans remain unaccounted for. Mudavadi said his March visit to Moscow put Kenya on a Russian recruitment "stop list," with no new Kenyans enlisted since.
Some African governments take steps
In August, Botswana stopped eight citizens from joining the Russian military at airports in Botswana, South Africa, and Ethiopia, Bloomberg reported.
Ghana accused Russia of luring its citizens into the war the same month, after Kenya and South Africa. The European Parliament said in March that Russia strips African recruits of their documents. Ukraine, meanwhile, is drafting its first Africa strategy.

articles.title: Raytheon wins up to $6.3B to build more SM-3 interceptors
articles.body:
- Raytheon received a contract worth up to $6.3 billion over five years, plus two option years, to produce and sustain SM-3 Block IB interceptors.
- The interceptor was first used in combat in 2024, and production will take place mainly in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The U.S. Department of War and the Missile Defense Agency have awarded Raytheon a multiyear contract worth up to $6.3 billion to build and sustain Standard Missile-3 Block IB interceptors, the ship- and land-launched missiles the U.S. Navy uses to shoot down ballistic missiles in space.
The contract runs five years with two additional option years. It was issued as an undefinitized contract action, which lets Raytheon start work immediately while final terms and pricing are still being negotiated. Neither the Pentagon nor the company said how many interceptors the contract will buy or how quickly deliveries will begin. Production will take place mainly at Raytheon plants in Tucson, Arizona, and Huntsville, Alabama.
The SM-3 Block IB is built to destroy short- to intermediate-range ballistic missiles during the midcourse phase of flight, while they are outside the atmosphere, by hitting them directly rather than with an explosive warhead. It is launched from Aegis-equipped U.S. Navy destroyers and cruisers and from Aegis Ashore land sites, alongside the larger SM-3 Block IIA. The Block IB was first used in combat in April 2024, when U.S. Navy ships intercepted Iranian ballistic missiles fired at Israel, and it has been used again during this year’s war with Iran.
Raytheon said the award supports urgent replenishment of missile defense stocks that have been drawn down in combat.
“This award underscores Raytheon’s commitment to increasing production of critical munitions, ensuring our customers have the defensive capabilities they need, when they need them,” said Raytheon President Phil Jasper. “SM-3 Block IB has proven its relevance in combat and this contract helps ensure we can replenish inventories and keep pace with the evolving threats the U.S. Navy, MDA and their partners face around the world.”
The Pentagon said the multiyear deal is meant to give industry the production certainty to invest in assembly lines, solid rocket motor suppliers and smaller domestic subcontractors, where shortages have limited how fast interceptors can be built.
“Our warfighters must never face a fair fight, and the SM-3 Blk IB has proven its operational superiority to dominate any adversary across the globe,” said Michael P. Duffey, under secretary of war for acquisition and sustainment. “This contract provides production certainty to our defense industrial base, breaks sub-tier manufacturing bottlenecks, and ensures that our fleets and combatant commands have the interceptors required to dominate the battle space.”
The award is the latest under five framework agreements Raytheon signed with the Department of War in February, covering expanded production of Tomahawk cruise missiles, AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, SM-3 Block IB, SM-3 Block IIA and SM-6 under deals of up to seven years. Last week, Raytheon received a contract worth up to $24.4 billion for SM-6 production under the same framework.
The SM-3 Block IB line had slowed before the current buildup. In March, the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon about $267 million for 23 more Block IB interceptors to restart production, bringing that order to 78 missiles, along with an $8.41 billion increase to the ceiling of a contract for SM-3 sustainment and engineering support.

articles.title: Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
articles.body:
Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
US President Donald Trump’s top envoys have begun two days of negotiations with Ukrainian and European representatives in Miami, focusing on preparations for the coming winter and potential ways to de-escalate the Ukraine conflict on terms that would be acceptable to Moscow.
Special Envoy Steve Witkoff described Friday’s discussions as “constructive,” saying US representatives had discussed prospects for a “lasting peace” with Kiev and its most hawkish European backers, including Britain, France and Germany, as well as officials from the European Commission and NATO.
The talks covered “near-term measures related to winter preparedness,” including energy resilience and grain exports, as well as longer-term security guarantees, post-war reconstruction and Ukraine’s potential accession to the EU, according to Witkoff.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on X.
Today, representatives from the United States, the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO met in Miami and held constructive discussions on potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace. The discussions covered a broad range of issues, including near-term measures related to winter preparedness (energy resilience, grains exports), security guarantees, as well as longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflicts, and support Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession. The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia. Participants reaffirmed their shared commitment to continuing diplomatic efforts toward a sustainable peace that strengthens security and creates opportunities for lasting stability and prosperity.
— Special Envoy Steve Witkoff (@SEPeaceMissions) October 9, 2026
The negotiations were scheduled to continue on Saturday, and no concrete agreements or breakthroughs have been announced so far.
The US delegation is led by Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Kiev is represented by Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, deputy chief of staff Sergey Kislitsa and senior lawmaker David Arakhamia.
The European delegation includes Bjoern Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and national security advisers from Britain, France and Germany. NATO is represented by Geoffrey van Leeuwen, chief of staff to Secretary General Mark Rutte, according to European media reports.
The talks follow reports that Witkoff and Kushner were preparing to present “new ideas and proposals” aimed at breaking the diplomatic deadlock. According to Axios, the pair could travel to Moscow later this month for further talks with Putin.
One proposal under consideration reportedly involves a partial ceasefire covering strikes on energy infrastructure, amid growing anxiety among Kiev’s European backers over the economic and energy consequences of the conflict.
“They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop,” a US source previously told AFP.
The Miami meeting also coincided with a 90-minute phone conversation between Trump and Putin on Friday, during which the leaders discussed Ukraine, Iran and a major agreement to resume Russian diesel supplies to American and global markets.
Zelensky lashed out at Trump, effectively accusing Washington of stabbing Kiev in the back by striking a separate diesel deal with Moscow. Zelensky branded the move “a weak decision by strong partners” and accused the US of using the Ukrainian delegation in Miami as a “smokescreen” while negotiating with Putin behind Kiev’s back.
Trump has repeatedly pressed Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming them for worsening a global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for American consumers. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, Trump promised Putin that he would convey Moscow’s position to the Ukrainian delegation in Miami.

articles.title: ‘We’re being used as a front,’ Zelensky says of Trump’s diesel deal with Putin
articles.body:
Russia and the U.S. have agreed on a deal to supply Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets. President Donald Trump announced the agreement on the evening of October 9 after a phone call with Vladimir Putin. Trump called the talks “highly successful.” Putin confirmed that Russia is ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. and global markets.
The U.S. said it is easing sanctions on Russian diesel. The Treasury Department has already issued a temporary license allowing sales of Russian diesel on the global market through April 7, 2027, despite U.S. sanctions. Washington previously eased sanctions on Russian oil temporarily because of a market crisis caused by the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran.
Russia has also begun lifting restrictions on diesel exports, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said. Sanctions and domestic export bans restrict exports of Russian oil and petroleum products worldwide. A ban on diesel and marine fuel exports by producers, for example, remains in effect through the end of October. Russia imposed it amid Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and a domestic fuel crisis caused by Ukrainian attacks over the summer.
Trump said the two sides agreed on the “immediate” delivery of more than 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel. Russia will supply another 500,000 metric tons in November, followed by an additional million metric tons. Novak said Russia is ready to supply additional diesel to the U.S. market as early as October. Exports are also expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after repairs.
Ukraine criticized the diesel deal between Moscow and Washington. President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media that any easing of sanctions on Russia without agreements on de-escalation shows “obvious weakness.” “Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis,” he said.
The deal comes as talks on ending the war resume. A Ukrainian delegation is reportedly meeting with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami on October 9 and 10. Reuters reported that the national security advisers of the U.K., France, and Germany, along with representatives of NATO and the EU, were invited to the talks. Axios reported that the U.S. negotiators plan to present the Ukrainian delegation with “new ideas and proposals” and then discuss them with Russia. No details of the proposals were given. “I think our team is simply being used as a front. That’s certainly dishonest, and it’s certainly no way to treat a partner,” Zelensky told reporters after the U.S. announced the diesel deal.
Russian authorities asked the U.S. to lift sanctions as part of talks on an “energy truce,” sources told The Kyiv Independent on the eve of the diesel deal. Officials in Kyiv said Ukraine was ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Russia agreed to stop striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Trump, who is under pressure over rising U.S. fuel prices ahead of the congressional midterm elections, has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil facilities. He said the attacks were causing global fuel shortages and price increases.
Putin rejected the idea of an “energy truce” with Kyiv on October 2. Speaking at the Valdai forum, he said stopping the strikes alone would not solve the problem of high diesel prices in the U.S. and around the world unless sanctions on Russia were lifted.

articles.title: Zelensky ‘doesn’t give a damn’ about Ukrainians – Russian envoy
articles.body:
Zelensky ‘doesn’t give a damn’ about Ukrainians – Russian envoy
Vladimir Zelensky’s continued attempts to target Moscow despite harsh retaliation against Ukraine’s military-related infrastructure prove that he doesn’t care about the well-being of his country’s people, Russia’s ambassador to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Dmitry Polyansky, has said.
Moscow Region came under a major aerial attack on Tuesday night, with Ukraine firing 650 drones towards the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said. Despite most of the UAVs being shot down by air defenses, the raid resulted in the death of two people. Another civilian was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the region on Thursday, according to Governor Andrey Vorobyev.
During his speech at an OSCE session in the Austrian capital, Vienna, on Thursday, Polyansky said that Zelensky “still harbors hopes of inflicting at least some noticeable damage on Moscow” in order to present this to the West as “proof that Ukraine is still capable of carrying out military operations that are painful” for Russia.
“At the same time, the head of the Kiev regime never tires of threatening Russia with escalation – something he is incapable of actually delivering – only to then complain about large-scale strikes by Russia,” he said, as cited by TASS.
Zelensky should remember the proverb that “people who live in glass houses shouldn’t throw stones,” the envoy noted.
According to Polyansky, Russian retaliatory strikes on facilities supporting Kiev’s war machine are “many times more powerful” than those attempted by Ukrainian forces. Because of those attacks, Ukraine is “losing the last remnants of its industry and infrastructure,” while also teetering on the brink of a “total energy and transport collapse” ahead of winter, he added.
Zelensky, however, “doesn’t give a damn about his citizens. His only concern is siphoning more money out of the country into the corruption system of his creation,” Polyansky said.
Ukraine has been rocked by a series of high-profile corruption scandals since last year, with the largest centering on a $100 million kickback scheme at state nuclear operator Energoatom, which was reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Zelensky. Other recent graft probes have targeted former Ukrainian ministers, prosecutors, diplomats, and senior officials.
In an interview with Reuters last week, Zelensky said he had ordered the Ukrainian military to double the number of attacks deep inside Russia, particularly against the country’s oil refining facilities.
The Russian Defense Ministry responded by announcing that “following Zelensky’s statement, the strikes... on military and military-industrial facilities… in Kiev and other regions of Ukraine will be intensified.” The ministry maintains that it never targets civilians.

articles.title: Putin offers help to end Iran war while Russia continues its own in Ukraine
articles.body:
The Russian president met Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan and pledged to do “everything in our power” to end the ongoing war between the US and Iran, despite Russia not being among the official mediators.
Vladimir Putin pledged to do "everything in our power" to help end the war between Iran and the US on Thursday, positioning Russia as a would-be Middle East mediator while continuing his own full-scale invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
The Russian president made the remarks at a bilateral meeting with his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian in Avazeh, on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast, praising Tehran for making what he called "genuine efforts" to resolve the war.
Pezeshkian said Iran and the US had exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that Tehran was reviewing and amending them before consolidating them through mediators. Despite ongoing US attacks, he said Iran would not leave the negotiating table.
"We are talking, but every time we negotiate with the United States, they attack again," Pezeshkian said. "Nevertheless, we will not abandon the negotiating table and dialogue."
He said the revisions, once finalised, would be put to mediators. "We are supposed to sit down through the existing mediators and consolidate them," he said.
It was the seventh meeting between the two presidents since Pezeshkian took office, following a phone call on 7 October — Putin's birthday — in which the pair discussed regional developments and the Iran-US negotiations.
The two previously met in person on 1 September on the sidelines of the Shanghai Co-operation Organisation summit in Bishkek.
Russia is not a mediator in the US-Iran negotiations. So far, Qatar and Pakistan have led the talks.
Ties further deepen
Military, diplomatic and economic relations between Iran and Russia have strengthened since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
The Iran war, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on 28 February, has sparked more frequent consultations between Moscow and Tehran on political and material support and financial co-operation.
Since 2022, Iran has supplied Russia with Shahed drone technology — which Moscow has since copied to create its own Geran-type variant, a key tool in its daily attacks on Ukrainian civilian and infrastructure targets — and short-range missiles.
Moscow also faces accusations of providing Tehran with targeting information for attacks on US interests in the Middle East.
Trade between the two countries rose by more than 21% in 2025 and continued on the same trajectory through the first seven months of 2026, Putin said, adding that relations were developing under a comprehensive strategic partnership agreement signed early last year.
Pezeshkian described the current situation as an opportunity to deepen co-operation and said Tehran and Moscow should coordinate "with greater speed and strength."
Billion-dollar loan delayed
Iranian state-run media reported in the days before the meeting that Russia was ready to extend a $1 billion loan to Tehran, described as the first tranche of a $20 billion package agreed at a meeting between Supreme National Security Council secretary Ali Larijani and Putin.
The semi-official IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said arrangements to disburse the sum were complete, but disagreements among Iranian authorities over how to spend the money prevented Tehran from providing the account number needed to complete the transfer.
Iran's Planning and Budget Organisation wants to use the funds to import cars and collect customs duties, the Oil Ministry wants them for oil equipment, and the Agriculture Ministry is seeking to allocate them to basic commodity imports, according to the same report.
The bilateral meeting took place on the eve of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders' summit — a gathering of nine former Soviet republic heads focused on regional co-operation — and a separate Caspian Sea environmental conference, also held in Turkmenistan, bringing together the leaders of Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Ground Robots Rescued 45 Soldiers Under Fire, Commander Says
articles.body:
Ukraine’s ground robots rescued 45 soldiers from under Russian fire and transported more than 41 tons of supplies to frontline positions during the summer of 2026, according to the Artan special unit under Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
Artan commander Col. Viktor Torkotiuk, call sign Titan, said crews operating the unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) worked continuously along the front, according to RBC-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
During the summer campaign, the platforms covered a combined distance of approximately 4,258 kilometers (2,646 miles), with tasks ranging from supporting frontline logistics to evacuating wounded Ukrainian troops and transporting captured Russian soldiers.
Robots enter areas too dangerous for vehicles
The ground platforms allowed Ukrainian forces to evacuate wounded troops from exposed positions without sending additional personnel or conventional vehicles into areas monitored by Russian drones.
Torkotiuk said the drones help free up valuable resources.
“Technology is transforming the combat capabilities of units on the front line,” Torkotiuk said. “Innovative logistics frees up capabilities and forces for active operations and offensive actions,” he added.
The unit did not specify how many vehicles took part in the missions, how many individual journeys they completed, or which ground-robot models they used.
Ground robotic systems vary in size and configuration. Some transport ammunition, food and other supplies, while others can carry wounded soldiers, conduct reconnaissance, clear mines or operate mounted weapons.
Russia Steps Up Production of Improved Su-34 ‘Fullback’ Bombers
Ukrainian troops have said such platforms are particularly useful inside the so-called kill zone, where ordinary evacuation vehicles can quickly be detected and targeted by surveillance and attack drones.
Frontline soldiers have previously told Kyiv Post that robots are not replacing troops but are increasingly performing the most dangerous logistical and medical evacuation missions.
Artan operates in Zaporizhzhia and near Lyman
Artan said its main area of operations is currently the Zaporizhzhia front in southern Ukraine, a region where over 70 percent is under Russian occupation, most of which since 2022.
The unit also participated in one stage of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi near Lyman in eastern Ukraine during the spring and summer campaign. The operation recovered at least 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory and disrupted Russian attempts to advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Analysts suggest the operation has reversed Russian gains made in 2026 and thwarted Moscow’s goal to capture eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
The HUR special operations unit was formed on June 1, 2022. Its personnel have fought in some of the war’s most contested areas and participated in land and Black Sea operations, including the 2023 campaign that helped open the road to Klishchiivka and create an escape route for Ukrainian forces encircled by the Russians in the Donetsk region’s Bakhmut.
Ukraine expands its robotic army
Ukraine is rapidly increasing its use of ground robots to reduce the number of soldiers exposed during supply runs and casualty evacuations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky set a target to provide the military with at least 50,000 ground robotic systems by 2026.
The systems are becoming a regular part of frontline operations as Ukraine seeks to compensate for personnel shortages and adapt to a battlefield where drones can detect and attack conventional vehicles several kilometers behind the contact line.

articles.title: Trump rules out Iran strikes as Pentagon draws up plans
articles.body:
(Getty Images)
The Pentagon has drawn up plans for an intensive three-day military campaign against Iran, the U.S. media reported on Oct. 8, even as President Donald Trump said Washington will not launch an attack before the Nov. 3 elections.
The U.S. military, acting on Trump’s orders, has developed options to strike Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, energy facilities and other military sites, The Times reported, citing U.S. officials.
Senior national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed the plans at Camp David last week, with the options centering on a short, intensive campaign lasting about three days, according to people briefed on the proposal.
The strikes would focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which has been rebuilt by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) since the early phase of the war, the newspaper said.
Other potential targets include Iranian energy facilities as well as IRGC command posts and headquarters.
Axios separately reported that the Pentagon ordered the US Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran.
The directive did not set a date for strikes and Trump had not made a final decision, Axios said, adding that any renewed major combat operations were expected to include large-scale bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets.
The military preparations come as Trump said on Oct. 8 that the US would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while pointing to ongoing diplomatic efforts.
“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections,” he wrote.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Washington and Tehran were having “productive discussions.”
Trump’s announcement on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to the elections.
The New York Times also reported that Trump has repeatedly declined proposals in recent months to resume major combat operations against Iran, despite ordering the Pentagon to prepare new options.
Three U.S. aircraft carriers are expected to be in the Middle East in the coming weeks as part of the major military buildup, according to the newspaper.

articles.title: Trump Makes Deal With Putin On Diesel Exports. Ukraine Calls It A 'Gift'
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump said he reached an agreement with President Vladimir Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a move Ukraine immediately criticized as a "gift" to the Kremlin.
Seeking to contain soaring energy prices, Trump said in a social media post on October 9 that the two leaders agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.
The move will see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote.
Diesel futures fell about 4 percent after the announcement but remained more than 110 percent higher than at the start of the year. Brent crude traded at around $104 a barrel, down just 0.3 percent on the day.
The decision came as Ukrainian, US, and European officials held talks in Miami aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. The discussions concluded without a breakthrough.
The waiver drew critical comments from Kyiv to lawmakers in Washington, who warned that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its war against Ukraine.
It also raised questions about US policy toward Russia following Trump’s recent signing of legislation intended to tighten sanctions against countries supporting Moscow’s energy trade.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis."
To enable the flow of diesel, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing the sale, delivery, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
Trump said that after the initial flows, Russia would supply a further 3 million tons “within a short period of time.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow was ready to increase supplies in October, with exports expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.
Diesel prices have climbed since the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran in February, sparking a conflict that is now in its eighth month.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing prices higher and urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian energy facilities.
“The problem I have with Ukraine and Russia is that, you know, a lot of the diesel comes … from Russia, and the Russia plants are being hit by Ukraine,” Trump told reporters recently.
Ukrainian officials have said they are prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Moscow halted its recent barrage of strikes on Ukraine’s energy and other civilian infrastructure installations.
As Ukraine’s negotiating team was in Florida, Zelenskyy also questioned the purpose of the Miami talks while Washington was allowing Russia to earn money from fuel exports.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” he said.
Earlier on October 9, Zelenskyy welcomed a bipartisan delegation of US senators to Kyiv and called for stronger pressure on Moscow.
Meanwhile, on Capitol Hill, the waiver for Russia drew the ire of several lawmakers.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia’s war economy is terrible,” Republican Representative Don Bacon told RFE/RL.
Democrat Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the bipartisan Russia sanctions legislation, called the decision an embarrassment, arguing that it would benefit Russia and China while undermining congressional efforts to pressure Moscow.
“This poorly concealed attempt to mitigate the havoc caused by Trump’s illegal war in Iran will only benefit the Chinese & Russian economies & lead to the slaughter of more innocents in Ukraine,” he wrote on social media.
Blumenthal called the agreement “a stain on our nation’s character” and said it ran counter to Congress’s intent in its recent passing of a sanctions bill.
He also warned US companies considering purchases of Russian fuel: “Congress is watching.”
Daniel Fried, a former US diplomat and sanctions expert, also criticized the timing of the waiver.
“General License allowing sale of Russian diesel, proceeds of which support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Not a promising start to the imminent talks on ending the war,” Fried said in a social media post.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior Treasury Department official who worked at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, said the move showed Trump was prioritizing the Iran conflict and its economic consequences over pressure on Russia.
“The Russia legislation put the onus, and the ability to act, in President Trump's hands,” Bitsoff told RFE/RL.
“Today's diesel license shows Trump is prioritizing the Iran conflict over pressure on Russia, and he likely doesn't intend to use a lot of the authorities in the bill,” she said.
Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said the waiver could also undermine Trump’s argument that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries were the main driver of rising diesel prices.
“If limiting diesel sanctions on Russia provides market relief then it’s clear the primary impact to the global diesel market was the Iran conflict and blockade, not Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, which would have had a secondary impact,” Vlasiuk told RFE/RL. “It lines up with price timelines.”
The decision also raises questions about the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has agreed to withdraw from Ukraine, recognized Ukrainian sovereignty, and poses no threat to NATO.
Supplied materials from officials on the decision does not establish how that provision applies to the new license.
The Miami discussions, initially expected to last two days, concluded on Friday, October 9, according to US envoy Steve Witkoff.
Representatives from the United States, the E3 group of European countries, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO held “constructive discussions” on ways to de-escalate and end the war before winter.
Witkoff said the agenda included winter preparedness, energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees, longer-term security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe, and support for Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction and eventual European Union accession.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on social media.
The Kremlin said Trump and Putin had also discussed prospects for resolving the war during their phone call, alongside the situation surrounding Iran and other bilateral issues.

articles.title: It became known how many Russian military personnel and pieces of equipment the Armed Forces of Ukraine eliminated on the front over the course of the day
articles.body:
It became known how many Russian military personnel and pieces of equipment the Armed Forces of Ukraine eliminated on the front over the course of the day
Kyiv • UNN
Russia lost 1,710 military personnel, 1,757 drones, 67 artillery systems, and 617 vehicles over the course of the day. Total losses reached 1,549,490 personnel.
Over the past day, October 8, the Russian army lost another 1,710 military personnel killed and wounded. Russia’s total personnel losses since the beginning of the full-scale invasion have reached approximately 1,549,490. The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
Details
According to the Ukrainian command, over the past day the Defense Forces destroyed 1,757 Russian operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles, 67 artillery systems, and 617 vehicles and fuel tankers.
In addition, the occupiers lost 3 tanks, 7 armored combat vehicles, 5 multiple rocket launchers, 1 air defense system, 18 ground robotic systems, and 4 pieces of special equipment.
Total losses of the Russian army as of October 9
Since the beginning of the full-scale war, the Russian army has lost 12,402 tanks, 25,509 armored combat vehicles, 50,950 artillery systems, 2,199 multiple rocket launchers, and 1,693 air defense systems.
Ukrainian forces have also destroyed 443 Russian aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,908 ground robotic systems, 555,335 operational-tactical unmanned aerial vehicles, and 5,126 cruise missiles.

articles.title: Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
articles.body:
Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
US media reports suggest he may be weighing strikes before the vote but the president has ruled that out.
United States President Donald Trump has said that he does not intend to bomb Iran again until the November midterm elections, even though several US media outlets have reported that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to relaunch attacks before that vote.
Trump has been accused of misdirection on the issue in the past. The US launched its initial attacks on Iran on February 28, as talks with Iran were ongoing and despite Trump saying just the day before that he had not made any decision. One year previously, the US struck Iran towards the end of Israel’s June 2025 12-day war, despite Trump saying he would announce a decision about attacks “in two weeks”.
Still, striking Iran ahead of the midterm elections would be risky for the administration as the war remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
Resuming the war afterwards may have less of a negative impact on Trump, who is not eligible to run for another term as US president anyway.
Here’s what we know about Trump’s plans.
What has been reported by US media?
In the past two days, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and other publications have reported claims by unnamed officials that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to attack Iran before the midterms, if authorised to do so.
On Wednesday, US publication Axios cited US and Israeli officials saying the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command (CENTCOM) to prepare for imminent major combat operations. The Atlantic also reported along similar lines.
What has Trump said?
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social media platform that he will not order a resumption of strikes on Iran before November 3, when the US midterm elections will be held.
“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition…we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” he said.
The president added that the US is presently “having productive discussions” with the Iranian side. However, that was also the case on February 28, the day the US and Israel first struck Iran, triggering the war.
Trump did not make any reference to preparing for potential military operations, nor did he provide more details on the state of talks.
Why might Trump be hesitant about resuming bombing before the midterms?
Trump and Republicans are worried about a voter backlash against the war at the polls. The US war on Iran is intensely unpopular domestically as Americans have had to grapple with surging prices of gas, food and other basic commodities because of the crisis in the Middle East.
Since the start of the war, surveys have shown that large numbers of Americans did not approve of striking Iran.
Now, about 65 percent of Americans say they “disapprove” of the way in which Trump has handled the Iran war overall, according to a Pew Research Center poll released on Thursday. Trump stated at the start of the war that it would go on for just a few weeks, however, it is now into its eighth month.
According to Pew, most Americans now believe the war will continue for at least another year. Even Republican or more conservative-leaning voters are growing more negative about the war, its poll found.
The conflict has also severely affected Trump’s personal ratings and eroded support for Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos poll on Thursday found that only 30 percent of his supporters were enthusiastic about voting in the midterms, compared with 48 percent of Democratic voters.
About 13 percent of those who voted for Trump in 2024 say they are not sure who to vote for in the congressional elections.
Delaying attacks until after the elections could potentially shield Republican candidates from voter backlash, analysts say.
While analysts say Trump will see a good performance at the polls as approval for renewed strikes, a Republican defeat at the polls could equally further incentivise him to hit Iran again as he will calculate that he has little to lose at that point.
While that could further affect Trump’s ratings, the president is not eligible to run in the next presidential election in any case.
Will the US restart the war after the midterms?
In recent weeks, the US president has threatened to “end” the war with force after the elections as talks with Iran have dragged on.
At a Republican convention in September, he accused Iran of trying to affect the outcome of the midterms and said that conflict “is going to end immediately after the elections”.
In an interview with Time magazine two weeks ago, he also said it would be “possible” to ramp up bombing in Iran after the elections, but declined to elaborate. Analysts say his comments were designed to calm voters, while at the same time warning Iran of potential aggression after the vote.
Last week, the US military dispatched about 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines aboard several ships now sailing to the Middle East amid threats of new attacks from Trump. The vessel formation included the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group.
The deployment increases the number of US troops in the region to 20,000, alongside hundreds of aircraft and at least three carrier strike groups.
In the past, US troop build-up in the Middle East and the Caribbean has subsequently resulted in military action.
In June, Washington and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement that quickly broke down over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump has repeatedly said that the US has the upper hand in the strait, citing more oil exports and Iran’s weakened economy. He has also voiced aversion to a deal with Tehran over management of Hormuz, but said he might consider it because “they’re willing to offer us anything to stop”.
Washington rejected a recent proposal from Iran to reopen the strait based on certain conditions it wants the US to meet, including the lifting of sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and guaranteeing an end to attacks. Last week, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran was considering a counterproposal from the US.

articles.title: Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed, Rogers spar over Iran, Israel
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Michigan Senate debate: El-Sayed and Rogers spar over Iran and Israel
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers traded barbs on Thursday over Iran and Israel during their first televised debate in the race for Michigan’s open Senate seat, ahead of November’s US midterm elections.
Held in Grand Rapids, Michigan, the debate opened with both candidates being asked whether they would support a pause on the federal petrol tax amid rising fuel prices linked to the war with Iran.
Fuel prices have surged since US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February triggered the conflict, adding to concerns over the cost of living among American voters.
Both candidates backed a pause on the federal petrol tax before turning to their respective positions on the war.
Rogers, who initially supported the US offensive against Iran, has since called for the months-long conflict to end.
The Republican Senate candidate reiterated that position during the debate, as did El-Sayed, who has repeatedly criticised the Trump administration over its handling of the war.
The Democrat also blamed the administration for Iran’s decision to close the Strait of Hormuz, a critical international trade route.
“This is what happens when you start wars you never should be fighting,” El-Sayed said.
“We literally taught the Iranian regime that they have a choke on the Strait of Hormuz, and now we’re living in that reality.”
Although Rogers agreed that “we need [the war] to come to an end”, he defended the military campaign, arguing that US attacks had set Iran’s uranium enrichment programme back by “twenty years”.
His remarks echoed claims by the Trump administration that military action was necessary to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Tehran has repeatedly denied US and Israeli accusations that it is seeking to develop nuclear weapons.
The Islamic Republic maintains that its nuclear programme is peaceful, while insisting that it will not compromise on its civilian nuclear activities or make structural concessions without the lifting of US economic sanctions.
El-Sayed criticised Rogers for his support of the war and for defending the Trump administration, accusing him of changing his position for political reasons rather than out of concern for Americans’ financial circumstances.
"The reason he’s flip-flopping has nothing to do with policy, has nothing to do with your costs. Has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers,” El-Sayed said.
He added moments later: “Weak, cowardly, won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.”
El-Sayed and Rogers clash over Israel
During the debate, El-Sayed faced questions over his criticism of Israel’s genocidal military campaign in Gaza, following his recent refusal to say whether he considers Israel or Iran a greater threat to the US in an interview with US cable news network NewsNation.
The candidates hold opposing positions on US military assistance to Israel, which has received more US foreign aid cumulatively than any other country since the Second World War.
Rogers reaffirmed his support for continued US aid to Israel, while El-Sayed called for an end to military assistance, arguing that American taxpayers’ money should instead be directed towards domestic priorities such as education and healthcare.
“He wants unconditional support for a foreign government,” El-Sayed said of Rogers. “I want unconditional support for kids in our schools, unconditional support for our healthcare, childcare.”
The Democrat also blamed Israel for drawing the US into military action against Iran.
“I don’t want to be pushed into war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in war with Iran,” El-Sayed said.
Rogers, meanwhile, argued that Israel had “the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood”, reiterating his support for the country.
“Is there anything Israel could do that would lose your support?” debate moderator Rick Albin asked.
“Listen, if they’re talking about using nuclear weapons, they would definitely lose my support,” Rogers replied.
Rogers targets El-Sayed over Muslim identity
Beyond their disagreements over foreign policy, the candidates repeatedly traded personal insults.
El-Sayed described his Republican rival as “weak”, “cowardly” and a “sock puppet for the Trump administration”. Rogers, in turn, called his opponent a “glitchy AI chatbot” who was running a “con” and would “say anything to win”.
The pair also challenged each other over campaign donations and their personal finances.
El-Sayed lambasted Rogers over a waterfront property he owns in Florida, while Rogers pointed to a rental property owned by El-Sayed’s wife in the United Arab Emirates.
According to Albin, the candidates continued arguing even when the cameras were off. The moderator repeatedly urged them to maintain order, telling them to “work with me” and adding: “I appreciate your passion, but please, let's try to keep this orderly.”
The debate also covered the trade dispute with Canada, immigration, healthcare, and the cost of living.
However, some of Rogers’ attacks arguably fixated on El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and alleged associations with extremist groups.
El-Sayed has repeatedly faced Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, with Trump leading attacks on the Democrat, including labelling him as an “extremist, terrorist sympathizer”.
Trump also claimed his history “goes back to the days of the Jihad” in a post on Truth Social.
During the debate, a discussion about healthcare led Rogers to claim that El-Sayed had “taken money from individuals on his campaign who openly support Hamas, Hezbollah, al-Qaeda”.
The former US congressman also challenged El-Sayed over his opposition to surveillance cameras operated by Flock Safety, arguing that the technology had helped apprehend people suspected of terrorism.
Rogers then suggested that El-Sayed’s concerns about the cameras warranted further scrutiny.
“Why would that bother you?” Rogers asked. “Well, if you have somebody in your family that might be on the terrorism watch list...”
El-Sayed interrupted, challenging Rogers to make explicit the implication he appeared to be suggesting.
“Are you going to go ahead and say that I’m a – go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said. “You’ve been tiptoeing about it the whole time. Just say it. Just say it. Go ahead and say it.”
The exchange comes amid repeated attacks on El-Sayed’s Arab and Muslim identity during his campaign, highlighting wider concerns about Islamophobia directed at Muslim and Arab candidates in US politics.
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the US Senate.
Michigan Senate race could shape control of Congress
A CBS News poll published earlier this week showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 45.6 per cent to 41.4 per cent, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
The race is among those expected to help determine which party controls the Senate following the midterm elections.
The elections will shape the final two years of Trump’s presidential term, with Republicans facing the prospect of losing their current hold on Congress amid the president’s declining popularity and the fallout from the war on Iran.
Trump himself has been holding numerous rallies to potentially reverse the party’s political fortunes.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Strike Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant, a Rocket Fuel Component Manufacturer
articles.body:
Strike drones attacked the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant in Russia’s Tver region overnight on October 9. The facility manufactures chemical products used by Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on this.
Footage published online shows strike drones flying overhead, followed by explosions and a fire near the plant. Local residents also reported Russian air defense activity in the area.
Tver region governor Vitaliy Korolyov confirmed that a fire broke out at the plant in the settlement of Redkino following a drone attack. According to him, the plant’s employees were evacuated to a shelter in time, and no one was injured. The fire has since been extinguished.
The facility is one of the major chemical industrial sites in the Tver region.
The plant produces specialty chemicals in small batches and manufactures more than 40 types of products for the aviation, aerospace, and other industries.
Its products include ferrocene derivatives, which are used as combustion catalysts in solid-propellant rocket engines, as well as specialty materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives.
According to the Security Service of Ukraine, the plant manufactures components for the special fuel Decilin-M, used in Russia’s Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
In September 2025, the United Kingdom imposed sanctions on the facility. The British government cited its activities in Russia’s strategically important defense and chemical sectors as the basis for the restrictions.
Militarnyi previously reported that the Redkino Experimental Chemical Plant was targeted twice by strike drones in a single night on June 27, 2024.
At the time, Russian sources reported that plant personnel had been evacuated, while Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that four drones had been intercepted over the Tver region.
The plant was also targeted in September 2023 and, according to monitoring channels, in February 2026.
