articles.title: NATO asks Russia ‘not to worry’ despite earlier threats
articles.body:
NATO asks Russia ‘not to worry’ about nuclear drills
NATO has asked Moscow “not to worry” about the US-led military bloc’s upcoming nuclear warfare drills, despite weeks of escalated war rhetoric from its member states, which are ostensibly preparing their populations for a war with Russia.
NATO’s forces will practice responding to launch orders, flying mock nuclear delivery sorties, and maintaining communications under the stress of nuclear war during its ‘Steadfast Noon’ exercises from October 13 to 23. The drill will involve 17 of the bloc’s 32 member states and will not involve live nuclear weapons.
This year alone, bloc forces have run three separate exercises on the borders of the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, after which Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski suggested a further buildup of NATO forces in the area in order to keep Moscow “uncertain of what we will do.”
The Kremlin issued a stern warning in response, stating that Russia is “ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad.”
The message apparently fell on deaf ears. On Wednesday, Estonia’s foreign minister claimed that NATO possessed the ability to close the Baltic Sea “within hours,” strangling Russia’s economic “lifeline” and creating an “existential” crisis for the country. Last week, Swedish Air Warfare Centre chief Colonel Carl Bergqvist said his country’s warplanes were ready to attack targets deep inside Russian territory in the event of a conflict with Moscow.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and European governments insisted in recent weeks that Russia is waging a “hybrid war” against the West. The accusations are by their nature unprovable, and have been described by analyst Thomas Fazi as a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, in which “Europeans are being subjected to a sustained campaign of cognitive or psychological warfare aimed at conditioning them to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia.”
NATO’s nuclear policy director, Nassima Barrows, told Politico on Thursday that the fact that the drills are held every year should serve as “a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry.”
Despite Burrows’ reassurances, and NATO’s description of Steadfast Noon as “not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country,” some of the bloc’s leaders evidently view their nuclear weapons as a tool with which to threaten Russia. After watching the test-launch of France’s latest nuclear-capable ballistic missile on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron released a video of the test, describing it as “a clear message…for wherever it must be received.”
Russia read the message “loud and clear,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded, adding that Russia will take “all necessary measures” to protect its national security.
During his speech at a session of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Vienna on Thursday, Russian envoy Dmitry Polyansky reiterated that Moscow “threatens no one and has no intention of attacking anyone.”
At the same time, however, the country “cannot ignore the development of plans by NATO for a direct military clash with Russia, nor the bloc’s simulation of scenarios involving a military-political blockade of Kaliningrad Region,” he stressed.
“Our response to any unfriendly moves will be swift,” Polyansky said, urging NATO not to test Russia’s patience or push the European continent “toward the point of no return.”

articles.title: Ukraine, Europe, US to meet in Miami for talks on ending war
articles.body:
Ukraine, Europe, US officials to meet for talks to end war
October 9, 2026
Ukrainian and European officials are set to meet US President Donald Trump's envoys in Miami on Friday to discuss "new ideas" to end Russia's war in Ukraine.
Ukraine's President Volodomyr Zelenskyy confirmed the meeting on Thursday evening, after a Russian attack on buses killed 30 civilians in the frontline city of Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.
Before the strikes in Kramatorsk, a Russian missile hit a five-storey apartment block in the northern Chernihiv region, killing 22 Ukrainians, including five children.
More than 70 people have been killed in Russian strikes on Ukraine in the past two days, Zelenskyy said.
What did Zelenskyy say about the Miami meeting?
"The Ukrainian negotiating team is due to meet Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in the US tomorrow," Zelenskyy said. "The meeting is expected to last two days. We are also counting on a European team to join our negotiating group."
Zelenskyy's chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, and other top officials, including Rustem Umerov, Sergiy Kyslytsya and David Arakhamia, will also attend, the Ukrainian president said.
"They will discuss new ideas and proposals that American negotiators began developing with the Russians and Ukrainians during their recent visit to the region", one of the US sources familiar with the talks told AFP.
"They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop," the US source said.
Zelenskyy blames US for inaction
Amid rising civilian casualties and fears of further escalation, Zelenskyy urged the US to accede to his request to expand Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite service, which would help it target Russian ballistic-missile launchers.
"Open Starlink for Ukraine. You did open it when you were responding to Iran ... I've said quite openly — give it to us, help us defend our skies and dominate there. And then Putin will sit down at the negotiating table," he said.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse the US of being unwilling to pressure Russia into negotiations, adding that enabling Starlink would cost Washington nothing.
"So where's the truth here, where's the honesty? Where's the stalemate? ... That's called unwillingness," he said.
Ukraine president rejects Rubio claim that war is deadlocked
Zelenskyy was responding to remarks on Wednesday from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said the war in Ukraine was at a stalemate.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that he agreed with Rubio's assessment, adding that he saw no immediate prospect for a three-way summit between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Zelenskyy and Trump.
"One cannot, on the one hand, negotiate with the Russians about future economic projects, whilst on the other hand say that we find ourselves in some sort of ... diplomatic stalemate," Zelenskyy said, countering the US narrative. "We are not a diplomatic dead end," he said.
Zelenskyy also called for tougher sanctions to cripple the Russian economy, a point Ukrainian officials are expected to press US envoys on at the meeting.
Edited by: Karl Sexton
If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

articles.title: How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice
articles.body:
How life has changed in a Moscow suburb where Ukrainian drones hit the same apartment building twice
On September 20, 2026, Ukraine launched another large-scale drone attack on the Moscow region. One drone hit a high-rise apartment building in Kotelniki, southeast of Moscow. Another had struck the same building in June. Neither strike killed anyone, but the attacks badly frightened many people in the neighborhood. Reporters from Bereg, a cooperative of independent journalists, visited the Novye Kotelniki residential complex to see how repairs were progressing after the two attacks and how residents had responded. Meduza is translating their report in full.
‘People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up’
Drivers struggle to find parking in this densely populated neighborhood in Kotelniki, outside Moscow. Shoppers wait in short lines at grocery store checkouts. It’s a warm, sunny weekend day, yet the courtyard of the Novye Kotelniki residential complex is unusually empty.
On September 20, a Ukrainian drone struck one of the complex’s high-rise buildings for the second time. The first strike came on June 18, 2026. The drone crashed into almost the same spot on the courtyard side, in the upper third of the building, and exploded.
A black scorch mark stands out against the beige-and-brown exterior, with a hole at its center. All that remains of the balconies on floors 19–22 is twisted metal and rebar. Some of the facade tiles have broken off.
The few residents walking in the courtyard occasionally look up at the building and whisper to one another. Many decline to tell Bereg how the constant drone alerts have changed their lives. “What is there to say?” says a woman of about 40 in a black hijab, waving off the question, though she had just been discussing that very subject with a friend.
Olga, a blonde woman in a trench coat, comes out of a neighboring building with her two-year-old daughter. She says this is their first walk in the courtyard since the recent attack.
This time, she says, the property management company quickly cleared the broken glass and other debris from the courtyard. But she’s still scared: “You never know, she could pick up a piece of glass or something. You’re more scared for her than for yourself.”
On the day of the attack, Olga woke to explosions at four in the morning. She woke her husband. At first, he thought she was imagining things, but then he heard the explosions, too. Deciding it wasn’t safe to stay in their apartment, they carried their sleeping daughter downstairs to the ground floor, where neighbors had already gathered.
Olga stayed in the lobby until eight in the morning. Throughout that time, she could hear explosions outside. “It was a nightmare: People were shaking, children were crying, older people’s blood pressure was shooting up, and we were all looking for medicine for them,” she tells Bereg. “You feel like you’re in a war zone, and you can’t believe this is happening to you.”
Olga missed the summer attack — her family was away. Perhaps that’s why, unlike many of her neighbors, she hadn’t put a “go bag” with documents, medicine, and other essentials in her entryway. Before the September attacks, she had felt less anxious than others. Afterward, she no longer felt safe.
Still, her family’s daily routine hasn’t changed. She and her husband decided against moving their bed farther from the windows, figuring it wouldn’t save them. “Look at the size of that hole,” she says, gesturing toward the damaged high-rise.
“You keep thinking: God, what if it happens again tomorrow?” Olga says. “I was on sedatives for two days. I definitely don’t feel safe here. I’m stressed every day.”
Her family is considering moving, but unless the attacks become more frequent — “not once or twice, but practically every day” — she and her husband are unlikely to “seriously start looking into it.” Olga hopes things will “get back to normal” because “they [the Ukrainians] have already hit what they wanted to hit, and now they’ll calm down.” She means the Moscow oil refinery, the Ukrainian military’s target. But the high-rise stood in the path of the drones flying toward it.
A few things help Olga manage her anxiety: She’s become even more absorbed in caring for her child and stopped reading the news, although she used to scroll through neighborhood chats even at night. “There’s so much noise now, so many planted stories, so much fake news,” she says. “Even the [real] news — there’s so much of it. You watch all this, and the whole situation keeps playing over in your head. What for?”
Ruslan, who lives in the same complex as Olga, takes the opposite approach: He tries to read all the news. He says the drone attacks don’t make him anxious.
“I knew there’d be an attack — the elections and all that,” Ruslan says. He says the neighborhood has only been quiet for the last few days. Before that, neighbors often heard air defenses in action at night and early in the morning.
On September 20, Ruslan and his family counted “at least 40 explosions.” “We could see flashes in the sky from our window — almost like the ones over Israel!” he says excitedly. “There were about 10 a minute at one point.” He saw the drone crash into the neighboring building. He and his family were about to head out into the stairwell when they heard a loud noise outside the window and red light flooded the apartment.
Like Olga, Ruslan doesn’t have a “go bag,” and he says he won’t be getting one. He sees no need, because “our air defenses have gotten better at their job.” “Yeah, there are screwups. Unfortunately, they can’t intercept everything. But overall, our guys are doing their job, and they’re doing it well,” Ruslan says. “Every day on my way home from work, I see the air defense systems changing locations.”
He tells Bereg he believes there won’t be any more strikes on the neighborhood because they’re no longer worth it for Ukraine: “They launched so many, and the results were really poor. They understand it’s a waste of money.”
With a smirk, Ruslan recalls wondering during the first attack whether the target might have been the apartment building rather than the refinery — “maybe some general lives here.” But he quickly dismissed the idea: First, it was a large-scale attack, and second, “what general would live here?”
Ruslan believes Moscow and its immediate surroundings are now “very well protected” and that the authorities should focus on deploying air defense systems in other regions. That’s his only complaint about the security measures. “I think our government will take care of us, and everything will be fine. Our army will handle it,” he says. “Maybe I’m not that well informed, or maybe I’m too optimistic. But I think everything really is fine.”
The toll of Ukraine’s October attacks on the Moscow region
The next large-scale attack on the Moscow region came overnight on October 6. It struck communities northwest of Moscow, damaging private homes and nonresidential buildings in settlements in the Solnechnogorsk, Volokolamsk, Istra, and Domodedovo districts. Ukrainian Telegram channels that monitor attacks and the Russian outlet Astra also reported a fire at the Volodarskaya oil depot, southeast of Moscow. The Ukrainian strikes and Russian air defense operations killed two people and injured nine.
Ruslan’s school-age daughter looks at him admiringly. They chuckle together as they recall a neighbor who panicked during the latest attack. “Run, run, we’re under attack!” Ruslan says, imitating her, though he quickly adds that “everybody’s different.”
His daughter says that after the summer attack, one of her classmates transferred to another school — her family had decided to move. “They were renting [their apartment]. Maybe if we rented here instead of owning, we’d feel better about moving, too,” Ruslan says. “Plus, we’ve got a mortgage here — where are we gonna go?”
‘I’ll be working to pay the rent. I’m just scared to live here.’
A man in a black jacket, probably an employee of the property management company, walks through the courtyard with a ring of keys. He unlocks a door marked “Shelter” leading to the basement, looks inside, locks it again, and moves on to the next building. Each of the complex’s more than 20 high-rises has a shelter.
Residents of Novye Kotelniki say the management company told them the basements are kept locked because they contain “technical equipment that the engineers are responsible for.” In the event of a real threat, residents are to call the dispatch office. A staff member will then come during the attack and unlock the basement door. The company promises this will happen quickly.
But on September 20, residents of some buildings complained in the neighborhood Telegram chat that they hadn’t been able to get into the basements until after seven in the morning, although the large-scale attack began at four.
Signs reading “Shelter” have been hung at the basement entrances, but the management company has done little to equip the rooms, residents say. Some have benches; others don’t even have those, leaving people to sit on the concrete or stand.
Aleksandra, a resident in her mid-40s, is smoking near the entrance to one shelter. Asked how she feels about the increasingly frequent attacks, she says emphatically: “It’s really bad, really bad!”
Aleksandra lives in the building that drones have struck twice. Or rather, she used to — after the recent strike, she realized she was afraid to stay in her apartment. “As they say, what happens once might never happen again, but what happens a second time…” she says.
Aleksandra was home during both attacks. On June 18, she and her husband woke to repeated explosions and began getting ready to go to the shelter. As she was tying her sneakers, a drone crashed into the building. “I hear this huge bang — and plaster starts falling down in our apartment!” she tells Bereg. “I opened the door, and there was already smoke in the stairwell. We didn’t know if we’d be able to get downstairs.”
No one opened the shelter, and neighbors crowded onto the ground floor. “It all ended around eight, and that’s when they opened the basement,” Aleksandra says indignantly. “Well, what’s the point of going down there once it’s all over?”
On the day of the second drone strike, Aleksandra again heard “a lot of activity” as explosions kept going off. First, she went out onto the communal balcony to take a look. From there, she could see several fires near the Moscow oil refinery, the Mega shopping mall, and the Sadovod market. She was horrified. “I wake my husband up: ‘Get up, there’s a real war out there — everything’s burning, everything’s in flames!’” she says.
To reach the stairs, Aleksandra and her husband had to pass through the communal balcony. As soon as they opened its door, there was a loud explosion, and a wave of heat hit them. “I knew it had hit the building,” she says. “Something went bang, and things started falling.”
As we talk in the courtyard, there’s a crash in the distance, quiet but distinct. Aleksandra flinches and abruptly turns toward the sound.
“I think something fell at the construction site.”
“I react like that all the time now [to sudden noises],” Aleksandra says. “My nerves are completely shot. I went a week without proper sleep, even with Novo-Passit, glycine, and things to calm me down. I’d sleep for two hours, then be awake again.”
On September 20, Aleksandra and her husband waited for the explosions to stop, went back up to their apartment, packed everything they needed, and left for their dacha. They’re staying there temporarily but return to their apartment in Novye Kotelniki every few days.
“We’re living out of bags: one in the car, one at the dacha, and one here. We come back, wash up, do the laundry, hang it up, and head back out,” Aleksandra says. “We try to get everything done as fast as we can. They’ve just posted [on Telegram channels] again that apparently another large-scale attack is expected. Who knows?”
But they can’t stay at the dacha for long: It has almost no amenities, and the trip to work takes three hours. Driving every day proved too expensive, so they switched to public transportation.
Aleksandra took out a mortgage to buy her apartment. She has no other home and no relatives who can take her in. Now she’ll have to pay both her mortgage and the rent on a new place in a safer neighborhood. “I’ll be working to pay the rent. What else can I do?” she says with a sigh. “I don’t know what I’ll eat, but I’m just scared to live here.”
“Looking at the windows, I could tell that lots of people had left — almost no one was still here,” she says. “Today we packed up a bunch of bags and took a heater. And everyone coming toward us had bags, too. People are leaving, and no one wants to come back.”
‘I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here.’
Far fewer people go into the high-rise hit by the two drone attacks than into the other buildings. Many residents emerge carrying large bags — clearly, they’re leaving for a long time.
The lobby has two entrances: one from the courtyard, the other from the road. The courtyard entrance is now cordoned off with barriers wrapped in red and white tape. The concierge warns that residents can’t leave through that door, either. A chair braces it shut from inside, and a sign on it reads: “No entry! Risk of death!” It doesn’t explain the danger.
Another notice asks residents not to use the elevators between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. so they can be available to “construction workers repairing the building.” Residents ignore the request, and there are no workers in sight.
Residents say that for the first few days after the attack, the elevators ran only in the evenings. Those with apartments on the upper floors of the 25-story building had to take the stairs or enter through the neighboring stairwell, use the elevator there, and cross the roof to reach their own building. The management company temporarily opened access to the roof for that purpose. The elevators are now running, and access to the roof has been closed off again.
On many floors, boxes and bags of belongings are scattered about, along with plastic-wrapped crates of toys, black bags of construction debris, window frames, packages of building materials, and parts from household appliances.
The smell of smoke still lingers on the fifth and sixth floors. On September 20, burning debris landed on a windowsill and started a fire. On the upper floors, it smells of burned plastic.
The 21st floor suffered the worst damage. Workers had to remove the front panels from one elevator and the structure surrounding the shaft opening. A padlocked grille has replaced the door separating the elevator lobby from the apartments. The apartment the drone struck is on this floor.
Georgy, whose name has been changed, was home in a neighboring apartment at the time. He and his wife, Yelena, whose name has also been changed, were about to head downstairs when he heard an unusual humming sound from the direction of the balcony. “I go over to the balcony and realize it [the drone] is getting closer, but I can’t see it. I can’t figure out where it’s coming from,” he tells Bereg. “I look down — and there it is, coming from the direction of the quarry, heading straight at me.”
Georgy managed to shout to Yelena to run. He didn’t have time to get out of the way himself. The drone hit the neighboring apartment and exploded. The blast wave and a hail of fragments hit him.
His arms and legs were badly cut. Bleeding heavily, he got dressed and pulled on his sneakers. His wife retrieved their cat, which had hidden under the bathtub. They grabbed a bag of documents and jewelry they had prepared in advance and ran downstairs.
“If it had flown just a little higher, that would’ve been it — we wouldn’t be talking now,” Georgy says, visibly shaken as he looks at his bandaged wrists. “The explosion was unreal. I’d never experienced anything like it in my life. I wouldn’t wish that on anyone.”
The couple went to the home of friends who lived nearby. From their friends’ window, Georgy saw an ambulance arrive at the complex. He went over to the medics himself for first aid and to have them “record [him] as one of the injured.” A few hours later, the couple returned to their apartment for belongings, then went back to their friends’ home. After that, they went to Yelena’s relatives’ home, where they’re now staying.
Georgy shows photos of the wrecked apartment on his phone. The stretch ceilings have melted. The windows and balcony are gone, and everything is covered in soot. Furniture and appliances have toppled over, and fragments and pieces of the walls are scattered everywhere. After what he’s been through, Georgy tries to avoid going to Novye Kotelniki unless he absolutely has to. He arranged to meet Bereg’s reporter at a shopping mall in Moscow.
“I thought the same place wouldn’t get hit twice. Turns out it doesn’t work that way here,” Georgy says. It wasn’t until several days later, he says, that he fully realized “what could have happened.” It’s been hard to cope with. The other day, he went to get a haircut, and the buzzing of the clippers made him uneasy.
“I barely slept for three nights. I asked my doctor to prescribe something to calm me down, but it’s still pretty tough,” Georgy says. “It’s okay, we’re strong, we’ll get through it. I think time heals.”
Moscow regional authorities are working out how to repair the apartment and pay compensation, but Georgy is avoiding those subjects for now. Over the past week, he’s had to return to the apartment several times to let in specialists who are to assess the damage from the attack, as well as local administration representatives and officers from the Investigative Committee, Russia’s criminal investigation agency. Those visits convinced him that he could no longer live in the complex, even if the building were fully repaired.
“When you go back there, you start shaking — the atmosphere’s different, the aura’s different,” he says. “I’ve developed a phobia of the place, so I want to get everything sorted out as soon as possible and put this nightmare behind me.”
Georgy’s neighbors are collecting signatures for a petition to the management company and the authorities. They’re demanding additional protection for the building that drones have now hit twice.
“It feels unfair that they can’t keep our homes or our lives safe. You don’t feel very safe in your own capital,” Georgy says.
He believes the air defenses can’t handle the number of drones flying toward Moscow. He sees only one way to guarantee an end to the attacks:
It wouldn’t hurt to end this military operation. One decision — and it would all be over.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Seeing Systems unveils Reaver drone carrier
articles.body:
A British company has launched an uncrewed vessel designed to carry, launch and recover as many as a hundred strike drones, controlled with the boat itself through a single command and control layer, the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday.
Matthew Le Maitre, chief technology officer at Seeing Systems, introduced the vessel at the end of a capability presentation. “Today, I am proud to announce that Seeing Systems stands ready to meet the challenge posed by this new paradigm,” he said. “Apex, please meet Reaver.”
Reaver 101 combines the strike power of UAVs with the endurance of an uncrewed surface vessel, and one command and control layer covers both sea and air for the whole mission. Maximum range is 2,000 nautical miles, it operates far from shore without a support ship, and it moves by road or inside a C-17 to wherever it is needed.
The four payload fits shown covered littoral strike against targets ashore, anti-surface strike against enemy vessels at sea, reconnaissance drones pushed out ahead of the force, and offshore air defence using interceptors against one-way attack drones. Reconfiguration is quick. “When the threat changes, the payload changes. The vessel does not,” Mr Le Maitre said.
“An adversary has no way of knowing which Reaver is doing which job, so every one of them has to be treated as an all-capable threat,” he said. “That is the decisive advantage of autonomous mass. It forces the enemy to solve thousands of problems at once.”
“Mass on its own is a useful advantage,” he said, “but it only becomes truly decisive if it can be controlled effectively. A thousand platforms that each need their own crew are not mass, they’re a manpower problem.” Autonomy allows one team to set the vessels’ routes and the drones’ tasks from a single interface.
The waters a Reaver would fight in will be jammed, spoofed and hostile. Navigation continues when GPS is denied, using inertial dead reckoning cross-checked against radar, and when communications degrade the system steps down through defined levels of autonomy so the mission continues until the link is restored.
The vessel carries its own autonomous deployment and retrieval system, designed and built by the company, which launches drones while the boat is under way and recovers them for reuse. “Recovery capability is what turns a single strike into a sustained operation,” Mr Le Maitre said, adding that the system has already launched and recovered drones at sea in trials.
Open architecture and standard drone protocols allow new airframes and sensors to be integrated without redesigning the vessel. Production runs on live lines in the United Kingdom, the hull from a partner that has already delivered uncrewed boats to the Royal Navy, and the drones from the company’s own lines. “The capital ship takes a decade to build. Reaver’s production lines are already running,” he said.
Mr Le Maitre built the case for the vessel on the cost of the ships it is meant to supplement. “For centuries, navies have measured their power by the size of their capital ships, and since the Second World War, the aircraft carrier has been the capital ship around which the rest of the fleet has been built,” he said. “Capital is a highly relevant word here. In today’s money, each of the Royal Navy’s two Queen Elizabeth class carriers would cost close to 4.6 billion pounds.”
“Now they are undoubtedly extraordinarily capable ships, but these vessels are so important to the Royal Navy that they also represent an extraordinary target. Our adversaries know that, and they plan accordingly. Protecting them effectively is now one of the hardest problems the fleet faces.”
Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed an asymmetry that upends the warfighting conventions of this century, in his account, and cheap mass-produced uncrewed systems are overwhelming platforms that used to dominate. Improvements in AI targeting and swarming will make those weapons more lethal over time, and efficiencies in mass production will make them cheaper.
“Iran has been severely disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz for over seven months, despite the US Navy committing three carrier strike groups to the region,” he said. “They’ve achieved this via a combination of drones, mines, small boats and USVs.” Iran managed it with a degraded green water navy and an air force heavily damaged by joint American and Israeli strikes.
“Just as Ukraine proved on land, Iran is proving at sea that the new asymmetry can be leveraged to frustrate a much stronger military adversary,” he said.
The arithmetic he showed sets one carrier against 4,600 fully armed Reavers. Each is designed to carry up to 100 Havoc strike drones carrying a two kilogram high explosive payload apiece, which across the fleet comes to 460,000 strike drones and more than 900 tonnes of warheads.
“An adversary facing an aircraft carrier has one rather large target to find and eliminate,” he said. “An adversary facing a comparable Reaver fleet has 4,600 targets to contend with.” Losing one costs a fraction of a per cent of the force, in his account, and “the rest of the force keeps fighting.”
The capital ship made sense while manpower was the limit on fielding mass, he argued, and autonomy has removed that limit.
“The Royal Navy has already announced its strategic shift to a hybrid navy,” he said. “We believe that Reaver will be an integral part of that new navy. Reaver will be ready to defend the UK as we move into a more uncertain world.”

articles.title: Zelensky Warns Against Easing Russia Sanctions as US Authorizes Russian Diesel Sales Through 2027
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced in a post on Truth Social Media that Russia agreed to supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets. Another 500,000 tons would follow in November and 1 million tons after that.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote, adding that Russia would then deliver 3 million tons of diesel within a short time, depending on the condition of its diesel refineries.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Combined with what he called a “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” the deal would quickly bring down diesel prices for Americans and the rest of the world, Trump claimed.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The new license came only three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, appearing to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as networks close to Putin.
Hours before the license was issued, President Volodymyr Zelensky appealed to the visiting US lawmakers to enforce the law, as it remains crucial for ending the war.
The move also gives Moscow something it had openly demanded. In late September, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russian diesel could flood international markets – but only if it reached them without sanctions or restrictions.
Sybiha Presses WTO Chief on Black Sea Shipping, Remote Audits
Since July, Russia has banned nearly all of its diesel exports, after Ukrainian drone strikes managed to halt a large share of its refining capacity.
Meanwhile, Trump has repeatedly pressed Kyiv to ease those strikes, pinning the blame on Ukraine for record diesel prices instead of the US-Iran war.
Zelensky warns against sanctions relief
Zelensky argued that easing sanctions on Russia without a clear and durable de-escalation agreement would be a sign of weakness that benefits Moscow. “In my view, this is a weak decision,” he said.
The Ukrainian president appeared to respond directly to Trump’s announcement. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” he said.
Zelensky also pointed to the EU’s decision to delist two Russian oligarchs – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman – both closely connected to Putin and the Kremlin’s war effort.
Since that move, he said, Russian strikes and terror of civilians have only intensified.
When the US lawmakers asked what it would take to end the war, Zelensky listed three conditions:
- enforcement of sanctions under the law championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham
- support for Ukraine in protecting lives
- and sustained pressure on Russia over the war.
De-escalation offered – again
Zelensky reiterated that Kyiv is prepared to take de-escalation steps that match Russia’s own, and that the American negotiating team is aware of this position.
Zelensky framed Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries and other oil facilities as a response to Moscow’s years-long campaign against Ukraine’s power grid. Halting them, he said, would depend on Russia ending its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Moscow, however, has repeatedly rejected such arrangements. In the very few times it had agreed to a ceasefire, it failed to honor it, with attacks resuming immediately.
The president stressed that any easing of the conflict must be reciprocal rather than one-sided, and pointed to Russia’s results on the battlefield. In his view, Russia is relying on strikes against civilians to make up for its failure to reach its military goals.
This year, he said, Russian forces are weaker on the front line than at any earlier point in the war.
“That is exactly why Putin relies on terror. That is exactly why he relies on attempts at backroom deals on one or another easing of pressure on Russia, to buy more time and more opportunities for war.”

articles.title: Defense Intel Chief: Russia targeting Ukraine's railways and Dnipro bridges in escalating strike campaign
articles.body:
Defense Intel Chief: Russia targeting Ukraine's railways and Dnipro bridges in escalating strike campaign
Moscow has introduced a new tactic and is attempting, through extensive long‑range strikes, to break Ukraine's infrastructure and the population's psychological resilience, says Col. Ants Kiviselg, head of the EDF Intelligence Center.
Kiviselg said at Estonian MoD briefing on Friday that in the battlespace, the downward trend in the number of combat contacts has continued, Russia continues to suffer heavy losses, and both sides continue long‑range strikes into each other's rear areas.
During this week, about 200 combat contacts per day have taken place, he noted.
"The most intense fighting has occurred in the same areas as in recent weeks: in Donetsk, the Pokrovsk and Konstantynivka directions; in Kharkiv oblast, the Southern Slobozhanske direction; in Zaporizhzhia, the Hulyaipole direction; and in Donetsk also the Lyman direction. Ukraine's counterattacks have continued in the Kupiansk direction in Kharkiv oblast, and in Donetsk in the Sloviansk, Lyman, and Kramatorsk directions," Kiviselg said.
"Losses of the Russian Federation have remained at an average of around 1,700 soldiers per day, which means the sixth consecutive week with more than 10,000 killed or wounded fighters per week. In response, Russia is slightly changing its behavior pattern: attempts are being made to break Ukraine's unity with intensive and very long‑lasting long‑range strikes," the military intel chief said.
Kiviselg pointed out that on 4 October Russia announced its intention to intensify long‑range strikes on Ukraine, and during the past 241st week such strikes hit various targets in 13 Ukrainian oblasts, followed in many places by power outages.
Ukraine setting up air defenses
Russia also repeatedly attacked bridges over the Dnipro River — both in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia — attempting to intimidate civilians, hinder everyday life in Ukraine, and thereby affect the economy.
"In Kyiv, air‑defense systems operating with artificial intelligence have begun to be placed to protect the bridges, and alternative solutions are being sought in case traffic on the bridges is halted for a longer period; the possibility of installing pontoon bridges over the Dnipro river is also being examined," Kiviselg said.
Kiviselg noted that according to Ukrainian data, about 330 educational institutions in Kyiv have been damaged in airstrikes during the war — roughly one‑third of all educational institutions there — and in the first eight months of this year, 107 educational institutions have been hit.
"Ukraine's rail transport is also in a very difficult situation. More than 500 locomotives have been damaged during the war, and this year alone 60 percent of them have been hit. Attacks against railway infrastructure are 40 percent higher this year than during the entire year 2025. So we see that Russia has intensified attacks both against educational institutions and against railway and transport hubs," Kiviselg said.
"Ukraine, for its part, has carried out medium‑ and long‑range strikes against Russian fuel‑industry facilities in Volgograd, Nizhny Novgorod, Samara, and Moscow oblast. Military‑strategic targets have also been attacked in occupied areas in Krasnodar, and in Bryansk and Oryol oblasts, and in the Republic of Adygea," he said.
Russia's fuel exports diminished
According to Kiviselg, the impact of Ukraine's long‑range strikes has begun to clearly appear in Russia's fuel exports. If in 2025 Black Sea ports exported an average of 200,000 tons of fuel per week, then according to public data this transport fell to zero in the third week of September. "Russia's diesel and gas‑oil exports are currently taking place through the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk and amount to about 81,000 tons," Kiviselg said.
Kiviselg said that between 1 and 30 September, Ukraine liberated, according to public sources, 25 to 80 square kilometers of territory, compared with last September, when Russia occupied 258 square kilometers.
"The trend is changing significantly, and last September Russia did not suffer such extensive losses as this year. Speaking of Operation Vivaldi, which began by the Ukrainians in late spring, it is likely that much larger areas have been liberated there — we are talking about more than 100 square kilometers," Kiviselg said.
Kiviselg emphasized that the Russian Federation has not come any closer to its stated goal of occupying the entire Donetsk oblast.
"Large personnel losses reflect rather that unit leaders and commanders on the ground are trying to fight their way to lines that have already been reported to higher leadership as occupied areas. We will likely see similar intensity in the coming weeks — perhaps intensity will decrease, but personnel losses on the front will continue. From this we also see that Putin's statements, as if Russians had additionally occupied 1,300 square kilometers during September, are not true; these are rather doomed attempts by commanders to achieve previously advertised results," Kiviselg commented.
--
Editor: Aleksander Krjukov, Argo Ideon

articles.title: NATO to hold major nuclear exercise amid escalating rhetoric with Russia
articles.body:
NATO to hold major nuclear exercise amid escalating rhetoric with Russia
NATO is seeking to reassure Russia that its upcoming nuclear exercise in Italy is nothing to fear, despite heightened tensions between the alliance and Moscow.
Source: European Pravda, citing Brussels-based politics and policy news organisation Politico
Details: NATO announced on 8 October that 17 member states would take part in its annual Steadfast Noon exercise, which will run from 13 to 23 October. This year's drills come amid a tense exchange of letters between Moscow and NATO after the allies held an exercise near Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast in August.
"We have been doing this every year and… this is also a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry. This is predictable and there is no reason to miscalculate," said Nassima Barrows, Deputy Director of Nuclear Policy at NATO.
"Its purpose is really essentially to train our allied forces so that we are ready and prepared, and we ensure the safety and security of our nuclear capability," she said.
Following a previous NATO exercise, Moscow sent the alliance a letter threatening to strike allied territory and referring to the possible use of its nuclear arsenal. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte publicly condemned the move last week.
Tensions are mounting as European countries are accusing Russia of carrying out sabotage and intensifying so-called hybrid attacks across the continent.
"Our intention is to really keep things calm," a senior NATO official said. Russian officials "keep ratcheting up this mood of tension and we are going to keep trying to calm the mood", they added.
US Army Colonel David Bull, Chief of NATO's Nuclear Operations, said the exercise would involve a "similar" number of participants as in previous years. It would cover everything from "simulated alert to [a] live flight exercise", but "no live nuclear weapons".
Dual-capable aircraft and ground personnel will also take part to support the exercise and practise aircraft loading, refuelling and maintenance procedures, a senior NATO military official added.
Background:
- It was previously revealed that Russia had handed NATO a document stating the possibility of using its entire available arsenal, including nuclear weapons, in the event of an attempt by the Alliance to isolate Kaliningrad Oblast.
- NATO responded by emphasising the defensive nature of the Alliance and calling on Russia to stop its irresponsible nuclear rhetoric.
- NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte emphasised that Russian leader Vladimir Putin knows he will never be able to defeat NATO.
- Lithuania described the new Russian threats regarding Kaliningrad as psychological pressure.

articles.title: Zelensky discusses Graham Act, anti-ballistic missile production with U.S. congressional delegation
articles.body:
Zelensky discusses Graham Act, anti-ballistic missile production with U.S. congressional delegation
President Zelensky announced this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
“I am grateful to the U.S. congressional delegation – Roger Wicker, Senator Kevin Cramer, Congressman Marc Veasey, and Congressman Dan Crenshaw – for being here with our people today amid virtually nonstop Russian attacks. Russia is not getting what it wants on the battlefield and is trying to make up for it through escalation,” Zelensky said.
According to him, an air raid alert remained in effect throughout the meeting in Kyiv because of the threat posed by jet-powered Shahed drones. The President stressed that in Kyiv alone, since the beginning of this month, Russian forces have damaged two schools with such drones and struck bridges, energy facilities and other critical infrastructure.
“We can only protect ourselves from this terror by working together, and we discussed how the United States can help save lives. Of course, we expect the Lindsey Graham Act to be implemented. This is a matter of political will, and it is now important to show leadership and fully cut off the financial flows sustaining Russia’s war machine,” Zelensky emphasized.
The sides also discussed other necessary steps, including accelerating licensing for the production of missiles for Patriot systems.
“Ukraine is ready not only to produce ballistic missile interceptors for its own needs, but also to strengthen the United States and its allies through joint production,” Zelensky stressed.
He thanked the United States for its unwavering support.
As Ukrinform reported, a bipartisan U.S. congressional delegation in Kyiv expressed support for expanding Ukraine’s access to Starlink capabilities and coverage.
Photo: Office of the President of Ukraine

articles.title: Pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk arrested in Montenegro
articles.body:
A leading pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger with reported ties to Russia’s intelligence services has been arrested in Montenegro, after warnings of attempts to destabilise the Balkan country, officials have said.
Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Rybar war blog, was detained on Friday alongside his wife and three other Russians by police and security agents in the Adriatic resort town of Risan, on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, local media reported.
Montenegro’s prime minister, Milojko Spajić, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X, saying it followed warnings that the country would face attempts at destabilisation and hybrid warfare.
The Montenegrin news outlet Vijesti reported later on Friday that Zvinchuk and the other detainees were to be expelled from the country on national security grounds.
The Russian Telegram news channel Baza said officers detained Zvinchuk at the luxury Mövenpick hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica, Montenegro’s capital, for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.
Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram. It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East. More recently, it has been accused of amplifying far-right narratives surrounding the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in north Africa.
“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation. Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released,” the channel said on Telegram.
Britain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine. The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.
The US has separately accused Zvinchuk of attempting to interfere in the 2024 presidential election, offering a reward of up to $10m for information about those involved.
Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban. He mocked a border guard who, he said, had searched his belongings but failed to check his name against a database.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow was aware of Zvinchuk’s detention and would work to secure his release.
Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev suggested Moscow could detain European and American citizens to use in prisoner exchanges to secure Zvinchuk’s release. “We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots in order to get our own people back,” he wrote on social media.
The arrest is likely to further strain relations between Montenegro and Russia, which have long been tense. In 2016, Montenegrin authorities accused Russian operatives of plotting with Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, allegations Moscow denied.
Montenegro, which joined Nato in 2017 and is seeking membership of the EU, imposed sanctions on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The country recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens from 1 November, closing off a popular holiday destination for Russian tourists as it brings its visa policy into line with the EU.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia will never break Yemen’s resistance: Ansarallah leader
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia will never break Yemen’s resistance: Ansarallah leader
TEHRAN — Speaking on the tenth anniversary of the Saudi airstrike on Sanaa’s Great Hall, Ansarallah leader Sayyed Abdul-Malik al-Houthi declared Thursday that Riyadh’s decade-long war to subjugate Yemen has collapsed into a strategic failure.
The October 2016 massacre, which left roughly 1,000 mourners dead or wounded inside a crowded funeral hall, remains a stark monument to Saudi war crimes carried out with direct American support.
The Ansarallah leader emphasized that every governorate across Yemen has suffered identical atrocities, with civilian homes, markets, and schools systematically targeted in a failed effort to force submission.
Al-Houthi dismantled the Saudi monarchy’s religious posturing, arguing that its claim to guard Islam’s holiest sanctuaries rings hollow.
The sword emblazoned on the Saudi flag has never drawn blood in defense of Muslims, he observed, but has consistently served Zionist and American ambitions to fragment the region and isolate the Resistance Front.
The address coincided with a sharp escalation on the ground.
On Thursday, the Yemeni Armed Forces shot down a Saudi-operated Turkish Bayraktar Akinci drone over Taiz and launched a ballistic missile strike at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, disrupting flight operations and triggering widespread alarms.
Parallel missile strikes hit Saudi troop concentrations at the Qa’wah camp near Ras al-Ara and positions along the Bab al-Mandab approach, inflicting dozens of casualties and detonating enemy ammunition depots.
Addressing regional governments, al-Houthi issued a direct warning to Qatar regarding its renewed political and media alignment with Saudi policies.
He reminded leadership in Doha that its previous involvement in the coalition against Yemen did not prevent Riyadh and Bahrain’s Al Khalifa regime from plotting regime change in Qatar and imposing a suffocating blockade.
Assisting Saudi Arabia now, the Ansarallah leader cautioned, makes Doha complicit in war crimes while exposing it once again to betrayal by its alleged allies.
Al-Houthi affirmed that Yemeni forces hold full operational authority to strike enemy assets across the Red Sea and Arabian Sea from any point in the country.
Rebuffing Western media claims, he placed full blame for maritime instability on Saudi and American militarization around Bab al-Mandab.

articles.title: Trump strikes deal for over 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel despite sanctions
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for more than 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel, a dramatic shift in U.S. policy toward Moscow as Washington seeks to ease soaring fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections.
The announcement came just weeks after Trump signed sweeping sanctions legislation targeting Russia's energy sector over its war in Ukraine, raising questions about Washington's commitment to maintaining economic pressure on the Kremlin.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly afterward. An additional 3 million tons would be delivered within a relatively short period, he said.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote on social media.
Shortly after the announcement, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a temporary license easing sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The authorization allows Russian diesel loaded onto tankers as of Friday to be supplied to global markets without triggering U.S. sanctions until April 2027.
The White House did not immediately clarify who would pay for the shipments, when the fuel would become available or whether deliveries scheduled for November would arrive before the November 3 elections.
The agreement comes as the war in Iran continues to disrupt global energy markets. According to AAA, the average price of diesel in the United States reached $6.23 per gallon Friday, after hitting a record $6.52 on September 22.
Zelensky: ‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace’
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky sharply condemned the agreement, warning that increased Russian energy revenues would help Moscow finance its continued war against Ukraine.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," Zelensky wrote on X.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," he added.
The Kremlin said the Trump-Putin phone call focused on prospects for resolving the war in Ukraine and also addressed developments in Iran.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev welcomed the agreement, saying cooperation between Moscow and Washington on diesel and energy would benefit the world.
The announcement also drew criticism from Democrats. Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called the decision "infuriating" and accused Trump of undermining sanctions intended to weaken Russia's war economy.
The latest Treasury authorization follows several temporary exemptions granted to Russian energy shipments since the outbreak of the Iran war. However, it marks a more substantial relaxation of restrictions, extending beyond the shorter waivers previously issued.
For Moscow, the agreement offers an opportunity to expand energy revenues despite Western sanctions. For Kyiv, it represents a potentially damaging reversal of efforts to constrain Russia's ability to finance its invasion.

articles.title: ‘Obvious weakness’: Zelenskyy criticizes Trump-Putin diesel deal over lack of de-escalation
articles.body:
Burç Eruygur
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Friday that easing sanctions on Russia without a de-escalation deal would be an "obvious weakness," following a diesel supply agreement announced by US President Donald Trump after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In a statement on US social media platform X, Zelenskyy said he had received a bipartisan delegation from the US Congress in Kyiv earlier Friday.
He said he called for stronger sanctions and increased pressure on Russia, as well as further support for Ukraine.
"And today, there was a conversation between the leaders of America and Russia. A conversation that leads to something different," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian president argued that Russia's recent increase in airstrikes against Ukraine was intended to compensate for Moscow's "inability to achieve their objectives on the battlefield."
He accused Moscow of attempting to "strike backroom deals to secure some form of pressure relief for Russia, in order to buy more time and more opportunities for war."
"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said. 
'Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in war'
Zelenskyy reaffirmed Kyiv's readiness to take reciprocal steps toward de-escalation with Moscow.
He said Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and other facilities were a response to Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy," Zelenskyy said.
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis," he added.
Zelenskyy's remarks followed Trump's announcement of what he described as a "highly successful discussion" with Putin.
Trump said on his Truth Social platform that the talks resulted in an agreement for Russia to "immediately supply" more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to US and global markets.
According to Trump, Russia would provide another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter."
He added that another 3 million tons would be delivered "within a short period," depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces strike facilities involved in missile launches and production of fuel for Kh-101 missiles
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces strike facilities involved in missile launches and production of fuel for Kh-101 missiles
Ukrainian forces struck Russian facilities involved in missile launches and the production of rocket fuel on the night of 8-9 October.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Telegram
Quote: "A facility belonging to the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Systems, a branch of the Centre for the Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure Facilities, was struck near the settlement of Dalneye Konstantinovo-5 in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast."
Details: The General Staff noted that the сentre is involved in the development, maintenance and operation of launch facilities, fuelling equipment and control systems for missiles.
The defence forces also struck the Redkino Experimental Plant near the settlement of Redkino in Tver Oblast. The plant is involved in the Russian military-industrial complex's production chains. It manufactures components of Decilin-M fuel for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, as well as additives for diesel fuel and aviation gas. The plant is subject to international sanctions.
"In addition, to weaken the enemy's military-industrial complex's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel, the Centre for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles was struck near the settlement of Surovatikha in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod Oblast," the General Staff added.
It stressed that strikes on such facilities constitute Ukraine's exercise of its inherent right to self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter and are aimed at reducing the military, economic and technological potential of the aggressor state.
Background: The General Staff previously reported that the defence forces struck the Omsk Oil Refinery, located more than 2,500 km from Ukraine's state border, on the afternoon of 8 October. This was the second attack on the facility since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: AFU General Staff: Facilities involved in missile launches, rocket fuel production inside Russia struck last night
articles.body:
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) reported strikes carried out last night against enemy facilities involved in missile launches and rocket fuel production, specifically in Nizhny Novgorod and Tver regions.

Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes—was hit near the settlement of Dalneye Konstantinovo-5 in Nizhny Novgorod region," the General Staff stated on Telegram on Friday.

articles.title: Pentagon prepares 3-day intensive Iran strike option as Trump says no attack before midterms: NYT
articles.body:
Seyit Kurt
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The Pentagon has drawn up plans for an intensive three-day military campaign against Iran, the New York Times reported on Thursday, even as President Donald Trump said Washington will not launch an attack before the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The US military, acting on Trump's orders, has developed options to strike Iran's missile and drone arsenal, energy facilities and other military sites, The Times reported, citing US officials.
Senior national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed the plans at Camp David last Friday, with the options centering on a short, intensive campaign lasting about three days, according to people briefed on the proposal.
The strikes would focus on Iran's missile and drone arsenal, much of which has been rebuilt by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) since the early phase of the war, the newspaper said.
Other potential targets include Iranian energy facilities as well as IRGC command posts and headquarters.
Axios separately reported that the Pentagon ordered the US Central Command (CENTCOM) several days ago to complete preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations against Iran.
The directive did not set a date for strikes and Trump had not made a final decision, Axios said, adding that any renewed major combat operations were expected to include large-scale bombing of Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear targets.
The military preparations come as Trump said on Thursday that the US would not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while pointing to ongoing diplomatic efforts.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said Washington and Tehran were having "productive discussions."
The NYT also reported that Trump has repeatedly declined proposals in recent months to resume major combat operations against Iran, despite ordering the Pentagon to prepare new options.
Three US aircraft carriers are expected to be in the Middle East in the coming weeks as part of the major military buildup, according to the newspaper.

articles.title: Montenegro to deport Russian pro-Kremlin war blogger and founder of Rybar propaganda project Mikhail Zvinchuk
articles.body:
Montenegrin authorities are set to deport Mikhail Zvinchuk, founder of the Russian pro-war propaganda project Rybar. Zvinchuk’s wife, Valeria, and three of the project’s employees, are also on the deportation list, local outlet Vijesti reported, citing Montenegro’s Police Directorate. Bosnian investigative journalists found that Zvinchuk entered Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina after flying there from Germany.
News of the detention of Zvinchuk, his wife, and other Rybar staff emerged earlier in the day on Oct. 9. Vijesti identified the other detainees as Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko. All five individuals have now been ordered to leave Montenegro, with law enforcement authorities saying the decision was made on the basis of national and internal security grounds.
According to Montenegrin police, Zvinchuk, his wife, and Rybar employees entered the country two days earlier. They stayed in the town of Risan on the Bay of Kotor, where they were ultimately detained. Officers seized cameras, a GoPro, a filming drone, and mobile phones from the group.
Bosnian investigative outlet Detektor found that Zvinchuk and his team entered Montenegro from Bosnia and Herzegovina. They arrived in Sarajevo on Oct. 2 on a flight from Germany. While Zvinchuk, his wife, and Rybar employees were in the country, elections were taking place in Bosnia. Bosnia’s Security Ministry has not yet commented on the information.
On Oct. 6, Rybar published a video roundup for the Solovyov Live program that was filmed in Bosnia. The following day, Oct. 7, the Rybar team entered Montenegro by land.
Zvinchuk later boasted that he had entered Montenegro despite the sanctions and travel ban levied against him. In a post on social media, Zvinchuk said Montenegro was the 26th country he had visited and described how he entered the country:
“Remember: even if you are under sanctions, like me, even if you have a travel ban, like me, even if you are traveling to a country that has pledged, out of solidarity, to enforce that travel ban, as in my case ... THERE IS A WAY!”
Zvinchuk added that travelers like him could always run into “an idiot border guard who turns out all your pockets but forgets to check the database.”
On Oct. 8, prior to his arrest, Zvinchuk again appeared on the Russian propaganda channel Solovyov Live, where he claimed that “Montenegro is in tears because visas are being introduced for Russian tourists.”
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X earlier today:
“The message following today's successful action in which the head of the information network ‘Rybar’ was apprehended is clear: out institutions are doing their job, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future.”
Rybar founder Mikhail Zvinchuk, a former employee of the Russian Defense Ministry’s press service, is under EU and UK sanctions. The EU’s sanctions justification says he is part of a working group created by Vladimir Putin to coordinate Russia’s mobilization efforts in support of the ongoing war against Ukraine. Rybar’s main Telegram channel has more than 1.5 million subscribers.
In 2024, the United States offered a reward of up to $10 million for information about people working on the project, which it said used social media to "sow discord, promote social division, stoke partisan and racial discord, and encourage hate and violence in the United States.” The U.S. State Department also listed Zvinchuk as being involved in attempts to influence the U.S. electoral process.
In February 2026, OpenAI blocked a network of accounts linked to Rybar. The project’s team had used ChatGPT as a content farm to generate social media and blog posts in Russian, English, and Spanish.
In September, Czech police detained and questioned Russian nationals Vitaly Chashchukhin and Igor Dolmatov, whom journalists from local outlet Seznam Zprávy had earlier lured to a meeting in Prague and secretly recorded discussing their work for the Rybar project. After questioning, both were ordered to leave the Czech Republic within three days as undesirable persons.
Chashchukhin and Dolmatov are known to live in Germany, where Chashchukhin performs work for sanctioned Russian media outlets Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV. In his reports, he portrays Germany as a country in economic decline, claiming its only hope for prosperity requires a halt to arms supplies for Ukraine and a return to the purchase of cheap energy from Russia.
Zvinchuk’s detention drew reactions from Russian government officials including Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov and ex-president Dmitry Medvedev, and also from media outlets, bloggers, and pro-war channels. Ivan Filippov, a propaganda researcher and author of the Telegram channel “All Quiet on the Zzzzzestern Front,” told the independent outlet Vot Tak that many commentators — regardless of their views — were asking why a sanctioned Russian propagandist who was aware of the risks had traveled to a NATO country that is seeking EU membership:
“Some people are expressing sympathy, but looking at the reactions now, the dominant question is why he went there in the first place. The pro-war “Z”-community is genuinely stunned. [Head of RT] Margarita Simonyan believed he would be extradited to Ukraine,” Filippov said.
Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 and is seeking to join the EU after adopting the euro in 2002 and applying for membership in the bloc in 2008. It imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The government recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens starting from Nov. 1, as Montenegro aligns its visa policy with the European Union ahead of a possible accession by 2028. Local media reported this spring that around 14,000 of the 21,000 Russians registered in Montenegro had left after the government announced plans to introduce visa requirements.
“Montenegro’s accession as the 28th member state by 2028 is within reach,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said at an EU-Western Balkans summit in June.

articles.title: Head of Russian military propaganda network to be expelled from Montenegro over suspected anti-EU operation
articles.body:
Montenegro has ordered the expulsion of Mikhail Zvynchuk, head of the pro-Kremlin military information network Rybar, and four other Russian citizens over national security concerns following a security operation targeting suspected Russian hybrid influence activities, Vijesti reported on 9 October.
Zvynchuk is the founder and head of Rybar, a prominent Russian military-focused information network known for its Telegram channels covering Russia's war against Ukraine. The network promotes pro-Kremlin narratives and has been associated with Russian propaganda and influence operations.
Montenegrin police announced on 9 October that the five Russians had their residence rights revoked and were ordered to leave the country on national and internal security grounds.
Montenegro investigates suspected Russian hybrid activity
The operation involved Montenegro's police and National Security Agency (ANB), which seized drones, high-resolution recording equipment, cameras, and several mobile phones for further examination, according to Vijesti.
According to Montenegrin authorities, the five had arrived in the country less than two days before the operation. The investigation is being conducted with support from international partners.
Montenegrin police identified the five Russian citizens as Zvynchuk, his wife Valeria Zvynchuk, Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko. Authorities said the case had been referred to prosecutors in Podgorica and Kotor.
The European Union has sanctioned Zvynchuk over activities that undermine or threaten Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence. He has also been sanctioned by the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Australia, and Ukraine, according to Vijesti.
Suspected influence operation targeting EU integration
Vijesti reported, citing security sources, that Montenegrin authorities suspected the group of planning a documentary intended to undermine public support for the country's European integration.
According to the outlet, the planned material would portray Montenegro's expected alignment of its visa policy with EU standards as a politically imposed measure that threatens tourism, economic stability, and national interests.
Security services had monitored the group's arrival before carrying out the operation in Risan, in the Bay of Kotor area, Vijesti reported. The equipment seized from the group will undergo expert analysis to establish its intended purpose and use in Montenegro.
Medvedev threatens imprisoning “European and American idiots” for prisoner exchanges
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev responded to the operation by suggesting Moscow might need to expand its pool of prisoners to exchange for Europeans and Americans to secure Zvynchuk's return.
“We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots,” Medvedev said, according to Vijesti.
Montenegro, a NATO member and EU candidate, has aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The expulsion comes amid broader European concerns over Russian intelligence activity, propaganda, and other forms of hybrid interference.

Russian Strikes Near Poland Trigger Military Aviation Deployment and Air Defense Alert
Poland activated military aviation and placed air defense and radar systems on alert on October 9 as Russia struck targets in western Ukraine.
Poland’s Operational Command of the Armed Forces announced the measures on the same day in a post on X, noting that military aircraft were operating in Polish airspace.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Ground-based air defense systems and radar reconnaissance assets have reached a state of readiness," the command stated.
The measures were described as preventive and intended to secure Polish airspace, particularly in areas bordering parts of Ukraine affected by the Russian strikes. The command added that its forces remained ready to respond while monitoring the situation.
Poland has repeatedly taken similar precautionary measures during Russian aerial attacks on western Ukraine, deploying military aircraft and increasing the readiness of air defense and radar systems near the Ukrainian border.
Earlier, on September 21, Poland scrambled military aviation and brought its ground-based air defenses to readiness during Russian strikes on Ukraine, standing down later that night with no airspace violation recorded.
Polish fighter jets had also taken off overnight on September 15 as Russia struck western Ukraine with jet-powered drones. Two days later, Russian drone strikes in Ukraine's Volyn region, where one drone came down roughly four kilometers from the Polish border, prompted Poland to deploy aircraft and briefly suspend operations at the Lublin and Rzeszów airports.
