articles.title: Australia asks U.S. for $300M Tomahawk planning system
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $300 million sale of Tomahawk mission planning systems and support to Australia.
- Australia first fired a Tomahawk from HMAS Brisbane in December 2024 and plans to field the missile on destroyers, frigates and future submarines.
The U.S. State Department has approved a possible $300 million sale to Australia of the systems and support it needs to plan Tomahawk cruise missile strikes, adding mission-planning capability to the long-range missiles the Royal Australian Navy began acquiring in 2023.
The package covers a Theater Mission Planning Center with its associated communications systems, the Tomahawk Mission Planning System, and program management, engineering, training and logistics support for developing and delivering the planning system, according to the Oct. 8 notification to Congress. The approval does not mean the sale is final; the quantities, contract terms and timeline will be set if Australia moves ahead.
A Tomahawk does not simply fly in a straight line to its target. Before launch, planners build a route for the missile, with waypoints over land and sea, terrain and navigation data, and the aim point it is meant to hit. The Theater Mission Planning Center is the system the United States uses to prepare and distribute that data to launching ships and submarines, and the State Department said the sale would strengthen Australia’s Tomahawk capability and deepen its interoperability with U.S. maritime forces.
The principal contractors would be BAE Systems in San Diego, California; Tapestry Solutions, a Boeing subsidiary in St. Louis, Missouri; Peraton in San Jose, California; and Leidos in Virginia Beach, Virginia. The State Department said the sale would not require sending additional U.S. government or contractor personnel to Australia and would not affect U.S. readiness.
Australia announced in 2023 that it would buy Tomahawks for its Hobart-class destroyers and later its Hunter-class frigates, with more than 200 missiles planned. The missiles are also intended for the Virginia-class nuclear-powered attack submarines Australia is set to receive under the AUKUS agreement in the early 2030s. Canberra says the Tomahawk has a range of up to 2,500 km (about 1,550 miles), making it the longest-reaching strike weapon in the Australian Defence Force.
In December 2024, the destroyer HMAS Brisbane fired a Tomahawk for the first time during a test off San Diego, making Australia the third country, after the United States and the United Kingdom, to acquire and fire the missile. That firing followed Australian Navy tests earlier that year of the Naval Strike Missile and Standard Missile-6 from another Hobart-class destroyer, HMAS Sydney.

articles.title: China denies report of reciprocal nuclear site visits with US
articles.body:
Faisal Mahmud
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
China on Friday denied a report that Beijing and Washington had discussed reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities, with further talks reportedly planned in the coming months.
"The relevant report is not true," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular news conference in Beijing, according to an official transcript of the briefing.
The denial came after CNN reported, citing sources familiar with the matter, that China and the US had discussed possible reciprocal visits to nuclear sites.
According to an earlier CNN report, preliminary discussions covered possible visits to US Department of Energy laboratories and corresponding Chinese research centers, alongside potential access to nuclear test sites.
The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), in its June report, estimated that China possessed 620 nuclear warheads as of January 2026, compared with more than 5,000 held by the US, including retired warheads.
According to SIPRI, the world's nine nuclear-armed nations possessed an estimated 12,187 warheads, including 190 held by India, 170 by Pakistan, 90 by Israel and 60 by North Korea. Russia and the US together accounted for nearly 86% of the global inventory.
SIPRI said China was expanding its nuclear arsenal faster than any other country, while Washington and Moscow continued extensive nuclear modernization programs.
The developments follow the expiration of the New START nuclear arms reduction treaty between Washington and Moscow in February.

articles.title: Zelensky slams Trump’s ‘weak decision’
articles.body:
Zelensky slams Trump’s ‘weak decision’
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has lashed out at US President Donald Trump over his decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, accusing Washington of striking a deal with Moscow behind Kiev’s back.
Zelensky described the move as “definitely unfair,” “definitely not partner-like” and “a weak decision by strong partners,” effectively portraying it as a stab in the back just as Ukrainian negotiators and Kiev’s European backers were meeting American officials to discuss a potential peace settlement in Miami.
In a voice memo sent to Western journalists on Friday, Zelensky suggested Trump had used Ukrainian negotiators as a “smokescreen” while pursuing a separate agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible,” he told Axios in a separate phone interview, referring to the Russian leader’s 74th birthday earlier this week.
Q: Zelenskyy said you're weak because of the Putin deal. He just criticized you TRUMP: Who said that? Q: Zelenskyy. He said you're weak TRUMP: Okay. *walks away* https://t.co/niHd2ynoVP
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 9, 2026
Trump initially ignored journalists’ questions about Zelensky calling him “weak” but later brushed aside the criticism, defending the agreement as necessary to ease soaring fuel prices.
Reporter: President Zelensky said that this is a weak move by a strong partner that will only prolong the war. Trump: We need oil for the world and this is diesel, which is what we need. So we're very happy to get it. https://t.co/8clgGPbJvv
— Faytuks Network (@FaytuksNetwork) October 9, 2026
“We need oil for the world and this is diesel, which is what we need. So we’re very happy to get it,” the US president said.
Earlier on Friday, Trump announced that following a “successful discussion” with Putin, Moscow had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another million tons shortly thereafter, and potentially 3 million additional tons depending on refinery capacity.
The US Treasury subsequently issued a six-month sanctions waiver allowing Russian diesel exports, as Washington seeks to contain a global fuel shortage exacerbated by the US-Israeli war on Iran and Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Trump has repeatedly blamed Kiev – and Zelensky personally – for worsening the global fuel crisis, accusing Ukraine of deliberately knocking out Russian refining capacity and driving up prices for American consumers.
During a visit to Ireland last month, Trump directly demanded that Zelensky halt the strikes. “Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia… Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world,” he said.
Trump doubled down earlier this week, arguing that the main driver of soaring US fuel prices was no longer the disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, but Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has similarly linked the strikes to a broader global “energy shock.”
Despite Washington’s repeated warnings, Zelensky pledged last weekend to intensify Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian oil facilities. A senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times on Friday that Kiev would ignore Washington’s deal with Moscow and “will burn their refineries.”
Frustrstion and anger in Kyiv tonight over Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Zelenskyy blasts Trump, calling the move "weak." A senior Ukrainian official tells me Kyiv will continue its long-range drone strikes on Russia's energy facilities "We will burn their refineries."
— Christopher Miller (@ChristopherJM) October 9, 2026
The fuel shortage has become an increasingly pressing domestic issue for Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. US diesel prices surged to record highs above $6.50 per gallon in September, with prices in California exceeding $8 in some areas.
Putin confirmed following Friday’s conversation that Russia was prepared to supply oil and petroleum products to American and global markets, expressing confidence that the move would have a positive effect on the world economy.

Trump says he’s reached a deal with Putin to supply Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets. Zelensky calls it ‘an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.’
U.S. President Donald Trump said he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets. Trump said they reached the agreement during “highly successful” talks by phone.
Russia agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets as soon as possible, Trump said. It will supply another 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons “immediately thereafter.”
“Based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries,” Moscow could also supply another 3 million metric tons of diesel “within a short period of time,” Trump said.
Trump’s announcement came as the U.S. Treasury Department issued a temporary license allowing Russian diesel fuel to be supplied to the global market until April 7, 2027.
“Thanks to our total control of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” Trump said.

Exports of Russian oil and petroleum products to countries around the world are restricted by sanctions and Russia’s own export bans. For example, a ban on producers exporting diesel fuel, marine fuel, and gas oil remains in effect until the end of October.

articles.title: Record 20 Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on headquarters in Donetsk, monitors say
articles.body:
Record 20 Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on headquarters in Donetsk, monitors say
Ukrainian missile strikes on Russian army command posts in Donetsk on Aug. 26 killed more Russian officers than in any other single attack during the war, independent monitors claim.
Mediazona, an independent Russian outlet that tracks Russian military deaths in collaboration with the BBC Russian Service, identified 20 officers killed in the attack.
Each of the dead Russian officers was identified by name, age, and rank by Mediazona. Seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain, and one senior lieutenant were killed in the strikes, which hit the headquarters of the Central Military District and the 41st Combined Arms Army in occupied Donetsk.
According to Mediazona, 18 of the Russian officers died immediately in the missile strike, while two succumbed to their injuries.
Denis Pushilin, the head of the Russian illegal occupation administration in Donetsk Oblast, confirmed in a post on Telegram that Ukraine had launched an attack on targets in Donetsk on Aug. 26, claiming that Anglo-French "Storm Shadow" air-launched cruise missiles were used, and that eight civilians were injured.
Mediazona also identified two other instances of "mass casualties" amongst staff officers of the 41st Combined Arms Army, according to their research, eight officers were killed on Aug. 4, with an additional four killed on Sept 8, 2025.
At least 276,113 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine since 2022, according to Mediazona, which tracks individuals killed by searching through obituaries, posts on Russian social media networks, and leaked Russian databases.

articles.title: Iran's IRGC strikes tanker and threatens to target vessels beyond Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned that vessels “violating” its designated routes would be pursued and "punished" anywhere in the region, as maritime agencies reported two further strikes on commercial ships in the Persian Gulf.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed responsibility on Friday for setting an oil tanker ablaze in the Strait of Hormuz and threatened to pursue vessels it deems in violation beyond the strait and across the wider region, as maritime security agencies reported two further strikes on commercial ships in the Persian Gulf.
The IRGC Navy said it targeted the engine room and propulsion system of the MV Sun Shine, a tanker belonging to the company Natwit, after the vessel attempted to use what it described as an unauthorised route through the strait's southern section. The attack caused a fire on board.
In a statement, the IRGC warned that action against "violating" vessels would no longer be confined to the Strait of Hormuz and that any ship using what it deems unauthorised routes would be pursued and "punished" anywhere in the region.
Companies it accuses of co-operating with the US would be sanctioned and all their vessels targeted, it added.
The IRGC laid blame for the incidents in the strait on the US military, accusing Washington of interfering in the decisions of shipping and insurance companies and paying "large bribes" to induce compliance.
"Direct responsibility for these incidents and the escalation of tensions in maritime transport in the region lies with the aggressive US army," the statement said.
Tehran's Friday prayer leader separately told his weekly sermon that the strait would remain closed until Iran's conditions were fully met.
Hojjatoleslam Mohammad Javad Ali-Akbari said Iran had set out "seven conditions" and would decide its next steps once they were met, adding that military readiness had improved, weak points had been addressed, and Iran's strategy had shifted from defence to offence.
Iran has said it controls the Strait of Hormuz and will not permit military forces from hostile countries in the area, vowing to respond "decisively" to any attempt to disrupt its management of the strait.
Lanes clear, CENTCOM says
US Central Command said on Friday it had cleared the strait's main shipping lanes, removed naval mines from principal transit routes, and declared them open to all vessels not in violation of US maritime sanctions against Iran.
Thousands of commercial ships had passed through safely as a result, CENTCOM said.
The competing claims came as the UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported that an LPG carrier was struck by unknown projectiles on Friday morning, 13 nautical miles west of Al-Jazira in the United Arab Emirates, causing a major fire that was later brought under control.
UKMTO had reported the previous day that an oil tanker north of Qatari waters was struck by several projectiles resulting in casualties, in the first such attack in six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, the maritime intelligence company Vanguard reported that a tanker had caught fire roughly 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, identifying the vessel as probably the Dalkut, sailing under the Marshall Islands flag.
At least 12 attacks, attempted attacks or harassment incidents targeting oil tankers and gas carriers were recorded in the strait between 28 September and 5 October, the highest weekly figure since the war began on 28 February, according to media reports.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments normally pass, has been effectively closed since the outbreak of the war, following Iranian missile and drone strikes on commercial vessels and a US Navy blockade of Iranian ports.
The latest data indicate that oil exports from other countries in the region, excluding Iran, have returned to pre-war levels in recent days.

articles.title: Ukraine far from producing Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles on its own — UK defense official
articles.body:
PARIS, October 9. /TASS/. Ukraine is still a long way from independently producing Western Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles due to the complexity of these weapons systems, UK Under-Secretary of State for the Armed Forces Louise Sandher-Jones told Le Figaro.
"I think we are still a long way from that due to the complexity of these weapons systems. We have already begun moving in this direction, but we are also considering other projects that could be implemented in the short term, including in the area of striking targets at operational depth," she said.
According to the defense official, Kiev’s needs are not limited to Storm Shadow and SCALP missiles. She noted that the UK military is working with Ukraine on the Brakestop project, which involves developing a low-cost, long-range cruise missile. Sandher-Jones noted that its development is focused on reducing production costs and ensuring the weapons can be manufactured in sufficient quantities.
In September, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that his government had agreed to allow the MBDA defense company to transfer classified data on UK components for the SCALP long-range missile to Kiev. At that time, he also discussed the matter with French President Emmanuel Macron, who had announced back in July that an agreement had been reached with Kiev on the licensed production of various weapons, including AASM guided bombs, Aster 30 missiles for the SAMP-T air defense system, and SCALP missiles.
The SCALP (the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow missile) is an air-launched cruise missile equipped with a subsonic turbojet engine, an infrared homing system, and an onboard processor with GPS. It can fly at extremely low altitudes (30-40 meters).

articles.title: Drone attack on Erbil renews Kurdish fears over Iran War fallout
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Drone attack on Erbil camp renews Kurdish fears over Iran War fallout
Two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil on Thursday night, raising fresh concerns about security in Iraq's Kurdistan Region following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces and their air defence systems.
The Kurdistan Region's Counter-Terrorism Service said the attack took place at 22:19 local time in the Kawergosk area of Khabat district, west of Erbil, the regional capital. No casualties were reported.
Local reports said the drones caused material damage near the site, although other accounts suggested they had crashed in an uninhabited area. The extent of the damage remains unclear, and no group has claimed responsibility.
The attack follows more than a month of relative calm in Erbil and has renewed concerns over the region's vulnerability to drone strikes, particularly after US-led coalition forces withdrew their air defence systems at the end of September.
Kurdish officials have repeatedly called for stronger air defences and greater coordination with the federal government in Baghdad, which holds primary responsibility for protecting Iraqi airspace.
A captain in the Kurdish Peshmerga forces told The New Arab that the latest attack highlighted the urgent need for air defence systems capable of intercepting drones, a role previously carried out by the international coalition.
"The renewed attacks make it necessary to accelerate the provision of air defence systems capable of dealing with drones," the officer said, speaking on condition of anonymity. He added that surveillance and interception measures alone could not provide sufficient protection without dedicated defensive capabilities.
The officer suggested the attack could be linked to Iran, citing the nature of targets struck in previous incidents. However, there has been no official confirmation of responsibility for Thursday's attack.
The Kurdistan Region has faced repeated drone and missile attacks in recent months amid escalating tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and associated refugee camps have been among the targets.
Earlier attacks have also affected areas of Erbil and Sulaimaniyah provinces, with Kurdish security authorities reporting the interception of drones targeting civilian and military sites. Some strikes blamed on Iran have killed members of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in northern Iraq.
The latest incident comes shortly after the US-led coalition completed its military withdrawal from Iraq under an agreement reached between Baghdad and Washington in 2024.
Coalition forces previously operated air defence systems in the Kurdistan Region that intercepted incoming drones and missiles. Kurdish political and military leaders had warned before the withdrawal that removing those systems without providing replacements would leave the region exposed to further attacks.
The Kurdistan Regional Government has argued that its airspace forms part of Iraq's national airspace and that the federal government must take responsibility for its protection.
Ali al-Harki, a member of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), told The New Arab that the renewed attacks threatened civilians and placed further pressure on the region's security arrangements.
"There is an urgent need for Baghdad to assert its authority over Iraqi airspace and take security measures to prevent further attacks," he said.
"Kurdistan's security is part of Iraq's security, and the Baghdad government cannot distance itself from the responsibility it must assume for protecting the country's airspace."
The attack has also raised concerns about the safety of refugee families living in camps across the region, particularly those associated with Iranian Kurdish opposition groups that have previously been targeted.
Those concerns have grown following the departure of US forces and their defensive equipment from Erbil, which has left regional authorities seeking alternative arrangements to protect civilian areas and critical infrastructure.
With the perpetrators of Thursday's attack still unidentified, Kurdish officials are pressing Baghdad to strengthen air defence capabilities and improve coordination between the Iraqi military and the Peshmerga to prevent further strikes.

articles.title: Ukrainian journalists say Austria detained them “like terrorists”: prosecutor says suspicion unsubstantiated
articles.body:
Austrian police detained Ukrainian investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko in Vienna yesterday, on 8 October. Both were later released, but the circumstances of their detention remain unclear, and the prosecutor’s office said suspicion against them had not been substantiated so far.
The detention lasted more than 12 hours, the first time Tkach had been held that long while on a reporting assignment abroad. The case unfolded alongside a separate Austrian espionage investigation involving two men suspected of working for Ukraine’s military intelligence. Authorities have not said whether the cases are connected.
Tkach describes detention
In a video published by Ukrainska Pravda, Tkach said seven people wearing masks and carrying weapons approached their car at a traffic light about 3–5 kilometers from central Vienna, broke its windows, and pointed weapons at them.
He said the people did not identify themselves or explain their actions. The journalists were pulled from the car, forced face down onto the road, searched, and had their hands taped behind their backs, according to Tkach. He said he initially thought they were being kidnapped because he did not see identification or have time to notice police markings. He realized they were police only after seeing police vehicles.
“As I felt it, they detained us like terrorists,” Tkach said.
He added that people shouted and pointed weapons, and there was no communication. He said one person put a knee on his neck and shouted at him to be quiet. He also saw glass from the broken window fly into Bondarenko’s face.
In a second report, Ukrainska Pravda said Tkach’s account of a document presented to him listed three allegations: espionage in the interests of Ukrainian military intelligence, participation in a criminal organization, and, as far as he remembered, causing harm to Austria. He said investigators did not explain the evidence behind the allegations.
Vienna prosecutor’s office spokesperson Nina Bussek told the Austrian Press Agency (APA) that suspicion against the two journalists had arisen during other investigations but had not been substantiated. She said it currently appeared that the suspicion was not holding up. Austrian officials have not publicly addressed Tkach’s account of the force used.
Diplomatic response and calls for an investigation
Tkach and Bondarenko were in Vienna on an assignment to find Ruslan Kravchenko, Ukraine’s former prosecutor general, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Kravchenko was dismissed on 15 September amid an investigation by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office into alleged protection of fraudulent call centers. He denied involvement. Der Standard reported that it remained unclear whether the journalists’ detention was connected to their reporting on him.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed Tkach’s release and said the Ukrainian consul had requested access to him, according to NV. Musaieva said Bondarenko had been injured and hospitalized.
A statement signed by Ukrainian media and civil society organizations, including Euromaidan Press, called for an immediate, transparent, and independent investigation of law enforcement’s actions. The signatories also demanded an independent review of the force used, the return of seized equipment, and necessary medical and legal assistance.
Separate espionage investigation
Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner confirmed the arrests of four Ukrainians, according to ORF. The two men detained on 5 October were placed in pretrial detention until 21 October on suspicion of secret intelligence activity against Austria. APA reported that they were suspected employees of Ukraine’s military intelligence service. Both deny the allegations.
